modules.title: Starting as an engineer
modules.prerequisites: None. Basic reading, arithmetic and the ability to save a file.
modules.project: Create a learning repository with a working motion program, an environment record, a prediction table and a one-page explanation of the input-to-display path.

lessons.title: What a program actually does
lessons.outcome: Explain state, instructions, input and output using a tiny game.
lessons.teach:
A program is a set of instructions that transforms information. Its state is the information that must persist: a player position, a health value, or a list of enemies. An input is a new observation or command. An output might be a picture, sound, file or network message. A game repeatedly reads inputs, changes state and produces outputs. The picture is a representation of the state, not the state itself.
A processor executes machine instructions; an operating system manages resources and access to devices. A game engine is software that organizes recurring tasks such as rendering and asset loading. A graphics processor is hardware that executes suitable workloads. Keep these layers distinct: changing a game rule is not the same activity as designing a processor.
lessons.example: For a player at x = 2, the command move-right by 3 units produces x = 5. Drawing the character twice must not move it twice. Rendering observes state; the simulation changes it.
lessons.lab: On paper, trace five commands: right 3, left 1, right 0, left 4, right 2, starting at x = 2. Draw boxes for input, simulation state and output. Save the trace. Pass: every state transition is explainable without running code.
lessons.reading: R03: introductory functions/variables lecture; R15: Basics of Information.

quiz.question: What is the difference between state and a displayed image?
quiz.answer: State is the underlying information; the image is one view of that information.

quiz.question: What final position results from the five lab commands?
Why should drawing a character not update its position?
quiz.answer: Rendering may occur at a different rate or multiple times; movement must follow simulation rules, not draw count.

lessons.title: Files, terminals and reproducible execution
lessons.outcome: Run a saved Python program and distinguish a shell from an interpreter.
lessons.teach:
A source file stores the instructions you write. A terminal presents a command-line interface; its shell starts programs and manages paths. The Python interpreter is a program that runs Python instructions. A shell prompt is not a Python prompt. Commands such as cd belong in the shell; expressions such as print(2 + 3) belong in Python code.
A working directory tells a process where relative paths begin. Many apparent programming errors are actually wrong-directory or wrong-file errors. Reproducibility starts by recording the exact command, file and tool version. Use a dedicated course folder. Do not run copied administrative commands or upload private files merely to make a tutorial work.
lessons.example: With day01_motion.py in the current folder, python3 day01_motion.py runs that file on many macOS/Linux setups. On Windows, py -3 day01_motion.py is a common launcher form. First confirm the available command with its --version option.
lessons.lab: Follow START_HERE. Run the included program twice from the same folder; save the command and output in your journal. Intentionally misspell the filename, read the error, then repair it. Pass: you can explain which program produced the error.
lessons.reading: R04: Using the Python Interpreter; installation links in START_HERE.

quiz.question: What does a relative filename depend on?
quiz.answer: The process working directory, unless the application explicitly resolves it another way.

quiz.question: Is cd a Python statement in an ordinary script?
quiz.answer: No. It is normally a shell command; Python has separate filesystem APIs.

quiz.question: What three facts help another person reproduce a run?
quiz.answer: The exact source revision/file, tool environment and command; inputs and working directory also matter.

lessons.title: Trace before running
lessons.outcome: Predict a program by following assignments in order.
lessons.teach:
An assignment evaluates the expression on the right and binds the result to the name on the left. In x = x + 1, the right-hand x means the old value. This is not an algebraic equation claiming that x equals x plus one forever. The order of instructions matters because later instructions can read changed state.
A trace table records values after each instruction. It is a small, executable model of your reasoning. Predict first, run second, and explain any difference. Copying code until it works trains recognition rather than independent reasoning. For an unfamiliar program, choose one tiny input and work through it before testing a large case.
lessons.example: Let x = 4; y = x + 2; x = 10. The final values are x = 10 and y = 6. The earlier calculation does not automatically rerun when x changes.
lessons.lab: Create three assignment sequences with at least four statements each. Predict their outputs, then check with Python. Include one swap attempt that fails because it overwrites a needed value. Pass: fix the swap and explain the lost information.
lessons.reading: R03: Functions, Variables; R04: An Informal Introduction to Python.

quiz.question: After a = 3; b = a; a = 8, what is b for these integers?
quiz.answer: 3. The earlier integer value was bound to b; changing a does not recompute b.

quiz.question: Why does x = y; y = x fail to swap two different values?
quiz.answer: The first assignment overwrites the old x, so both names end with the old y.

quiz.question: What makes prediction useful when a run disagrees?
quiz.answer: It exposes the specific mistaken assumption, which can then be tested instead of hidden by random edits.

lessons.title: Units, budgets and engineering notebooks
lessons.outcome: Use units and simple arithmetic to check game calculations.
lessons.teach:
A number without a unit can be misleading. Position may be measured in meters or pixels, time in seconds or milliseconds, and speed in units per second. Multiplying speed by elapsed time yields displacement. Adding a time directly to a position has no coherent physical meaning. Naming variables with units makes mistakes visible.
A performance budget is also arithmetic. At a target of f frames per second, the time available per frame is 1000/f milliseconds. This is a planning limit, not a guarantee that the machine will meet it. Record hypotheses, observations and conclusions separately. A measurement describes a particular workload on a particular system, not every possible game.
lessons.example: A speed of 6 units/second for 0.25 seconds gives 1.5 units of travel. At 60 frames/second, the frame interval is about 16.67 milliseconds. A 20 ms frame exceeds that interval.
lessons.lab: Calculate travel at 2, 6 and 10 units/second for 0.1 and 0.5 seconds. Calculate frame intervals for 30, 60 and 120 frames/second. Pass: show units at every step and identify which assumptions are chosen targets.
lessons.reading: R03: Variables and arithmetic; R15: Performance Measures.

quiz.question: How far does 8 units/second travel in 0.125 seconds?
quiz.answer: 1 unit, because 8 multiplied by 0.125 is 1.

quiz.question: What is the interval for 120 frames/second?
quiz.answer: 1000/120 = approximately 8.33 milliseconds.

quiz.question: Why record hardware and workload with a timing result?
quiz.answer: The result depends on the environment and work performed; without them it cannot be meaningfully reproduced or generalized.

modules.title: Values, decisions and repetition
modules.project: Build a terminal-based resource-gathering simulation with bounded health, inventory and a fixed number of turns. Include invalid-input handling and a complete trace for a five-turn run.

lessons.title: Types and expressions
lessons.outcome: Choose integers, real-valued numbers, strings and booleans appropriately.
lessons.teach:
A type determines what operations mean and which values are representable. Integers suit counts; floating-point numbers approximate many real-valued measurements; strings store text; booleans represent true or false. Python performs some conversions automatically, but a text value such as "12" is not the same thing as the integer 12. Input from a text prompt begins as text.
Floating-point arithmetic is finite precision. Some simple decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly in a binary format. Do not begin by adding arbitrary rounding everywhere: first decide whether a quantity is a count, a continuous measurement or an exact monetary amount. Record assumptions about ranges and units before choosing the representation.
lessons.example: "3" + "4" produces the string "34" in Python, while 3 + 4 produces 7. An inventory count of 7.5 swords indicates a modeling problem unless partial items are deliberately supported.
lessons.lab: Write a resource-cost calculator that converts two text inputs to integers and reports total cost. Test zero, a positive count and malformed text. Pass: invalid input produces a useful message rather than an unexplained crash.
lessons.reading: R03: Functions, Variables and Exceptions; R04: Numbers and Text.

quiz.question: Why are "12" and 12 different?
quiz.answer: One is text and one is an integer; their operations and validation rules differ.

quiz.question: What does "ab" + "cd" produce?
quiz.answer: The string "abcd".

quiz.question: Would an exact item count normally use floating point? Why?
quiz.answer: No. An integer directly represents whole counts and avoids fractional or approximation ambiguity.

lessons.title: Conditions and boundary cases
lessons.outcome: Write decisions with complete and non-overlapping rules.
lessons.teach:
A condition selects behavior according to a boolean expression. Comparison operators such as < and >= make boundaries explicit. An if/elif/else chain evaluates conditions in order and takes the first matching branch. Independent if statements may execute more than one branch. These are different designs.
Boundary cases reveal missing rules. For a door that opens at level 5, level 4, level 5 and level 6 are more informative initial tests than three arbitrary large values. Compound conditions use and, or and not. Write parentheses when they improve clarity. Name complex conditions so that the code expresses the game rule rather than making readers reconstruct it.
lessons.example: A purchase is allowed when gold >= price and stock > 0. Having enough gold is insufficient when stock is zero. A zero price still requires a policy for availability.
lessons.lab: Implement a door requiring either a key or both level >= 5 and stamina >= 10. Enumerate all key/no-key cases around the two numeric boundaries. Pass: explain why each case succeeds or fails.
lessons.reading: R03: Conditionals; R04: if Statements.

quiz.question: Does gold > price allow buying an item when gold equals price?
quiz.answer: No. Use >= when exact funds are sufficient.

quiz.question: Evaluate False or (True and False).
quiz.answer: False: the parenthesized conjunction is false, and neither side of or is true.

quiz.question: Why test immediately below, at and above a threshold?
quiz.answer: Those cases expose incorrect inclusive/exclusive comparisons and missing boundary rules.

lessons.title: Loops and invariants
lessons.outcome: Use repetition that terminates and preserves a stated property.
lessons.teach:
A loop repeats a body. A for loop commonly processes a known sequence; a while loop repeats while a condition holds. Every loop needs a reason it will terminate or an explicit design for ongoing operation. A changing progress measure, such as remaining turns, is often the simplest termination argument.
An invariant is a statement that remains true at a chosen point in every iteration. For example, gold never becomes negative if every purchase first checks affordability. Distinguish the number of iterations from the final value of a loop variable. Off-by-one errors often arise from forgetting whether an endpoint is included.
lessons.example: In Python, range(5) supplies 0, 1, 2, 3, 4: five values, not six. To process turn numbers 1 through 5, range(1, 6) makes the intended numbering explicit.
lessons.lab: Simulate ten turns, collecting three units each turn and spending five only when affordable. Print a trace. Pass: exactly ten updates occur and the resource count is never negative. Add a test for zero turns.
lessons.reading: R03: Loops; R04: for Statements and range.

quiz.question: How many values does range(2, 7) produce?
quiz.answer: Five: 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6.

quiz.question: What must change in while remaining > 0 to make progress?
quiz.answer: The body must eventually reduce remaining or otherwise make the condition false, unless it exits explicitly.

quiz.question: Give an invariant for an inventory limited to ten items.
quiz.answer: At the chosen loop boundary, the item count is always between zero and ten inclusive.

lessons.title: Functions and contracts
lessons.outcome: Separate a calculation from interaction and state its valid inputs.
lessons.teach:
A function packages an operation behind a name and parameters. Returning a value is different from printing it: the caller can use a returned value in another calculation or test. A contract describes valid inputs, promised outputs and relevant side effects. A pure function depends only on its inputs and does not change outside state. Such functions are usually easier to test.
Break a program into responsibilities rather than arbitrary lengths. A movement calculation should not also prompt for a username, write a save file and change global audio settings. Handling invalid inputs is part of the interface. Decide whether to reject, clamp or represent failure; do not silently choose inconsistent policies.
lessons.example: advance(position, velocity, dt) returns position + velocity * dt. With inputs 2, 8 and 0.25, it returns 4. A negative dt should be deliberately supported or rejected, not accidentally ignored.
lessons.lab: Implement advance with a documented nonnegative finite dt contract. Test stationary motion, negative velocity, zero dt and invalid dt. Pass: the function returns a value and the caller controls printing.
lessons.reading: R03: Functions and Unit Tests; R04: Defining Functions.

quiz.question: What is the result of advance(2, 8, 0.25)?
quiz.answer: 4, because 2 + 8 times 0.25 equals 4.

quiz.question: Why is returning a value more reusable than only printing it?
quiz.answer: Other code can consume and test the result without parsing console output.

quiz.question: What belongs in a function contract besides parameter names?
quiz.answer: Valid ranges/types, units, outputs, side effects and failure behavior.

modules.title: Organizing data and small programs
modules.project: Build a data-driven turn simulator with functions, a list of entities, a validated configuration file and save/load round-trip tests.

lessons.title: Sequences, dictionaries and identity
lessons.outcome: Choose collections according to the operations the program needs.
lessons.teach:
A sequence organizes values by position. A dictionary associates keys with values. Use a list when order and iteration matter; use a dictionary when lookup by a meaningful key is central. The container is part of the model, not merely syntax. An entity name may change, so a stable identifier is often safer than using its displayed name as its permanent identity.
Mutable containers can be shared. Assigning a list to another variable does not automatically create an independent deep copy. Mutating a shared object can therefore surprise callers. Before modifying a collection during iteration, understand whether the iterator remains valid and whether elements will be skipped. Building a new collection is often clearer at this stage.
lessons.example: If a = [1, 2] and b = a, then b.append(3) also changes the list seen through a. By contrast, b = list(a) makes a new outer list, but nested mutable objects can still be shared.
lessons.lab: Store five units with stable IDs, names and health. Look up a unit by ID and create a filtered list of living units. Pass: renaming a unit does not break lookup, and the original collection is unchanged by filtering.
lessons.reading: R04: Data Structures; R03: Loops and dictionaries.

quiz.question: When is a dictionary preferable to a list?
quiz.answer: When the main operation is association or lookup by a stable key rather than by position.

quiz.question: Does b = a copy a Python list?
quiz.answer: No. Both names refer to the same list object.

quiz.question: Why can a shallow copy still share changes?
quiz.answer: Its nested objects can remain the same mutable objects referenced by the original.

lessons.title: Decomposition, modules and interfaces
lessons.outcome: Divide a small game into parts that can be tested independently.
lessons.teach:
A module groups related definitions. An interface is the set of operations other code is expected to use. Good boundaries hide unnecessary details while exposing the information a caller needs. Start with a small separation: simulation logic, input handling and presentation. This is enough to prevent many tangles without inventing a large framework.
Dependencies should be intentional. Simulation can accept commands as data rather than directly reading a keyboard. Then the same simulation can run from recorded input, a test or a future network client. Avoid circular dependencies: if every module imports every other module, a local change can become a system-wide problem.
lessons.example: A simulate_turn(state, command) function can run in a terminal game, in a unit test and in a replay tool. It should not need to know which window or controller produced command.
lessons.lab: Refactor the resource simulation into simulation.py and a separate command-line entry point. Pass: importing simulation.py does not start a game or prompt the user, and a test can call its logic directly.
lessons.reading: R04: Modules; R03: Libraries and Unit Tests.

quiz.question: What is an interface?
quiz.answer: The supported operations and contracts through which another part of the system interacts with a component.

quiz.question: Why avoid starting a game as a side effect of importing simulation.py?
quiz.answer: Imports should make reusable definitions available; automatic interaction prevents tests and other tools from using them cleanly.

quiz.question: How does command-as-data design help replays?
quiz.answer: Recorded commands can be fed back through the same simulation interface.

lessons.title: Files, serialization and validation
lessons.outcome: Save structured data without assuming every file is trustworthy.
lessons.teach:
Serialization converts an in-memory representation into a storable or transmittable form. Deserialization reconstructs a representation from that form. The file format needs a schema: which fields exist, their types and their valid ranges. A syntactically valid JSON file can still contain impossible health values or missing required fields.
Treat file contents as inputs, even when you normally create the files yourself. Files can be truncated, edited or come from a different program version. Do not use unrestricted evaluation to load a save. A round-trip test checks that saving and loading preserve the intended information, but it must be complemented by malformed-input tests.
lessons.example: A save with {"version": 1, "health": 50} is structurally clearer than an undocumented sequence of numbers. Validation should reject a string health or an unsupported version with an actionable explanation.
lessons.lab: Create JSON save/load functions for a small state. Test a normal round trip, missing field, wrong type, unsupported version and truncated file. Pass: the original working save remains usable after a failed load.
lessons.reading: R04: Input and Output, json documentation linked from the standard library.

quiz.question: Does valid JSON imply a valid game state?
quiz.answer: No. Syntax validity does not establish schema, range or game-rule validity.

quiz.question: What does a round-trip test check?
quiz.answer: That the intended data survives serialization and deserialization without unacceptable change.

quiz.question: Why include a format version?
quiz.answer: It lets the loader detect compatibility requirements and choose migration or a clear rejection.

lessons.title: Classes, composition and state machines
lessons.outcome: Represent behavior without creating an unnecessary inheritance hierarchy.
lessons.teach:
A class can combine state and operations that maintain its rules. Encapsulation means that other code uses an interface rather than directly violating those rules. Composition builds a larger object from smaller capabilities. Inheritance describes an is-a relationship and can support substitution, but it is not a requirement for every game object.
A finite state machine models a system using named states and transitions. A character might be idle, moving or stunned. Writing allowed transitions explicitly prevents contradictory combinations such as being both stunned and actively attacking, unless the design intentionally allows that. The model should follow actual behavior, not a fashionable pattern.
lessons.example: A door has Closed and Open states. An Open command succeeds only when its lock policy permits the Closed-to-Open transition. Repeated Open commands should have a documented harmless or rejected result.
lessons.lab: Implement a three-state character controller with a transition table. Pass: test every allowed transition and at least three forbidden transitions. Explain why composition would help add inventory independently of movement.
lessons.reading: R04: Classes; R03: Object-Oriented Programming.

quiz.question: What does encapsulation protect?
quiz.answer: An object's invariants by controlling how its state can be changed.

quiz.question: Why can independent booleans create contradictory states?
quiz.answer: They allow combinations that may not correspond to any valid behavior unless separately constrained.

quiz.question: When is composition useful?
quiz.answer: When independent capabilities should be combined without forcing them into one rigid inheritance tree.

modules.title: Debugging, testing and collaboration
modules.project: Publish a local tagged release of the terminal simulation with tests, a reproducible bug report, a reviewed change and an evidence-based development journal. A remote public upload is not required.

lessons.title: Debugging as an experiment
lessons.outcome: Find a defect by narrowing evidence rather than making random edits.
lessons.teach:
A bug report distinguishes expected behavior from observed behavior and supplies reproducible steps. A debugger lets you pause, inspect variables and follow control flow. Logging records selected events over time. Neither tool replaces a hypothesis: identify what you believe is wrong, choose an observation that could disprove it, and change one relevant thing.
Reduce failing examples. A ten-line reproduction is easier to reason about than a full game. Check the earliest point at which state becomes incorrect, not only where a crash finally happens. Keep the original failure and its fix in a regression test so that future changes do not silently reintroduce it.
lessons.example: If a unit loses health twice, log command receipt and damage application separately. Two damage events could come from duplicate commands or from one command processed twice; the two hypotheses require different fixes.
lessons.lab: Introduce a double-damage bug into a copy of the simulator. Write expected/actual behavior, reduce the reproduction and use a breakpoint or trace to identify the first incorrect update. Pass: fix it with a regression test.
lessons.reading: R03: Exceptions and Unit Tests; R11: assertions and error-handling guidance.

quiz.question: What information makes a bug report actionable?
quiz.answer: Reproduction steps, inputs/environment, expected behavior, actual behavior and useful evidence.

quiz.question: Why inspect the earliest wrong state?
quiz.answer: The final crash may be a downstream symptom; the first deviation is closer to the cause.

quiz.question: What is a regression test?
quiz.answer: A test that preserves a previously failing case to detect reintroduction of that defect.

lessons.title: Unit, integration and property tests
lessons.outcome: Choose tests that challenge the contract instead of repeating the implementation.
lessons.teach:
A unit test checks a small responsibility. An integration test checks that components work together. A property test checks a rule over many inputs, such as inventory never becoming negative after valid purchases. The expected result should come from the specification, a simpler reference implementation or a mathematical property, not a copy of the same potentially wrong algorithm.
Tests are evidence, not proof of all behavior. Passing tests cannot demonstrate untested requirements. Include empty inputs, boundaries, invalid inputs and representative workloads. Keep tests repeatable by controlling randomness and time. A flaky test teaches people to ignore alarms and should be investigated rather than routinely rerun until it passes.
lessons.example: For clamp(x, 0, 100), examples include -1 -> 0, 50 -> 50 and 101 -> 100. A useful property is that every output lies in [0, 100] and clamping an already clamped value changes nothing.
lessons.lab: Write at least twelve tests across motion, resource spending and save/load. Include one property-style loop over many small inputs. Pass: temporarily insert a known bug and demonstrate that a relevant test fails.
lessons.reading: R03: Unit Tests; R04: unittest standard-library documentation.

quiz.question: How does an integration test differ from a unit test?
quiz.answer: It checks cooperation between components rather than one isolated responsibility.

quiz.question: Why is copying the implementation into the test oracle weak?
quiz.answer: The test can reproduce the same mistake and falsely agree with the implementation.

quiz.question: What does a test suite passing establish?
quiz.answer: The exercised checks passed in that environment; it does not prove every requirement or input is correct.

lessons.title: Git, branches and recoverable changes
lessons.outcome: Use small commits to preserve reasoning and collaborate safely.
lessons.teach:
Git records snapshots of tracked files. The working tree is what you edit; the staging area selects the content for the next commit; a commit stores a snapshot and history relationship. A branch is a movable reference to a line of development, not a complete independent copy of every file.
Small commits with meaningful messages make review and recovery easier. Inspect differences before committing. Exclude generated files, credentials and large unnecessary binaries. A remote repository is useful for collaboration and additional copies, but it is not permission to publish someone else's assets or secrets. Learn revert on a practice repository before using destructive history operations on shared work.
lessons.example: A commit message such as "Reject negative purchase quantities; add boundary tests" explains an intent. "Updates" forces a reviewer to reconstruct it from every changed line.
lessons.lab: Initialize the course repository, make three focused commits and implement one feature on a branch. Merge it and practice reverting an intentionally bad commit in a disposable copy. Pass: identify exactly what changed and why.
lessons.reading: R05: Getting Started, Git Basics and Basic Branching and Merging.

quiz.question: What does the staging area control?
quiz.answer: Which current file changes become part of the next commit.

quiz.question: Why should secrets not be committed even if later deleted?
quiz.answer: Earlier commits may still retain them and copies may already exist.

quiz.question: What makes a useful commit message?
quiz.answer: It identifies the behavior or purpose of the change and, when needed, its reasoning.

lessons.title: Review, documentation and responsible AI help
lessons.outcome: Explain a change and verify assistance without surrendering understanding.
lessons.teach:
A review asks whether a change meets its requirements, preserves contracts and is understandable to the next maintainer. Critique behavior and evidence rather than the person. Documentation should explain setup, decisions and limitations; comments should add intent rather than merely restating each statement.
An AI assistant can explain errors, suggest test cases and compare approaches. Its output is untrusted until checked. Do not submit generated code you cannot explain, and do not expose private data or licensed material without permission. For this course, attempt each quiz unaided, label assisted work and complete a small no-assistance transfer task before marking a skill mastered.
lessons.example: Instead of asking "write the whole engine," ask for three possible causes of a reproducible failure, then test them. Preserve your prediction, the suggestion and the evidence that accepted or rejected it.
lessons.lab: Review a ten-line change using a checklist: requirement, correctness, boundary cases, readability and tests. Write a README that a second person can follow. Pass: explain every changed line and recreate a small related feature without assistance.
lessons.reading: R05: Distributed Git; R11: philosophy and interface guidance; course assessment policy.

quiz.question: What should a review criticize?
quiz.answer: The change, its behavior and evidence, not the author's character.

quiz.question: Why is compiling AI-generated code insufficient validation?
quiz.answer: Compilation checks only some structural rules; logic, security, performance and requirements can still be wrong.

quiz.question: What demonstrates understanding beyond copying a solution?
quiz.answer: Explaining the reasoning, testing edge cases and solving a related new task independently.

modules.title: A complete first game
modules.project: Complete Gate A: a deterministic terminal grid game with movement, obstacles, win/loss states, replay, tests and a clean-start README. Use the detailed project brief in the program handbook.

lessons.title: The update loop and command model
lessons.outcome: Separate simulation ticks from input collection and presentation.
lessons.teach:
A simulation tick is one application of the game's update rules. A frame is one produced image. They need not occur at the same rate. Start with a turn-based loop so each command advances exactly one tick. Store commands as values and let update(state, command) apply the rules.
Do not put important state transitions in rendering or sound playback. This separation allows headless testing, where no window is needed. It also makes failures reproducible: the same initial state and command sequence should produce the same state when the simulation is deterministic. Later lessons will address numerical and scheduling obstacles to cross-platform determinism.
lessons.example: For a grid game, command Right can move from (2, 3) to (3, 3) only when the destination is valid. Render reads the resulting grid but performs no additional move.
lessons.lab: Build a 10-by-10 terminal grid with one player and an exit. Pass: one command causes one update, drawing twice changes nothing, and the update function works without printing.
lessons.reading: R20: runtime systems course overview; R27: fixed-step concepts, read without copying its implementation.

quiz.question: Are a simulation tick and a rendered frame necessarily identical?
quiz.answer: No. Simulation and presentation can run at different rates.

quiz.question: What should happen when render is called twice without an update?
quiz.answer: The simulation state should remain unchanged.

quiz.question: Why is headless simulation useful?
quiz.answer: It enables automated tests, replays and server-style execution without a graphical interface.

lessons.title: Collision rules and complete behavior
lessons.outcome: Specify edge cases before implementing a playable rule.
lessons.teach:
A rule is incomplete when it defines only the happy path. Movement must say what happens at a wall, at the grid boundary, when two commands arrive or after the game is over. A collision system answers questions about overlap or blocked motion, but the game design decides what the answer means.
For this project, use integer grid coordinates and a set of blocked cells. Reject invalid moves without partially changing state. This is a simple transaction: validate, then apply. Separate win/loss detection from input text parsing so a typo does not accidentally consume a game turn unless that is the documented rule.
lessons.example: On a grid with x in 0 through 9, moving right from x = 9 must not yield x = 10. A chosen policy is to keep the old state and report blocked; wrapping is a different valid game rule.
lessons.lab: Add five obstacles, a goal and a terminal win state. Test every edge of the board, blocked movement, reaching the goal and commands after victory. Pass: no partial movement occurs on rejected commands.
lessons.reading: R20: game-programming projects; course transition and testing lessons.

quiz.question: What is missing from "move right increases x"?
quiz.answer: Boundary, obstacle, terminal-state and invalid-command policies, among other possible rules.

quiz.question: Under the reject policy, what happens at x = 9 on a 0-9 grid?
quiz.answer: The right move is rejected and x stays 9.

quiz.question: Why validate before applying a multi-part state change?
quiz.answer: It avoids leaving the system partially updated when one requirement fails.

lessons.title: Deterministic replay and simple measurement
lessons.outcome: Reproduce a run and measure the work actually performed.
lessons.teach:
A replay stores initial conditions and commands in their intended order. If randomness is used, record the seed and the generator policy as well. Determinism means the relevant outputs match for the same defined inputs and environment. It does not follow merely from setting one random seed when other sources of variability remain.
Measure update cost separately from printing; terminal output can dominate a small program. Use a monotonic timing source for elapsed durations. Repeat a representative workload and report the workload size, repetitions and environment. Avoid claiming that a small terminal benchmark predicts the performance of a future three-dimensional game.
lessons.example: A replay of Right, Right, Down from (0, 0) ends at (2, 1) on an unobstructed grid where Down increases y. A blocked cell at (1, 0) changes that result under the rejection policy.
lessons.lab: Save and replay a twenty-command session. Run the same replay repeatedly and compare final states. Time 10,000 headless updates separately from display. Pass: report exact inputs and no invented performance target.
lessons.reading: R27: reproducibility motivation; R04: time and random standard-library references.

quiz.question: What information does a replay need besides button names?
quiz.answer: Initial state, order/tick placement, relevant configuration and controlled randomness/environment assumptions.

quiz.question: Why exclude printing from a simulation microbenchmark?
quiz.answer: Otherwise the measurement may primarily reflect terminal I/O instead of simulation work.

quiz.question: Does one matching replay prove determinism for all inputs?
quiz.answer: No. It is evidence for that case; broader tests and analysis are still required.

lessons.title: Finishing, usability and the first portfolio artifact
lessons.outcome: Deliver a tiny game another person can run and understand.
lessons.teach:
A finished small project teaches integration that disconnected exercises cannot. Define a limited scope and complete it: startup, instructions, gameplay, termination and error messages all matter. Include a way to quit and restart. Avoid relying on color alone to convey important information. Clear controls and readable output are engineering responsibilities even in a terminal game.
A portfolio artifact should include source, tests, run instructions, a short demonstration and a discussion of decisions. Explain what you built yourself and what came from references. Do not inflate a simple project into a claim of production-engine expertise. An honest account of a difficult bug and a measured improvement is more informative than an unsupported adjective.
lessons.example: A useful release note says "Added obstacle rejection and a replay test for the top-right boundary." A useful limitation says "Keyboard commands are turn-based; there is no real-time renderer yet."
lessons.lab: Complete Gate A and ask a tester to start from the README without verbal help. Record three observations and fix at least one usability issue. Pass: the tester can start, play, quit and rerun the tests.
lessons.reading: R29: Input, UI navigation and error-message guidelines; R05: tagging releases.

quiz.question: What belongs in a clean-start README?
quiz.answer: Prerequisites, exact run/test commands, controls, expected behavior and known limitations.

quiz.question: Why should color not be the only important cue?
quiz.answer: Some players cannot reliably distinguish it; a second channel such as text or shape preserves the information.

quiz.question: What evidence should accompany a claimed improvement?
quiz.answer: A reproducible comparison with the same workload and clearly stated measurement conditions.

modules.title: Discrete mathematical reasoning
modules.prerequisites: Volume 01; complete the algebra diagnostic in START_HERE before proceeding.
modules.project: Write a mathematical notebook containing a truth-table specification, an induction proof, a graph model and a justified operation-count estimate. Include counterexamples to three false claims.

lessons.title: Algebra, functions, logarithms and trigonometry
lessons.outcome: Translate a game relationship into an equation with a defined domain.
lessons.teach:
A function maps each allowed input to one output. Its domain matters: dividing by zero or taking a real square root of a negative number is not repaired by notation. Rearranging an equation must preserve its conditions. Exponents model repeated multiplication; logarithms invert exponentiation. log2(n) often counts how many times a size can be halved.
Angles connect geometry to periodic motion. In radians, a full revolution is 2*pi. For a unit circle, a direction at angle t has components (cos(t), sin(t)). Check units before calling a trigonometric function. Degrees and radians are different representations of the same angle, not interchangeable numeric inputs.
lessons.example: At 90 degrees, or pi/2 radians, the unit-circle direction is (0, 1). A list of 1024 items can be halved ten times to reach one because 2^10 = 1024.
lessons.lab: Solve distance = speed*time for each variable and state forbidden inputs. Convert 0, 90, 180 and 360 degrees to radians. Pass: solve ten algebra problems and explain logarithms using repeated halving before advancing.
lessons.reading: R08: prerequisite algebra review and trigonometric functions; R06: sums and asymptotics.

quiz.question: What is log2(64)?
quiz.answer: 6, because 2^6 = 64.

quiz.question: Convert 180 degrees to radians.
quiz.answer: pi radians.

quiz.question: What restriction applies when computing speed = distance/time?
quiz.answer: Time cannot be zero; also state the physical units and whether negative time is meaningful.

lessons.title: Logic, sets and quantified claims
lessons.outcome: Express requirements precisely enough to test or prove.
lessons.teach:
Propositional logic combines true/false statements. Implication P -> Q fails only when P is true and Q is false. It does not claim that P actually happens. A universal claim says a property holds for every allowed input; an existential claim says at least one input has it. Negating a universal claim requires one counterexample.
Sets group distinct elements; relations describe connections; functions are relations with exactly one output for each domain element. These ideas support requirements such as every live entity has one valid transform. Ambiguous language like "usually valid" cannot serve as an invariant until its exceptions are specified.
lessons.example: "Every saved entity has an ID" is disproved by one saved entity without an ID. "Some entity is visible" requires only one witness and does not imply all entities are visible.
lessons.lab: Formalize five requirements for the grid game using sets and quantifiers. Construct truth tables for a door-access rule. Pass: provide a counterexample or witness for each negated requirement.
lessons.reading: R06: propositions, predicates, sets and relations.

quiz.question: When is P -> Q false?
quiz.answer: When P is true and Q is false.

quiz.question: Negate "every unit has positive health."
quiz.answer: There exists a unit whose health is not positive.

quiz.question: Why must the domain of a quantified statement be explicit?
quiz.answer: The claim can change meaning or truth when it ranges over different objects or inputs.

lessons.title: Proofs, induction and invariants
lessons.outcome: Justify a program property instead of testing only examples.
lessons.teach:
A proof is a chain of justified steps from assumptions to a conclusion. Direct proof, contradiction and induction solve different kinds of questions. Induction establishes a base case and shows that validity at one step implies validity at the next. Both parts are necessary.
A loop invariant connects mathematical reasoning to implementation: establish it before the loop, preserve it in each iteration, and combine it with the exit condition to prove the result. Testing complements proofs by checking whether code matches the modeled assumptions. A proof of an ideal algorithm does not automatically establish the correctness of its floating-point implementation.
lessons.example: To prove the running sum after k iterations equals 1+...+k, start at k=0 with sum=0. If the claim holds at k, adding k+1 produces the required sum for k+1.
lessons.lab: Prove the formula 1+...+n = n(n+1)/2 by induction. Then write an invariant for counting living units in a prefix of a list. Pass: show initialization, preservation and termination explicitly.
lessons.reading: R06: induction, invariants and proof methods.

quiz.question: What are the two essential parts of induction?
quiz.answer: A valid base case and an implication from the inductive hypothesis to the next case.

quiz.question: Why does a mathematical proof not eliminate implementation tests?
quiz.answer: The code, machine arithmetic or environmental assumptions may differ from the proven model.

lessons.title: Counting, graphs and recurrences
lessons.outcome: Model combinations and recursive work without brute-force guessing.
lessons.teach:
The product rule counts independent sequential choices; the sum rule counts disjoint alternatives. A graph represents vertices and edges, which may be directed or weighted. A level map, dependency graph and network topology are different applications of the same abstraction. Decide what an edge means before choosing an algorithm.
A recurrence describes a quantity in terms of smaller instances. Repeatedly halving a search space gives logarithmic depth, but doing linear work at every level changes total cost. Do not confuse possible states with states actually explored by a particular algorithm. Counting provides upper bounds and exposes when exhaustive search becomes unrealistic.
lessons.example: Four independent equipment slots with three choices each give 3^4 = 81 combinations. An undirected simple graph with n vertices has at most n(n-1)/2 edges because each unordered pair appears once.
lessons.lab: Build a dependency graph for game startup and identify an invalid cycle. Count loadout combinations with and without a restriction. Pass: explain the recurrence for halving a search range and distinguish depth from total work.
lessons.reading: R06: counting, graphs, recurrences and asymptotic notation.

quiz.question: How many combinations arise from five independent binary choices?
How many edges can a simple undirected graph with five vertices have?
Why is a dependency cycle a problem for a simple startup order?
quiz.answer: No member can be initialized first while requiring another member of the cycle to be ready.

modules.title: Linear algebra and game geometry
modules.project: Build a tested vector/matrix library for a two-dimensional scene, then demonstrate a three-dimensional camera transformation with written coordinate conventions.

lessons.title: Vectors, dot products and projections
lessons.outcome: Use vectors for direction, distance and component measurements.
lessons.teach:
A vector represents a magnitude and direction in a chosen coordinate system. A point represents a location; subtracting points yields a displacement vector. The Euclidean length of (x,y,z) is sqrt(x*x+y*y+z*z). Normalization divides by length, so the zero vector needs a deliberate policy.
The dot product measures alignment and produces a scalar. For unit vectors it equals the cosine of the included angle. Projection onto a unit direction u is dot(v,u)*u. In three dimensions the cross product produces a perpendicular vector with orientation determined by the coordinate convention. Do not use a cross-product sign without declaring handedness.
lessons.example: For v=(3,4), length is 5 and its unit direction is (0.6,0.8). Dotting v with u=(1,0) gives 3, the component along the x axis.
lessons.lab: Implement length, dot and safe normalization. Use dot products to determine whether a target is in front of a character. Pass: test zero vectors, perpendicular vectors and opposite directions.
lessons.reading: R07: vectors and projections; R23: Geometry and Transformations / Vectors.

quiz.question: What is the length of (6,8)?
What is the dot product of (1,0) and (0,1)?
quiz.answer: 0, indicating perpendicular directions.

quiz.question: Why cannot the zero vector be normalized by the ordinary formula?
quiz.answer: Its length is zero, so division is undefined and it has no unique direction.

lessons.title: Matrices, bases and linear systems
lessons.outcome: Understand a matrix as a transformation rather than a table to memorize.
lessons.teach:
A matrix describes how basis vectors are mapped. Matrix-vector multiplication combines those images to transform a vector. A basis is a set of independent directions spanning the space. Changing basis changes coordinates without necessarily changing the underlying geometric object.
Matrix multiplication composes transformations, and order generally matters. Solving Ax=b is not the same task as explicitly computing A inverse; elimination or factorization is often preferable. A singular matrix loses information and cannot be uniquely inverted. In graphics, a zero scale along an axis is a concrete example of collapsing multiple points to the same location.
lessons.example: In two dimensions, scaling x by 2 maps (1,1) to (2,1). Rotating and then applying a nonuniform scale generally differs from applying the scale and then rotating.
lessons.lab: Implement 2-by-2 multiplication and solve two small linear systems by elimination on paper. Pass: show a pair of transforms that do not commute and explain a singular example geometrically.
lessons.reading: R07: matrix multiplication, elimination, inverses and vector spaces.

quiz.question: Do matrices generally satisfy AB = BA?
quiz.answer: No. Transformation order usually changes the result.

quiz.question: What happens to invertibility when an axis is scaled to zero?
quiz.answer: Information on that axis is lost, making the transformation singular.

quiz.question: Why solve Ax=b without explicitly forming an inverse?
quiz.answer: Factorization can be more efficient and numerically preferable, especially for repeated or large solves.

lessons.title: Homogeneous transforms, cameras and quaternions
lessons.outcome: Compose a scene using explicit coordinate conventions.
lessons.teach:
Homogeneous coordinates allow translation to be represented with matrix multiplication. In a common three-dimensional convention, points use w=1 and directions use w=0. A model transform maps local coordinates into world space; a view transform maps world coordinates into camera space. Perspective projection introduces a division by w and changes how depth is represented.
Choose row or column vectors, multiplication order, handedness and depth range, then document them. A unit quaternion represents orientation compactly and supports interpolation, but multiplication order still matters and accumulated error may require normalization. Euler angles remain useful for interfaces; their limitations do not make them meaningless.
lessons.example: With column vectors and a local-to-world matrix M, a point is p_world=M*p_local. A parent-child chain is M_parent*M_child*p_local. Reversing it changes the coordinate interpretation.
lessons.lab: Create a parented object and camera using documented conventions. Pass: test identity, inverse round trips within tolerance, a translated direction that remains unchanged, and a parent rotation that moves its child correctly.
lessons.reading: R23: Coordinate Systems and Transformations; R19: geometric transformations.

quiz.question: Why commonly use w=0 for directions?
quiz.answer: Translation should not change a pure direction; the homogeneous form makes the translation term vanish.

quiz.question: What does the view transform do?
quiz.answer: It expresses world-space geometry in the camera coordinate system.

quiz.question: Why document multiplication order even when using a library?
quiz.answer: The library convention and application convention must agree; otherwise valid arithmetic produces the wrong geometry.

lessons.title: Eigenvalues, least squares and singular values
lessons.outcome: Recognize stability and approximation problems in game data.
lessons.teach:
An eigenvector keeps its direction under a linear transformation; its eigenvalue is the scale applied along that direction. These concepts help analyze repeated updates and dynamical systems. Least squares fits an approximate solution when equations are inconsistent or measurements are noisy. It minimizes a chosen squared residual, not necessarily every meaningful error.
Singular values describe how strongly a matrix stretches different directions. Very small singular values can make inversion sensitive to input errors. Condition number measures sensitivity of the problem; algorithmic stability concerns how a method handles arithmetic error. A well-written algorithm cannot remove information absent from a badly conditioned problem.
lessons.example: The diagonal matrix diag(2,0.5) stretches the x direction by 2 and y by 0.5. Repeated application expands one component while shrinking the other.
lessons.lab: Fit a line to five noisy position/time observations and report residuals. Analyze repeated multiplication by a diagonal matrix. Pass: distinguish data noise, poor conditioning and a programming error in your report.
lessons.reading: R07: eigenvalues, least squares and singular value decomposition.

quiz.question: What are the eigenvalues of diag(3,2)?
quiz.answer: 3 and 2, with the coordinate axes as eigenvector directions.

quiz.question: What objective does ordinary least squares minimize?
quiz.answer: The sum of squared residuals under its specified model.

quiz.question: Can a stable algorithm make an ill-conditioned problem insensitive?
quiz.answer: No. It can limit added numerical error but cannot eliminate the problem's inherent sensitivity.

modules.title: Calculus, mechanics and numerical simulation
modules.prerequisites: Modules 06.1 and 07.1; work through the linked calculus problem sets.
modules.project: Build a projectile and spring simulator with analytic comparison cases, timestep refinement, unit checks and a report separating model error from numerical error.

lessons.title: Limits, derivatives and rates
lessons.outcome: Connect derivatives to velocity, acceleration and local approximation.
lessons.teach:
A derivative measures the local rate of change of a function. Velocity is the derivative of position with respect to time; acceleration is the derivative of velocity. The derivative carries units: meters differentiated by seconds gives meters per second. Product and chain rules explain how composed calculations change.
A finite difference approximates a derivative from samples. Making the step smaller reduces some approximation errors but can worsen floating-point cancellation. The derivative of an ideal formula and the difference between two measured samples answer related but not identical questions. Always distinguish the mathematical function from the noisy or discretized data available to your program.
lessons.example: For x(t)=t*t, velocity is 2*t. At t=3, velocity is 6. The forward difference using h=0.1 is ((3.1)^2-3^2)/0.1=6.1, an approximation rather than the exact derivative.
lessons.lab: Compare analytic and finite-difference derivatives of three functions over several step sizes. Pass: include units, an error table and an explanation of why the smallest tested h need not be best.
lessons.reading: R08: differentiation, product rule and chain rule.

quiz.question: Differentiate x(t)=3*t*t.
quiz.answer: dx/dt = 6*t.

quiz.question: What units does acceleration have when position is in meters?
quiz.answer: Meters per second squared.

quiz.question: Why can excessively small finite-difference steps be inaccurate?
quiz.answer: Subtracting nearly equal floating-point values magnifies rounding and cancellation error.

lessons.title: Integrals, accumulation and continuous probability
lessons.outcome: Interpret integration as accumulated contribution.
lessons.teach:
An integral accumulates contributions over a domain. Integrating velocity over time gives displacement; integrating acceleration changes velocity. The fundamental theorem of calculus connects derivatives and integrals. A definite integral is a signed accumulation, so negative contributions can cancel positive ones.
Numerical quadrature approximates an integral with samples and weights. Rectangle, trapezoid and higher-order rules have different accuracy assumptions. More samples do not repair a wrong model or omitted discontinuity. In graphics, integration will later accumulate incoming light over directions; in probability, a density integrates to a probability over an interval.
lessons.example: With constant velocity 4 meters/second over 3 seconds, displacement is 12 meters. For v(t)=2*t from 0 to 3, integrating gives 9 meters, not the final velocity multiplied by the whole duration.
lessons.lab: Implement rectangle and trapezoid integration for v(t)=2*t and a curved function. Pass: compare to an analytic integral, halve the step and report how error changes.
lessons.reading: R08: integration and the fundamental theorem; R23: Monte Carlo Integration introduction.

quiz.question: Integrate constant velocity 5 over two seconds.
quiz.answer: Displacement is 10 units of length.

quiz.question: What is the integral of 2*t from 0 to 3?
quiz.answer: [t^2] from 0 to 3 = 9.

quiz.question: Why can an integral be zero despite nonzero motion?
quiz.answer: Positive and negative displacement can cancel; total distance is a different quantity.

lessons.title: Newtonian mechanics and differential equations
lessons.outcome: Model motion from forces with clear simplifying assumptions.
lessons.teach:
Newton's second law relates net force to mass times acceleration. Position and velocity form the state of a basic particle model. Gravity, springs and damping provide forces with different dependencies. A differential equation specifies how state changes; initial conditions select a particular trajectory.
For a simple spring, force is proportional to displacement from rest and opposite its sign. Damping depends on velocity and dissipates energy in the model. Distinguish mass from weight and force from impulse. Games often choose simplified models for control and performance; simplification is legitimate when its behavior and limitations are explicit.
lessons.example: A 2 kg body under a constant 6 N net force has acceleration 3 m/s^2. Over 0.5 seconds, its velocity changes by 1.5 m/s. This says nothing about drag unless drag is included in the net force.
lessons.lab: Implement a particle under constant acceleration and a damped spring. Pass: compare the constant-acceleration trajectory to its analytic solution and state what collision, rotation and air-resistance effects are omitted.
lessons.reading: R28: simulation, bodies, forces and impulses; R08: differential-equation applications.

quiz.question: What acceleration results from 10 N on a 2 kg mass?
How does impulse differ from force?
quiz.answer: Impulse is force integrated over time and changes momentum; force is a rate of momentum change.

quiz.question: Why must initial conditions accompany a differential equation?
quiz.answer: Many trajectories can satisfy the same differential rule; initial state selects the intended one.

lessons.title: Time integration, stability and error
lessons.outcome: Choose and test a numerical update rather than assuming smaller code is correct.
lessons.teach:
Explicit Euler advances state using derivatives at the old state. Semi-implicit Euler updates velocity first and then uses the new velocity for position. Other methods trade more work for different accuracy and stability properties. A method can have small local error yet accumulate unacceptable global drift.
Timestep choice depends on the system, method and acceptable error. Stiff springs can require much smaller explicit steps than slow motion. Fixed timesteps aid repeatability but do not guarantee stability or identical results across machines. Compare against analytic cases, inspect energy where meaningful and repeat with a refined step before trusting a visually plausible animation.
lessons.example: For explicit Euler: x_next=x+v*dt; v_next=v+a*dt. For semi-implicit Euler, compute v_next first and use x_next=x+v_next*dt. The methods differ even with identical inputs.
lessons.lab: Compare explicit and semi-implicit Euler on an undamped spring at three timesteps. Pass: plot or tabulate position and energy error, identify an unstable case, and avoid calling visual smoothness proof of physical accuracy.
lessons.reading: R23: physically based animation topics via R19; R28: simulation stepping guidance.

quiz.question: Which velocity does semi-implicit Euler use for the position update?
quiz.answer: The newly updated velocity.

quiz.question: Does a fixed timestep guarantee a stable simulation?
quiz.answer: No. Stability still depends on the equations, method and step size.

quiz.question: What is a useful check beyond watching the animation?
quiz.answer: Compare to an analytic solution or conserved quantity and perform timestep-refinement tests.

modules.title: Probability, statistics and evidence
modules.project: Create a reproducible benchmark experiment and a loot-distribution simulation. Report assumptions, uncertainty, representative workloads and one result that did not support the original hypothesis.

lessons.title: Probability and conditional reasoning
lessons.outcome: Model uncertainty without confusing independent and conditional events.
lessons.teach:
Probability assigns weights to events under a model. Conditional probability restricts attention to cases where another event occurred. Independence means learning one event does not change the probability of the other; it is an assumption to justify, not a default for every repeated observation.
Bayes' rule reverses conditioning using prior probabilities and evidence likelihoods. Rare-event base rates matter when interpreting an apparently accurate detector. In games, these ideas apply to randomized systems, telemetry and testing. A measured frequency approaches a model probability only under suitable sampling assumptions; a small sample can be very noisy.
lessons.example: For independent fair coin flips, the probability of two heads is 1/4. If the second outcome is deliberately copied from the first, the probability is 1/2, demonstrating why dependence changes the calculation.
lessons.lab: Simulate independent and dependent binary events. Build a small contingency table for a hypothetical bug detector. Pass: calculate both P(alert|bug) and P(bug|alert) and explain why they differ.
lessons.reading: R09: probability, conditional probability and Bayes' theorem.

quiz.question: What is the probability of two independent events with probabilities 0.5 and 0.2 both occurring?
quiz.answer: 0.1, the product under the stated independence assumption.

quiz.question: Is P(A|B) generally equal to P(B|A)?
quiz.answer: No. They condition on different populations.

quiz.question: Why do rare-event base rates matter for an alert?
quiz.answer: Even a small false-positive rate can produce many alerts when true events are very rare.

lessons.title: Random variables, distributions and sampling
lessons.outcome: Distinguish an expected value from a guaranteed outcome.
lessons.teach:
A random variable maps outcomes to numbers. Its expectation is a probability-weighted average; variance measures spread around that average. A distribution describes the possible values and their probabilities. Bernoulli, binomial and normal models have different assumptions and should not be chosen only because their names are familiar.
Pseudorandom generators are deterministic algorithms with internal state. A seed supports repeatable experiments, but a generator suitable for gameplay is not automatically suitable for security. Sampling can be biased by how data is collected. Use separate random streams when independent subsystems should not change each other's results merely by making extra draws.
lessons.example: A reward of 10 with probability 0.2 and 0 otherwise has expected value 2. A player still receives either 10 or 0 on one trial, not necessarily 2.
lessons.lab: Implement a weighted reward sampler and compare observed frequencies to the intended distribution over several sample sizes. Pass: record seed, generator, counts and expected values; explain finite-sample variation.
lessons.reading: R09: random variables, expectation and variance; R04: random reference.

quiz.question: What is the expectation of 20 with probability 0.25 and 0 otherwise?
Does an expectation of 5 guarantee a reward of 5 on a trial?
quiz.answer: No. It describes an average under the model, not an individual outcome.

quiz.question: Why separate random streams for unrelated systems?
quiz.answer: An extra draw in one system should not unintentionally alter another system's sequence.

lessons.title: Inference, uncertainty and benchmark design
lessons.outcome: Compare implementations without hiding variance or bias.
lessons.teach:
A sample statistic estimates a property of a larger process. Confidence intervals express uncertainty under a sampling model; they are not a probability that a fixed frequentist parameter lies in a specific realized interval. Hypothesis tests require defined assumptions and do not measure practical importance by themselves.
For performance work, control workload, build mode, warmup and environmental changes. Use repeated independent runs where possible; adjacent frames are often correlated. Report distributions and tail latency rather than only an average. A statistically detectable difference may be too small to matter, while a rare long pause can be important despite little change in the mean.
lessons.example: Implementation A might average 5 ms but occasionally take 100 ms; B might average 6 ms with no large pauses in the tested sample. The preferred design depends on throughput and latency requirements, not the mean alone.
lessons.lab: Compare two implementations using the same inputs, randomized test order and repeated runs. Pass: report median, a tail percentile, sample count and limitations; distinguish observations from causal claims.
lessons.reading: R09: confidence intervals, hypothesis testing and experimental reasoning.

quiz.question: Why can adjacent frame times violate an independence assumption?
quiz.answer: They share workload phases, caches, thermal state and other correlated conditions.

quiz.question: Does a small p-value establish a large useful improvement?
quiz.answer: No. Statistical evidence and practical effect size are different questions.

quiz.question: Why report a tail percentile alongside a mean?
quiz.answer: It exposes slow cases that can affect responsiveness despite an acceptable average.

lessons.title: Regression, correlation and ethical telemetry
lessons.outcome: Fit a model while recognizing confounding and data limits.
lessons.teach:
Regression relates an outcome to predictors under a chosen model. Correlation is association, not proof of causation. A confounder can influence both the apparent cause and the outcome. Models should be evaluated on held-out observations or a suitable validation scheme, not only on the data used to fit them.
Telemetry collection should have a defined purpose and minimize unnecessary personal data. For course projects, use synthetic or consented data rather than harvesting real players. Do not optimize only the easiest-to-measure metric. Session length, for example, is not equivalent to enjoyment, accessibility or wellbeing.
lessons.example: Players with better hardware may both buy more games and achieve higher frame rates. Observing a purchase/frame-rate correlation does not establish that purchases caused faster rendering.
lessons.lab: Fit a simple performance model using entity count and measured update time. Hold out some workloads. Pass: report prediction error and one confounder; write a short data-minimization plan for the experiment.
lessons.reading: R09: regression and inference; R01: ethics and data-management breadth.

quiz.question: Why is training-set fit alone insufficient?
quiz.answer: A model can overfit and fail on new observations or workloads.

quiz.question: What is a confounder?
quiz.answer: A variable that influences both the proposed explanatory factor and the outcome, complicating causal interpretation.

quiz.question: Why should telemetry collect only what the question requires?
quiz.answer: It reduces privacy exposure and unnecessary data handling while keeping the experiment focused.

modules.title: Signals, optimization and numerical foundations
modules.project: Complete Gate B: a mathematical engineering notebook plus tested transforms, numerical integration, signal filtering and an uncertainty-aware experiment.

lessons.title: Multivariable calculus and gradients
lessons.outcome: Use partial derivatives to reason about spatial fields and optimization.
lessons.teach:
A multivariable function depends on several inputs. A partial derivative varies one input while holding the others fixed. The gradient collects partial derivatives and points toward steepest local increase under the usual Euclidean metric. The Jacobian describes the local linear behavior of a vector-valued function.
Gradients support terrain normals, inverse kinematics and parameter fitting. A gradient is local information, not a guarantee of the global best direction over a large step. Chain-rule reasoning must follow every transformation. Numerical derivatives are useful checks for analytic code, but choose perturbations that account for scale and rounding.
lessons.example: For f(x,y)=x*x+y*y, the gradient is (2*x,2*y). At (3,4), it is (6,8). Taking a small step in the negative gradient direction reduces f locally.
lessons.lab: Derive gradients for three functions and check them with centered differences. Pass: test nonzero and stationary points, vary perturbation size and report errors rather than claiming exact equality.
lessons.reading: R07: linearization foundations; R23: geometric differential quantities; use the program's multivariable extension reading.

quiz.question: What is the gradient of x*x + 3*y*y?
What does a Jacobian describe?
quiz.answer: The first-order local mapping from small input changes to output changes for a vector-valued function.

quiz.question: Does a zero gradient always identify a minimum?
quiz.answer: No. It may identify a maximum, saddle or other stationary point.

lessons.title: Sampling, aliasing and Fourier ideas
lessons.outcome: Explain why discrete samples can misrepresent a continuous signal.
lessons.teach:
Sampling records a signal at discrete positions or times. Different high-frequency signals can produce the same samples, creating aliasing. Reconstruction needs assumptions about bandwidth and a suitable filter. For a strictly band-limited signal, the familiar sampling criterion requires a rate greater than twice its highest frequency; practical systems need transition bands and margin.
The Fourier viewpoint decomposes signals into frequency components. It connects audio, textures, animation and display artifacts. Increasing resolution helps only relative to the signal content. Filtering before downsampling removes frequencies that the lower rate cannot represent; filtering afterward cannot generally recover information already aliased.
lessons.example: A 900 Hz tone sampled at 1000 samples/second can appear as a 100 Hz tone. The samples do not uniquely preserve the original high-frequency oscillation.
lessons.lab: Generate low- and high-frequency sine samples, then downsample a checker pattern with and without prefiltering. Pass: explain the artifacts using frequency content rather than calling them random noise.
lessons.reading: R10: sampling and Fourier representation; R23: Sampling and Reconstruction.

quiz.question: What is the Nyquist frequency at 48,000 samples/second?
quiz.answer: 24,000 Hz, the half-sampling-rate boundary; practical filtering requires additional care.

quiz.question: Why filter before downsampling?
quiz.answer: To remove frequencies that would fold into misleading lower frequencies at the new sample rate.

quiz.question: Can post-filtering always undo aliasing?
quiz.answer: No. Distinct original signals may already have become indistinguishable in the samples.

lessons.title: Convolution, filters and systems
lessons.outcome: Predict a filter's effect on data and latency.
lessons.teach:
Convolution combines a signal with a kernel by weighted summation of shifted values. A moving average smooths high-frequency variation, but it also changes edges and can introduce delay depending on implementation. A linear time-invariant system is characterized by its impulse response under the model assumptions.
Boundary handling is part of a filter definition. Zero padding, wrapping and edge replication produce different results. Filters also have numeric and performance costs. In audio, a stable and bounded processing path is essential; in images, color-space assumptions matter when averaging values. Test an impulse and a constant signal before trusting a complex input.
lessons.example: A three-sample average of [3,6,9] is 6. Sliding this kernel across a sequence produces a smoothed sequence; values near either end require an explicit boundary policy.
lessons.lab: Implement a one-dimensional convolution with documented boundary handling. Test an impulse, a constant and a step. Pass: predict the output before running and identify the filter's delay convention.
lessons.reading: R10: convolution, impulse response and linear time-invariant systems.

quiz.question: What does convolving with an impulse reveal?
quiz.answer: The filter's impulse response, including its alignment convention.

quiz.question: What is the average of 2, 5 and 8?
Why is boundary handling not an implementation footnote?
quiz.answer: It changes the mathematical result at the edges and may create visible or audible artifacts.

lessons.title: Optimization, conditioning and approximation budgets
lessons.outcome: Choose an objective and distinguish convergence from correctness.
lessons.teach:
Optimization minimizes or maximizes a specified objective under constraints. Gradient descent takes steps opposite the gradient; its behavior depends on step size, scaling and the shape of the objective. A local optimum need not be global. Constraints can be as important as the objective, such as keeping error below a visible threshold while reducing work.
Numerical engineering combines error sources: model approximations, finite precision, sampling and iterative termination. Define an error budget and a reference case. More iterations can reduce one error while leaving others unchanged. Stop according to a justified criterion and report failure to converge rather than silently returning a plausible number.
lessons.example: For f(x)=(x-3)^2, gradient descent uses x_next=x-alpha*2*(x-3). An excessively large alpha can oscillate or diverge even though the function has a simple minimum.
lessons.lab: Implement gradient descent on a quadratic and a two-variable problem. Pass: compare step sizes, record residuals and state a stopping rule; complete Gate B with no unsupported claim of global optimality.
lessons.reading: R07: least squares and conditioning; R23: numerical utilities; graduate optimization reading in the handbook.

quiz.question: Where is the minimum of (x-3)^2?
quiz.answer: At x=3, with objective value zero.

quiz.question: Why can reducing step size help an unstable iteration?
quiz.answer: It can prevent updates from overshooting the region where local information is useful, though convergence can become slower.

quiz.question: What should happen when an iterative method reaches its iteration limit?
quiz.answer: Report nonconvergence or the achieved residual explicitly rather than pretending the requested accuracy was met.

modules.title: Native programming with C++
modules.prerequisites: Volume 01, Modules 06-07; do not skip the ownership module that follows.
modules.project: Port the deterministic grid simulation to C++20, with a command-line build, automated tests, warnings enabled and an explicit account of representation differences from Python.

lessons.title: Compilation, linking and build systems
lessons.outcome: Explain how source code becomes a runnable native program.
lessons.teach:
A C++ translation unit is compiled into object code; linking resolves references and combines the required pieces into a program or library. Headers usually provide declarations shared across translation units. A declaration describes an entity; a definition supplies its implementation or storage. Build errors therefore occur at different stages and require different evidence.
A build system records dependencies and compiler settings. Use a small CMake target rather than hardcoding paths throughout source files. Keep build products outside the source tree. Debug and optimized builds can differ substantially, so record which configuration produced a measurement. For this course, C++20 is a selected teaching baseline, not a claim that every feature is supported by every compiler.
lessons.example: A function can compile at a call site when its declaration is visible yet fail to link when no matching definition is supplied. A missing header usually fails earlier during compilation.
lessons.lab: Build the included C++ starter, then split one function into a header and source file. Pass: reproduce and explain one compile error and one link error, then restore a warning-clean build.
lessons.reading: R12: Getting Started and libraries; R11: Source Files.

quiz.question: What task does the linker perform?
quiz.answer: It resolves symbol references and combines object code/libraries into the requested output.

quiz.question: Can valid declarations alone supply every function implementation?
quiz.answer: No. A referenced function generally needs a matching definition unless special language rules apply.

quiz.question: Why record build configuration with a benchmark?
quiz.answer: Optimization, instrumentation and assertions can materially change behavior and performance.

lessons.title: Integer, floating-point and object representations
lessons.outcome: Choose native types with explicit range and precision assumptions.
lessons.teach:
Native representations have finite range and precision. Do not assume int is a particular width in every environment. Fixed-width integer types are available when the implementation provides them; use them where a format or interface requires that width. Unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo its range, while signed integer overflow in ordinary C++ arithmetic is undefined behavior.
Floating-point operations approximate real arithmetic and have special values such as infinity and NaN on common IEEE-style implementations. Object layout can contain padding, so raw struct bytes are not a portable save or network format. Byte order, alignment and field encoding require explicit decisions. An apparently correct result on one machine does not establish portability.
lessons.example: An unsigned 8-bit value has 256 distinct values, 0 through 255. A 32-bit byte count can be too small for a large asset. Converting a negative signed value to an unsigned type may produce a very large number.
lessons.lab: Print relevant sizes and numeric limits on the available compiler. Write checked conversions for a file length and tests for boundary values. Pass: do not trigger signed overflow as a test oracle; reject out-of-range input before converting.
lessons.reading: R11: arithmetic and conversion guidance; R15: information encoding and arithmetic.

quiz.question: How many distinct bit patterns fit in eight bits?
Is ordinary signed integer overflow defined to wrap in C++?
quiz.answer: No. It is undefined behavior; use checked arithmetic or an intentionally suitable representation.

quiz.question: Why is writing raw struct bytes not a portable format?
quiz.answer: Padding, byte order, alignment, type widths and representation may vary.

lessons.title: Values, references, pointers and lifetimes
lessons.outcome: Track where an object lives and how long access remains valid.
lessons.teach:
A value is an object's stored information. A reference aliases an existing object; a pointer stores an address-like value and can represent no object with nullptr. Neither a raw pointer nor a reference automatically owns what it refers to. Ownership determines who must release a resource; lifetime determines when the object exists.
Automatic storage duration often corresponds to stack allocation, but storage-duration rules are the reliable language concept. Returning a pointer or reference to a local object leaves a dangling access after that object's lifetime ends. Const expresses permitted modification through an interface, not universal thread safety or deep immutability. Draw ownership and lifetime diagrams before clever pointer code.
lessons.example: Passing const State& can avoid copying while allowing observation of a state owned by the caller. Returning a State by value can be safe and efficient; do not assume every value return causes an expensive extra copy.
lessons.lab: Implement functions taking values, const references and pointers with a documented null policy. Pass: explain each lifetime and identify a deliberately supplied dangling-reference example without executing undefined behavior.
lessons.reading: R11: Interfaces, Resource Management and lifetime safety guidance.
