quiz.question: Does a raw pointer necessarily own its target?
quiz.answer: No. Ownership must be established by the interface or an owning type.

quiz.question: Why is returning a reference to a local variable invalid?
quiz.answer: The local object is destroyed at function exit, leaving a dangling reference.

quiz.question: Does const by itself make shared access thread-safe?
quiz.answer: No. Thread safety depends on all accesses, object behavior and synchronization.

lessons.title: Standard containers, iterators and error handling
lessons.outcome: Use library abstractions while respecting invalidation and failure contracts.
lessons.teach:
Standard containers provide reusable storage and algorithms. std::vector offers contiguous elements and amortized growth behavior, but reallocation can invalidate pointers, references and iterators into its storage. Size is the number of live elements; capacity is storage reserved for possible growth. Reserving capacity does not construct that many elements.
Use standard algorithms when they make intent clearer. Check container preconditions and distinguish exceptional failure from ordinary absence. An optional value, status type or exception may each be appropriate under a documented policy. Do not catch every error and pretend success; preserve useful diagnostic context and avoid leaving partially updated state.
lessons.example: For a vector with size 3 and capacity 8, valid element indices are still 0, 1 and 2. Accessing index 7 is not allowed merely because storage has been reserved.
lessons.lab: Port the unit list to std::vector and implement lookup with an explicit not-found result. Pass: test empty input, missing ID and growth; document which operations invalidate stored references.
lessons.reading: R11: standard-library use and error handling; R12: testing integration.

quiz.question: Does reserve(100) make a vector's size 100?
quiz.answer: No. It changes capacity, not the number of constructed elements.

quiz.question: Why can a pointer to a vector element become invalid after growth?
quiz.answer: Reallocation may move elements to a different storage region.

quiz.question: What is wrong with ignoring every exception?
quiz.answer: It hides failures and may allow incorrect or partially updated state to appear successful.

modules.title: Ownership, abstractions and C++ design
modules.project: Build a small resource manager with explicit ownership, safe move behavior, bounded interfaces, fault-injection tests and a written comparison of composition and inheritance.

lessons.title: RAII and resource ownership
lessons.outcome: Make cleanup follow object lifetime on success and failure paths.
lessons.teach:
Resource acquisition is initialization, or RAII, ties a resource to an owning object whose destructor releases it. The resource can be memory, a file, a mutex guard or a graphics handle. This makes cleanup occur on normal scope exit and during supported exception unwinding. Ownership should be visible in types rather than scattered comments.
Prefer unique ownership when one component controls lifetime. Shared ownership is useful for genuinely shared lifetimes but adds costs and can form cycles. Non-owning views must not outlive their owner. Wrapping an operating-system or GPU handle requires the correct release operation and context; a destructor is not magic if it runs after the device is gone.
lessons.example: A unique_ptr owns one object and releases it automatically. Passing a raw pointer to inspect that object can be fine when the caller guarantees the owner remains alive throughout the call.
lessons.lab: Wrap a mock file/device resource whose open/close counters can be inspected. Inject failure after acquisition. Pass: each acquired resource is released exactly once and no view outlives its owner.
lessons.reading: R11: Resource Management and smart-pointer ownership rules.

quiz.question: What does RAII connect?
quiz.answer: Resource ownership and release to the lifetime of an object.

quiz.question: Can shared ownership create a leak through cycles?
quiz.answer: Yes, if owning references keep each other alive; weak/non-owning links may be needed.

quiz.question: Why must device-resource destruction order be planned?
quiz.answer: A release operation may require a live device or context; destroying the device first invalidates that assumption.

lessons.title: Copy, move and exception safety
lessons.outcome: Define what transferring a resource means without duplicating ownership.
lessons.teach:
Copying creates an independent value according to a type's contract. Moving transfers or reuses resources where appropriate; it is not merely a guaranteed byte copy. A moved-from standard-library object remains valid but may have an unspecified value unless its specific contract says more. std::move is a cast enabling move-aware overload resolution, not an operation that itself moves bytes.
Exception safety asks what remains true if an operation fails. A basic guarantee preserves validity and prevents leaks; a strong guarantee leaves observable state unchanged on failure. Build a replacement first and commit only after success when that guarantee is important. Prefer the rule of zero: compose well-behaved members rather than writing custom special-member functions unnecessarily.
lessons.example: To replace a loaded asset, validate a new asset before swapping it into the live slot. A failed parse then leaves the old working asset available instead of an empty or half-filled replacement.
lessons.lab: Implement a move-only mock resource and transactional asset replacement. Pass: copying is prohibited, moving does not double-release, and injected load failure preserves the old asset.
lessons.reading: R11: class special members, rule of zero and exception safety.

quiz.question: Does std::move itself guarantee that an object is moved?
quiz.answer: No. It permits move-aware overload selection; the selected operation determines what happens.

quiz.question: What is the strong exception guarantee?
quiz.answer: On failure, the operation leaves the relevant observable state unchanged.

quiz.question: Why prefer the rule of zero?
quiz.answer: Correct member types can manage resources without fragile custom copy/move/destruction code.

lessons.title: Interfaces, composition and polymorphism
lessons.outcome: Choose abstractions according to substitutability and measured cost.
lessons.teach:
An interface should expose a coherent capability with a clear contract. Runtime polymorphism chooses behavior through a dynamic type, often via virtual functions. Static polymorphism resolves behavior through compile-time types. Neither is always faster or better; ownership, extensibility, binary boundaries and workload matter.
Composition keeps independent capabilities separate. An inheritance hierarchy is appropriate when derived objects can honor the base contract. A base class deleted polymorphically normally needs a virtual destructor. Avoid embedding every engine subsystem in one universal object. Small explicit interfaces make tests, replacement implementations and dependency analysis easier.
lessons.example: A Renderer interface might accept a scene description and produce a frame. A test renderer can record calls without drawing. It should not need to own gameplay rules or the network session.
lessons.lab: Create interchangeable console and recording renderers behind one small interface. Pass: both satisfy the same contract, tests run without display output, and ownership/destructor behavior is explicit.
lessons.reading: R11: Interfaces, Class Hierarchies and composition guidance.

quiz.question: What does substitutability require?
quiz.answer: An implementation used through an interface must preserve that interface's behavioral contract.

quiz.question: Why can a polymorphic base need a virtual destructor?
quiz.answer: Deletion through a base pointer must invoke appropriate derived cleanup.

quiz.question: Why not put every responsibility into one engine class?
quiz.answer: It increases coupling, obscures contracts and makes isolated testing or replacement difficult.

lessons.title: Templates, concepts and data-oriented choices
lessons.outcome: Use generic code without hiding costs or exploding complexity.
lessons.teach:
Templates express algorithms and types parameterized by compile-time information. Concepts constrain acceptable operations and improve interface meaning. Generic code still needs tests for relevant instantiations and clear compilation errors. Excessive instantiation can increase build times and binary size, so abstraction costs include developer time as well as runtime.
Data-oriented design starts from access patterns: which fields are processed together, how often, and in what order? Array-of-structures and structure-of-arrays layouts trade convenience, locality and vectorization opportunities. Do not adopt either as doctrine. Measure a representative loop and preserve correctness while comparing designs.
lessons.example: If a movement pass reads only positions and velocities, a structure-of-arrays layout can avoid fetching unrelated names and inventory fields. If each operation needs the complete object, that advantage may shrink or reverse.
lessons.lab: Write a constrained generic clamp or interpolation function and benchmark two simple entity layouts. Pass: test contracts, record compiler/build mode and explain why the result is workload-specific.
lessons.reading: R11: Templates and Generic Programming; R15: memory hierarchy motivation.

quiz.question: What does a concept constrain?
quiz.answer: The compile-time requirements a type or expression must satisfy for a template interface.

quiz.question: Is structure-of-arrays universally superior?
quiz.answer: No. Its benefit depends on access pattern, workload and architecture.

quiz.question: Name a cost of templates beyond runtime.
quiz.answer: Compilation time, error complexity, binary size or maintenance burden.

modules.title: Data structures and their costs
modules.project: Implement educational versions of a dynamic array, queue, hash table and heap, each with invariants and tests. Compare them to standard containers without replacing standard code in production merely for practice.

lessons.title: Complexity, arrays and linked structures
lessons.outcome: Predict asymptotic work while recognizing locality and constants.
lessons.teach:
Asymptotic notation describes how cost grows with input size under a stated model. Big-O is an upper bound, not an exact time or a synonym for worst case in every context. Arrays provide indexed access and contiguous storage. Linked structures connect separately located nodes and can support local insertion when the location is already known.
Searching for that location still costs work. Pointer chasing and allocation affect real performance beyond operation counts. A dynamic array can grow geometrically to achieve amortized constant-time append, even though some individual appends require linear relocation. Amortized analysis concerns a sequence of operations, not an average over random inputs.
lessons.example: Doubling capacity after each expansion makes total copied elements across n appends proportional to n. Growing capacity by one each time can copy approximately 1+2+...+(n-1), which is quadratic.
lessons.lab: Implement a growable integer buffer for study. Count copied elements under doubling and one-at-a-time growth. Pass: derive the growth behavior and separately measure elapsed time without equating it to the proof.
lessons.reading: R13: arrays, cost models and asymptotic analysis; R06: sums.

quiz.question: Does O(n) specify an exact runtime?
quiz.answer: No. It bounds growth under a cost model and omits constants and environment details.

quiz.question: What is the total 1+...+(n-1) proportional to?
quiz.answer: n squared, since the sum is n(n-1)/2.

quiz.question: How does amortized analysis differ from random-input average-case analysis?
quiz.answer: It bounds total cost over an operation sequence without requiring a probability distribution over inputs.

lessons.title: Stacks, queues and ring buffers
lessons.outcome: Match ordering semantics to the intended workflow.
lessons.teach:
A stack is last-in, first-out; a queue is first-in, first-out. Stacks support nested calls and undo-like history; queues support pending work and messages. A ring buffer reuses a fixed storage region by wrapping indices. It needs an unambiguous policy to distinguish empty from full.
Bounded structures force an overload decision: reject, overwrite, block or drop according to requirements. Silently overwriting input commands may be unacceptable even if overwriting old diagnostic samples is permitted. A single-threaded ring buffer is not automatically safe for concurrent producers and consumers; synchronization is a separate lesson.
lessons.example: Enqueue A, B and C into a FIFO queue, then dequeue twice: A and B leave first. Push the same values onto a stack, then pop twice: C and B leave first.
lessons.lab: Implement a bounded queue with explicit full/empty results and wraparound tests. Pass: preserve FIFO order through more than three times its capacity in operations and never read an uninitialized slot.
lessons.reading: R13: elementary data structures; R16: later concurrency comparison.

quiz.question: Which item leaves first after pushing A then B onto a stack?
quiz.answer: B.

quiz.question: Why does a ring buffer need a full/empty convention?
quiz.answer: Equal index values can otherwise be ambiguous after wrapping.

quiz.question: Does a correct single-threaded queue imply a thread-safe queue?
quiz.answer: No. Concurrent access introduces ordering, atomicity and ownership requirements.

lessons.title: Hash tables and collision policies
lessons.outcome: Explain expected lookup behavior and its assumptions.
lessons.teach:
A hash table maps keys to buckets using a hash function. Different keys can share a bucket; collision handling is therefore required, not optional. Equality decides whether keys are actually the same. Load factor measures occupancy and affects performance according to the collision strategy.
Expected constant-time lookup relies on assumptions about hashing, load and inputs. Worst-case behavior can be much worse. Rehashing can invalidate references according to a container's contract. For untrusted inputs, adversarial collisions may matter. Hash values are not unique identifiers, encryption or proof that two objects are equal.
lessons.example: Keys 12 and 22 both map to bucket 2 under key modulo 10. A correct table retains both and compares actual keys during lookup.
lessons.lab: Implement chaining or open addressing with collision tests and resizing. Pass: deliberately force many collisions, test missing keys and verify that distinct equal-hash keys remain distinct.
lessons.reading: R13: hashing and dictionary data structures.

quiz.question: Does a matching hash prove two keys are equal?
quiz.answer: No. Collisions are possible; equality must still be checked.

quiz.question: What is the load factor for 30 entries in 10 buckets?
quiz.answer: 3 entries per bucket on average for this definition.

quiz.question: Why is expected O(1) not an unconditional guarantee?
quiz.answer: It depends on hashing, occupancy and input assumptions; worst cases can be much slower.

lessons.title: Trees, heaps and priority queues
lessons.outcome: Preserve structural invariants and choose the right query behavior.
lessons.teach:
A binary search tree orders keys so that search can follow comparisons down a path. Its height determines many operation costs; an unbalanced tree can degrade to a chain. A heap maintains a different invariant: each parent has priority no worse than its children. It efficiently exposes an extreme element but does not globally sort all positions.
Priority queues are central to scheduling and pathfinding. Updating priorities requires a supported policy, such as handles, indexed heaps or inserting a new entry and ignoring stale ones. State the ordering and tie-break rules so tests and replays behave consistently.
lessons.example: A min-heap containing 2, 5 and 9 must expose 2 at the root, but its internal array is not promised to be a sorted sequence. A sorted insertion stream can make a naive search tree height n.
lessons.lab: Implement a binary min-heap with push/pop and randomized comparison to a sorted reference. Pass: validate the heap invariant after every operation and test duplicate priorities.
lessons.reading: R13: binary search trees, balanced trees and heaps.

quiz.question: Does a heap provide a fully sorted array?
quiz.answer: No. It guarantees the heap ordering relation, especially access to the extreme element.

quiz.question: What can the height of an unbalanced n-node search tree become?
quiz.answer: n in the chain-like worst case, depending on height convention by one.

quiz.question: Why define a tie-break rule in a priority queue?
quiz.answer: Equal priorities otherwise may produce inconsistent processing order, complicating tests and deterministic behavior.

modules.title: Algorithms for maps, simulation and tools
modules.project: Build a pathfinding visualizer and asset-dependency planner. Provide correctness arguments, unreachable cases, complexity analysis and measured comparisons on multiple map families.

lessons.title: Searching, sorting and algorithm selection
lessons.outcome: Choose an algorithm from its preconditions and the data distribution.
lessons.teach:
Binary search discards part of an ordered range after each comparison. Its invariant must preserve where a possible answer can remain. Sorting establishes order but incurs a cost; whether sorting first is worthwhile depends on how many later queries will reuse it. Stable sorting preserves relative order of equivalent keys.
Comparison sorting has well-known lower bounds under its model, while specialized methods can exploit bounded integer keys or other structure. Algorithm selection also considers memory, input size, nearly sorted data and worst-case behavior. Never apply a performance claim without its assumptions.
lessons.example: For 1024 ordered elements, binary search takes roughly ten halving decisions to narrow to one candidate, with exact comparisons depending on the implementation. An unsorted list does not satisfy the required invariant.
lessons.lab: Implement binary search with a documented interval convention and test empty, one-element, duplicate and missing cases. Compare two sorts on random and nearly sorted inputs. Pass: verify output order and element preservation.
lessons.reading: R13: binary search, sorting and comparison models.

quiz.question: What precondition does ordinary binary search require?
quiz.answer: A range ordered consistently with its comparison rule.

quiz.question: What does stable sorting preserve?
quiz.answer: The original relative order of elements considered equivalent by the comparison.

quiz.question: Why test element preservation as well as sortedness?
quiz.answer: An output can be sorted yet incorrectly omit, duplicate or change input elements.

lessons.title: Graph traversal and dependency ordering
lessons.outcome: Use graph algorithms with explicit edge semantics.
lessons.teach:
Breadth-first search explores an unweighted graph by distance in edges; depth-first search follows a path before backtracking. Both need visited-state handling to avoid repeated traversal in cyclic graphs. A topological ordering exists only for a directed acyclic graph and places prerequisites before their dependents under the chosen edge convention.
Graph representation affects cost. Adjacency lists suit many sparse graphs; adjacency matrices can simplify dense or constant-time edge-existence queries at greater storage cost. A navigation graph is a model of movement, not the world itself: missing edges, one-way passages and dynamic obstacles change the problem.
lessons.example: With edges A->B and B->C meaning "must precede," A,B,C is a valid topological order. Adding C->A creates a cycle, so no such order exists.
lessons.lab: Implement BFS and topological sorting. Pass: recover a shortest unweighted path, report unreachable goals, reject a cyclic dependency graph and justify the O(V+E) traversal bound for adjacency lists.
lessons.reading: R13: graph representations, BFS, DFS and topological sorting.

quiz.question: When does BFS find a shortest path by edge count?
quiz.answer: On an unweighted graph, or when all traversed edges have equal cost.

quiz.question: Can a directed graph with a cycle have a topological order?
quiz.answer: No.

quiz.question: Why mark visited nodes?
quiz.answer: To avoid repeated exploration and nontermination on cycles while preserving the traversal's intended behavior.

lessons.title: Dijkstra, A* and admissible heuristics
lessons.outcome: Build a correct pathfinder before optimizing its queue.
lessons.teach:
Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths with nonnegative edge costs. A* adds a heuristic estimate of remaining cost, prioritizing f=g+h. An admissible heuristic never overestimates the true remaining cost. A consistent heuristic also respects a triangle-like condition across edges.
Implementation details matter: closed-set policies, stale queue entries and reopening nodes affect correctness when a heuristic is not consistent. Negative edge costs invalidate ordinary Dijkstra assumptions. For a four-neighbor unit-cost grid, Manhattan distance is a useful lower bound; diagonal motion or terrain costs require reconsidering the model. Faster search that returns an invalid route is not an improvement.
lessons.example: From (1,2) to (4,6), Manhattan distance is |4-1|+|6-2|=7 on a four-neighbor unit-cost grid. Allowing inexpensive diagonals changes the appropriate estimate.
lessons.lab: Implement Dijkstra and A* against the same grid model. Pass: compare path costs on many small maps, include no-path cases and demonstrate a deliberately overestimating heuristic that can sacrifice optimality.
lessons.reading: R13: shortest paths; R20: game navigation context.

quiz.question: What edge-cost condition does ordinary Dijkstra require?
quiz.answer: Nonnegative edge costs.

quiz.question: What is Manhattan distance from (0,0) to (3,4)?
Why can inconsistent heuristics require reopening nodes?
quiz.answer: A better path to a previously processed node may be discovered later; permanently closing it can discard that improvement.

lessons.title: Dynamic programming, complexity limits and approximation
lessons.outcome: Recognize repeated subproblems and justify a practical solution.
lessons.teach:
Dynamic programming stores solutions to overlapping subproblems under a recurrence. The difficult step is defining sufficient state and a valid dependency order. Memoization evaluates on demand; tabulation fills an ordered table. More dimensions can make a state space explode even when each transition is simple.
Complexity classes describe families of problems and reductions under formal models. NP-complete does not mean impossible on every instance, and a polynomial algorithm is not automatically fast enough in practice. Approximation, heuristics and bounded search can be appropriate when their guarantees and limits are explicit. Do not label an algorithm optimal merely because it found a good result once.
lessons.example: A budgeted loadout problem can use state (item_prefix, remaining_budget). Remembering only remaining_budget loses which items remain available and can produce an invalid recurrence.
lessons.lab: Solve a small 0/1 knapsack instance by exhaustive search and dynamic programming. Pass: compare answers, derive state count, and describe how a heuristic would be evaluated without claiming a guarantee it lacks.
lessons.reading: R13: dynamic programming; R06: reductions and asymptotic reasoning.

quiz.question: What two features motivate dynamic programming?
quiz.answer: Overlapping subproblems and a valid way to combine their solutions through sufficient state.

quiz.question: Does NP-complete mean no instance can be solved quickly?
quiz.answer: No. It concerns worst-case problem-family complexity, not every individual instance.

quiz.question: Why keep a brute-force solver for tiny inputs?
quiz.answer: It provides a simple correctness oracle for testing more sophisticated algorithms.

modules.title: Programming languages, compilers and computability
modules.project: Complete Gate C: a tested C++ simulation plus a tiny expression language with lexer, parser, evaluator, bytecode execution and resource limits.

lessons.title: Language paradigms and type systems
lessons.outcome: Separate language semantics from syntax and implementation habits.
lessons.teach:
Imperative code describes updates; functional style emphasizes expression evaluation and controlled side effects; object-oriented design organizes behavior through objects and interfaces. Real languages combine paradigms. A type system rejects certain invalid combinations according to its rules, but no ordinary type system proves all game requirements.
Static versus dynamic typing concerns when and how types are checked, not a simple ranking of language quality. Ownership-aware languages offer useful comparisons for systems design, while C remains important at binary interfaces and embedded boundaries. Learn enough C syntax and layout rules to read those interfaces, then preserve explicit ownership when calling them from C++.
lessons.example: A pure damage calculation can be tested independently of an imperative combat loop. The two styles cooperate: the loop manages time and effects, while the function computes a value.
lessons.lab: Write one rule in imperative and pure-functional styles, then define a small typed C-compatible interface for a mock subsystem. Pass: state allocation ownership and reject type-invalid expressions in a toy checker.
lessons.reading: R14: language frontend concepts; R11: interfaces and C-style boundary guidance.

quiz.question: Does static typing prove all logical requirements?
quiz.answer: No. It enforces its type rules, which cover only part of correctness.

quiz.question: What advantage does a pure calculation offer tests?
quiz.answer: The same explicit inputs determine the result without hidden state or side effects.

quiz.question: What must a C-compatible ownership boundary specify?
quiz.answer: Who allocates and frees resources, valid lifetimes, error signaling and compatible representations.

lessons.title: Lexing, parsing and syntax trees
lessons.outcome: Convert source text into a structured representation with diagnostics.
lessons.teach:
A lexer groups characters into tokens such as numbers and operators. A parser applies a grammar to produce a syntax tree. Precedence and associativity determine structure: multiplication normally binds more tightly than addition, and subtraction usually groups left-to-right. An evaluator should operate on that structure rather than repeatedly guessing meaning from raw text.
Parsing failures need locations and useful messages. An input can be syntactically valid but semantically invalid, such as referring to an unknown variable. Keep these phases separate enough to test. Never implement a game-data parser by unrestricted execution of input text.
lessons.example: For 2+3*4, the tree has addition at the root and multiplication on the right, yielding 14. Parsing it as (2+3)*4 would yield 20 and violate the chosen precedence.
lessons.lab: Implement tokens, recursive-descent parsing and evaluation for numbers, parentheses and four arithmetic operators. Pass: test precedence, associativity, malformed input, unknown names and division-by-zero policy.
lessons.reading: R14: Kaleidoscope lexer, parser and abstract syntax tree chapters.

quiz.question: What separates lexing from parsing?
quiz.answer: Lexing identifies tokens; parsing organizes tokens according to grammar.

quiz.question: Under ordinary precedence, what is 2+3*4?
Why preserve source locations in a syntax tree?
quiz.answer: They allow later semantic or runtime errors to point back to meaningful user code.

lessons.title: Bytecode, virtual machines and bounded execution
lessons.outcome: Implement a small execution model with explicit limits.
lessons.teach:
A virtual machine executes a defined instruction set in software. A stack machine can use instructions such as push, add and multiply. Compiling an expression tree to bytecode separates source syntax from execution. A VM still needs a specification: stack effects, value types, branch behavior and error conditions.
Scripts and mods must be treated as potentially faulty input. Bound instruction count, memory use and access to host capabilities. A VM is not automatically a secure sandbox; unsafe host functions can defeat isolation. Keep the educational VM offline and limited, and do not equate a few checks with production security review.
lessons.example: The expression 2+3*4 can become PUSH 2, PUSH 3, PUSH 4, MUL, ADD. MUL consumes two values and pushes one, so the stack height drops by one.
lessons.lab: Compile the expression language into stack bytecode and compare results to the tree evaluator. Pass: reject stack underflow, invalid opcodes and over-budget execution; preserve source context for errors.
lessons.reading: R14: code generation and execution concepts; course security requirements.

quiz.question: What is the stack-height change of a binary add that pushes one result?
quiz.answer: Minus one: two values are removed and one is added.

quiz.question: Why compare VM output to the tree evaluator?
quiz.answer: Independent execution paths provide a useful differential check on compilation and interpretation.

quiz.question: Does using bytecode automatically create a secure sandbox?
quiz.answer: No. Host capabilities, memory safety, limits and implementation flaws still determine isolation.

lessons.title: Automata, computability and compiler optimization
lessons.outcome: Know what analysis can establish and when transformation is legal.
lessons.teach:
Finite automata recognize patterns using bounded state. More expressive computation models explain parsing and general programs. Some questions about arbitrary programs, including universal termination, are undecidable. This does not prevent proving termination for restricted programs or enforcing execution budgets.
Compiler optimization must preserve the language's observable semantics under its assumptions. Constant folding, dead-code elimination and inlining are examples, but floating-point reassociation can change results and undefined behavior can invalidate a programmer's intuition. Inspect generated code to learn, not to assume one assembly listing predicts every target. Correctness precedes instruction-count reduction.
lessons.example: Replacing 2+3 by 5 is straightforward for the defined integer literals. Reassociating (a+b)+c into a+(b+c) can change finite-precision floating-point results when magnitudes differ greatly.
lessons.lab: Add constant folding to the toy compiler and test it against the unoptimized evaluator. Pass: include a finite-state recognizer, explain a termination restriction and document transformations deliberately excluded for semantic reasons.
lessons.reading: R14: optimizer support; R06: computation models and proof limitations.

quiz.question: Does undecidability mean no individual program can be proven to terminate?
quiz.answer: No. Many restricted or specific programs admit termination proofs.

quiz.question: Why can floating-point reassociation change a result?
quiz.answer: Rounding occurs after operations, so changing grouping can change which information is lost.

quiz.question: What is the primary correctness condition for an optimization?
quiz.answer: It must preserve the required observable behavior under the language and application assumptions.

modules.title: Processor architecture and assembly
modules.project: Trace a compiled C++ loop through a small assembly example and a cache model. Deliver an instruction/data-flow explanation and a controlled locality experiment.

lessons.title: Instruction sets, registers and calling conventions
lessons.outcome: Read a small machine-level routine without confusing ISA and implementation.
lessons.teach:
An instruction-set architecture defines visible operations, registers and relevant behavior. A microarchitecture implements that contract using particular pipelines, caches and execution units. Different implementations can run the same machine code while achieving different performance. A calling convention specifies how functions pass arguments, preserve registers and return values.
Begin with a small load/store ISA such as the selected RISC-V subset, then compare your host's generated assembly. Do not assume an educational subset implements every extension or privileged feature. Assembly understanding helps explain costs and interoperability, but handwritten assembly is rarely the first optimization step.
lessons.example: A load reads a value from memory into a register; an add combines register values; a store writes a result back. A C++ array loop may contain all three, plus loop-control instructions.
lessons.lab: Annotate a ten-to-twenty-instruction routine with register meanings and memory accesses. Pass: predict its output for two inputs and identify caller/callee responsibilities from the chosen ABI reference.
lessons.reading: R15: Assembly Language and Procedures and Stacks; R35: selected base integer ISA.

quiz.question: How does an ISA differ from a microarchitecture?
quiz.answer: The ISA is the software-visible contract; the microarchitecture is a particular implementation.

quiz.question: What does a calling convention specify?
quiz.answer: Argument/return placement, register preservation and related function-call rules.

quiz.question: Why identify the exact ISA subset in a simulator?
quiz.answer: Unsupported instructions or extensions cannot be assumed to behave like a complete implementation.

lessons.title: Pipelines, dependencies and branch prediction
lessons.outcome: Explain why instruction count alone does not predict latency.
lessons.teach:
A pipeline overlaps stages of multiple instructions. Dependencies can prevent later work from proceeding until earlier results are ready. Modern processors may issue or complete operations out of order while preserving required architectural behavior. Branch prediction speculates about control flow, and mispredictions can discard work.
Throughput measures sustained work per time; latency measures delay for a particular result. A long dependency chain can have poor latency even when the processor can execute many independent operations per cycle. Do not infer performance from clock frequency alone. Instruction mix, memory stalls and available parallelism matter.
lessons.example: Summing one running accumulator creates a dependency chain. Several independent accumulators may expose more instruction-level parallelism, but final combination and numeric-order effects must be considered.
lessons.lab: Compare dependent and independent arithmetic loops while preventing dead-code elimination. Pass: preserve observable results, inspect generated code and explain measured differences as evidence rather than universal CPU facts.
lessons.reading: R15: Pipelining and Performance Measures.

quiz.question: What is a data dependency?
quiz.answer: An operation requires a result produced by an earlier operation.

quiz.question: Does higher clock frequency guarantee a faster program?
quiz.answer: No. Work per cycle, stalls, memory and workload behavior also matter.

quiz.question: Why can extra independent accumulators help?
quiz.answer: They can expose parallel operations instead of one serial dependency chain, subject to resource and numerical constraints.

lessons.title: Caches, locality and memory hierarchy
lessons.outcome: Relate access patterns to cache lines and working sets.
lessons.teach:
Processors use a hierarchy of storage with different capacities and access costs. Caches transfer data in blocks called cache lines. Spatial locality reuses nearby data; temporal locality reuses recently accessed data. A working set is the data actively needed during a phase. Once it exceeds a cache level, behavior can change sharply.
Cache associativity and replacement influence conflicts. A cache miss is not always a main-memory access, because another cache level may satisfy it. Prefetching can help predictable patterns but can also waste bandwidth. Measure several working-set sizes and avoid attributing every slow access to one guessed cache characteristic.
lessons.example: If a hypothetical cache line is 64 bytes and each element is a 4-byte integer, one line can contain 16 consecutive elements when aligned appropriately. A stride of 16 elements can use only one integer from each line.
lessons.lab: Benchmark sequential, strided and randomized access over multiple array sizes. Pass: record assumed versus measured hardware information and explain spatial locality without claiming exact cache behavior from one timing curve.
lessons.reading: R15: Caches and the Memory Hierarchy.

quiz.question: What is spatial locality?
quiz.answer: Accessing data near data that was recently accessed.

quiz.question: How many 4-byte values fit in a hypothetical 64-byte line?
quiz.answer: 16, ignoring boundary misalignment and other storage.

quiz.question: Does every first-level cache miss access DRAM?
quiz.answer: No. Another cache level or other hierarchy component may satisfy it.

lessons.title: Virtual memory, SIMD and architectural limits
lessons.outcome: Recognize address translation and vector execution as separate mechanisms.
lessons.teach:
Virtual addresses belong to a process view; address translation maps them to physical storage subject to permissions. A translation lookaside buffer caches recent translations. Large working sets and access patterns can stress translation independently of ordinary data caches.
Single-instruction multiple-data execution applies operations across several lanes. It benefits suitable regular work but needs attention to alignment, tails, masks and numerical semantics. Vector width is not a guaranteed speedup factor. Some workloads are limited by memory bandwidth or serial dependencies instead. Later co-design lessons will connect these observations to roofline and Amdahl-style limits.
lessons.example: Processing four independent additions in vector lanes can reduce instruction overhead, but loading and storing the same bytes may still dominate. The last three elements of a non-multiple-sized array still require correct handling.
lessons.lab: Inspect compiler vectorization reports for a simple loop and compare aligned/misaligned or tail cases safely. Pass: test lengths 0, 1, lane_width-1 and lane_width+1 and explain translation versus caching.
lessons.reading: R15: Virtual Memory and Parallel Processing; R11: bounds and arithmetic contracts.

quiz.question: What does a TLB cache?
quiz.answer: Virtual-to-physical address translation information and associated access details.

quiz.question: Does four-lane SIMD guarantee a fourfold speedup?
quiz.answer: No. Memory, dependencies, overhead and other resources can limit improvement.

quiz.question: Why test array lengths not divisible by vector width?
quiz.answer: The remainder must be handled without out-of-bounds accesses or omitted elements.

modules.title: Operating systems and resource management
modules.project: Create a systems lab report covering processes, memory, scheduling and file I/O. Use unprivileged programs and disposable data; do not alter kernel or device settings on a primary machine.

lessons.title: Processes, threads, system calls and protection
lessons.outcome: Explain which resources are isolated and which are shared.
lessons.teach:
A process is an execution environment with an address space and operating-system-managed resources. Threads within a process share memory but have their own execution state. A system call requests a kernel service through a controlled boundary. User/kernel separation protects privileged operations; it does not make application code automatically safe.
Process isolation helps contain faults, while threads allow lower-overhead sharing at the cost of synchronization complexity. Starting a worker process, a thread and an asynchronous task are not interchangeable choices. Identify ownership, failure propagation and communication needs before choosing a mechanism.
lessons.example: Two threads can see the same game-state object, creating race risk. Two isolated processes normally need an explicit communication mechanism to exchange equivalent information.
lessons.lab: Write a program that reports its process identity and runs independent worker tasks. Pass: explain what memory is shared in the chosen approach and how worker failure is reported without privileged operations.
lessons.reading: R16: Processes, Process API and Threads.

quiz.question: What do threads in one process typically share?
quiz.answer: The process address space and many resources, while retaining separate execution state.

quiz.question: What is a system call?
quiz.answer: A controlled request from application code for an operating-system kernel service.

quiz.question: Why might processes be preferable to threads for a risky tool?
quiz.answer: Stronger isolation can contain faults, though communication and resource costs may be higher.

lessons.title: Allocation, paging and memory-mapped data
lessons.outcome: Distinguish reserved address space, committed storage and live objects.
lessons.teach:
An allocator manages storage for application objects; the operating system manages virtual memory and backing resources. Reserving an address range is not the same as having every page physically resident. Page faults can occur when access requires additional mapping or data movement. Application allocation behavior and operating-system paging interact but are not identical.
Memory mapping can present file data through an address range, but it still requires lifetime, bounds and error handling. It does not guarantee zero I/O latency. Avoid assuming that freeing an object immediately reduces the process's visible memory usage: an allocator may retain storage for reuse.
lessons.example: A large mapped file can occupy a large virtual range while only accessed pages become resident. Reading a new region can still incur page faults and storage activity.
lessons.lab: Compare sequential file reads with a read-only mapped-file approach on a small disposable file. Pass: verify identical content and report virtual/resident concepts separately without promising one method is faster.
lessons.reading: R16: Address Spaces, Address Translation, Paging and Memory API.

quiz.question: Does reserving virtual address space imply all pages are resident?
quiz.answer: No.

quiz.question: Why may process memory usage stay high after freeing objects?
quiz.answer: The allocator or runtime may retain storage for later reuse rather than returning it immediately to the OS.

quiz.question: Does memory mapping eliminate storage latency?
quiz.answer: No. Access can still trigger page faults and underlying I/O.

lessons.title: Scheduling, responsiveness and real-time constraints
lessons.outcome: Distinguish average completion from meeting a deadline.
lessons.teach:
A scheduler chooses runnable work according to its policy. Context switches have costs, and oversubscription can create contention rather than useful parallelism. Throughput-oriented scheduling is not necessarily suitable for a time-critical audio or input path. Real-time reasoning concerns deadlines and worst-case behavior under stated assumptions.
General desktop operating systems do not make arbitrary user programs hard-real-time merely because a thread has high priority. Priority inversion occurs when high-priority work waits indirectly on lower-priority work holding a needed resource. Design short critical sections and bounded work before experimenting with priorities.
lessons.example: An audio callback needed every few milliseconds can glitch if it waits for a worker holding a mutex during a long file load, even when average CPU usage is low.
lessons.lab: Simulate a scheduler or instrument a bounded producer/consumer workload without changing privileged priorities. Pass: show one contention-induced latency spike and propose a structural fix rather than only raising priority.
lessons.reading: R16: Scheduling, Multi-Level Feedback Queue and Concurrency Bugs.

quiz.question: What is priority inversion?
quiz.answer: Higher-priority work is delayed by lower-priority work through a shared-resource dependency.

quiz.question: Does low average CPU use guarantee deadlines are met?
quiz.answer: No. Bursts, blocking and scheduling delays can still cause misses.

quiz.question: Why avoid blocking I/O in an audio callback?
quiz.answer: Its unpredictable delay can exceed the callback deadline and cause audible interruption.

lessons.title: Filesystems, persistence and asynchronous I/O
lessons.outcome: Design data operations that survive partial failure.
lessons.teach:
A filesystem organizes persistent data and metadata. A successful write call does not always mean data has reached durable storage. Buffering, ordering and crash consistency require explicit treatment when durability matters. A robust save process avoids overwriting the only valid copy with partially generated data.
Asynchronous I/O lets work proceed without blocking the caller, but completion can occur later and fail. Buffers and request objects must remain valid until completion according to the API. Cancellation is a request with a contract, not necessarily immediate erasure of all work. Separate correctness, durability and performance goals.
lessons.example: A common save strategy writes a new temporary file, validates it and performs an appropriate replacement operation. The exact durability guarantee still depends on filesystem/API synchronization and failure assumptions.
lessons.lab: Build a save pipeline with injected failures before, during and after serialization. Pass: recover a valid prior or new save under your documented model and never reuse an asynchronous buffer before completion.
lessons.reading: R16: Files and Directories, Crash Consistency and Journaling.

quiz.question: Does every successful write imply durable storage?
quiz.answer: No. Data may remain buffered unless the required durability operations and guarantees are satisfied.

quiz.question: Why retain an asynchronous I/O buffer until completion?
quiz.answer: The operation may still read or write that storage after the initiating call returns.

quiz.question: What should a save-recovery test inject?
quiz.answer: Partial writes, malformed data, interruption points and replacement failures under an explicit failure model.

modules.title: Concurrency and parallel programming
modules.project: Implement a bounded job system with dependency handling, shutdown, failure propagation and stress tests. Compare one-thread and multi-thread execution on a real workload.

lessons.title: Races, mutexes and happens-before
lessons.outcome: Protect shared invariants using a clear synchronization model.
lessons.teach:
Concurrent execution interleaves operations. A C++ data race occurs when conflicting accesses are not properly ordered and at least one is a write, with the relevant accesses not atomic; this leads to undefined behavior. A race condition is a broader logical timing defect and can exist even when individual accesses are atomic.
A mutex protects a shared invariant only when all relevant participants follow the same locking protocol. The critical section must cover the complete operation that needs to be atomic at the application level. Ownership and message passing can reduce shared mutable state. Document the happens-before relationships rather than relying on "it usually runs first."
lessons.example: Checking balance >= price and then subtracting price in separate unlocked steps can allow two purchases to spend the same funds. Making each field read atomic does not automatically make the whole purchase transaction atomic.
lessons.lab: Implement a shared counter and a compound inventory transaction with proper synchronization. Pass: stress test, inspect with an available race detector and explain why detector silence alone is not proof.
lessons.reading: R11: Concurrency and Parallelism; R16: Locks and Concurrency Bugs.

quiz.question: Can individually atomic reads/writes still form a logical race?
quiz.answer: Yes. A multi-step invariant can be violated by interleaving even when each access is atomic.

quiz.question: What must a mutex protocol protect?
quiz.answer: The entire shared invariant and every conflicting access that participates in it.

quiz.question: Why is "this thread usually runs first" insufficient?
quiz.answer: Scheduling is not the required synchronization guarantee and can change across runs or systems.

lessons.title: Condition variables, deadlocks and cancellation
lessons.outcome: Make waiting and shutdown correct under adverse timing.
lessons.teach:
A condition variable allows a thread to wait for a predicate to become true while coordinating with a mutex. Wait in a loop because wakeups do not by themselves prove the predicate. Notifications and state changes must follow a consistent protocol to avoid missed progress.
Deadlock can arise from circular resource dependencies. A lock-order rule or reduced lock scope can prevent common cases. Shutdown deserves the same rigor as steady-state execution: wake waiters, stop accepting work, define what happens to queued jobs and join threads safely. Cancellation must specify whether work is abandoned, completed or rolled back.
lessons.example: A consumer waits while queue_empty and not stopping. On shutdown, the producer changes stopping under the agreed synchronization and notifies waiters so they can exit even when no work arrives.
lessons.lab: Create a producer/consumer queue with graceful shutdown and failure propagation. Pass: test stopping with an empty queue, a full queue and active consumers; no thread remains blocked indefinitely.
lessons.reading: R16: Condition Variables, Semaphores and Concurrency Bugs; R11: locking guidance.

quiz.question: Why test a condition-variable predicate in a loop?
quiz.answer: Wakeups can be spurious or another thread can consume the condition before the waiter proceeds.

quiz.question: What does a consistent lock order prevent?
quiz.answer: A common source of circular wait and deadlock.

quiz.question: Why must shutdown notify blocked workers?
quiz.answer: Without new work or a notification, they may never observe the stop condition.

lessons.title: Atomics, memory ordering and false sharing
lessons.outcome: Use low-level synchronization only with a complete correctness argument.
lessons.teach:
Atomic operations provide indivisible access according to their type and memory-order rules. Acquire/release synchronization can publish earlier writes when the specified read observes the release sequence appropriately. Relaxed ordering does not provide the same cross-object publication guarantees. Volatile is not a substitute for C++ thread synchronization.
False sharing occurs when independent frequently written data occupy a shared cache line, causing coherence traffic. Padding may help a measured case but increases footprint. Lock-free algorithms also face reclamation and progress issues; an atomic pointer alone does not make referenced storage safe to free. Prefer a proven library design unless low-level implementation is the explicit learning goal.
lessons.example: A producer writes payload, then publishes a ready flag with release ordering; a consumer that observes the corresponding flag with acquire ordering can safely observe the published payload under the complete protocol.
lessons.lab: Write a publication litmus test with a documented happens-before diagram. Measure a padded versus unpadded counter layout. Pass: do not claim stress tests prove memory-model correctness or assume a fixed cache-line size without labeling it.
lessons.reading: R11: atomics and memory model; R16: concurrency; R37: later GPU memory-model comparison.

quiz.question: Is volatile a C++ inter-thread synchronization mechanism?
quiz.answer: No.

quiz.question: What is false sharing?
quiz.answer: Coherence contention caused by independent data sharing a cache line.

quiz.question: Why is freeing a node difficult in lock-free structures?
quiz.answer: Another thread may still hold or access the node; safe reclamation needs a separate protocol.

lessons.title: Task graphs, work stealing and scaling limits
lessons.outcome: Parallelize independent work and measure end-to-end benefit.
lessons.teach:
A task graph expresses jobs and dependencies. Parallel execution is possible among ready tasks that do not conflict. Work stealing distributes queued tasks dynamically, but scheduling overhead can exceed the benefit of tiny jobs. Batch work at a granularity that matches the workload and hardware.
Amdahl's law models the limit from a serial fraction: speedup = 1/(s+(1-s)/p) under its simplifying assumptions. Communication, contention and load imbalance can reduce real speedup further. A job system must handle exceptions, ownership, completion and shutdown, not only start threads. Benchmark the actual simulation rather than an empty task loop.
lessons.example: If 20% of a workload remains serial, an infinite number of ideal workers cannot exceed a 5x speedup. Four ideal workers give 1/(0.2+0.8/4)=2.5x.
lessons.lab: Implement a small task graph for independent entity updates followed by aggregation. Pass: compare 1, 2 and available worker counts, verify results and explain a case where more workers hurt.
lessons.reading: R15: Parallel Processing; R16: concurrency; R11: task-oriented concurrency guidance.

quiz.question: What is the ideal maximum speedup with a 25% serial fraction?
quiz.answer: 4x, since the parallel portion cannot eliminate the remaining 0.25 of runtime.

quiz.question: Why can very small tasks reduce performance?
quiz.answer: Scheduling, synchronization and bookkeeping can cost more than the useful work.

quiz.question: What does a task dependency express?
quiz.answer: A required ordering or data-availability relationship before a dependent task may execute.

modules.title: Networks, storage and data services
modules.project: Build a local-only client/server message exercise and a small relational game-data service. Test malformed framing, transaction rollback and duplicate requests without exposing a public service.

lessons.title: Network layers, latency and transport semantics
lessons.outcome: Choose transport behavior from application requirements.
lessons.teach:
Networks exchange data through layered protocols. IP provides packet delivery without guaranteeing arrival or order. TCP presents a reliable ordered byte stream, not a stream of application messages. UDP preserves datagram boundaries but does not itself supply delivery, ordering or congestion-control behavior. Applications still need explicit protocols.
Latency, jitter, loss and bandwidth describe different constraints. A high-bandwidth link can still have long round-trip delay. Reliable delivery can involve waiting for missing information, which affects real-time design. Use localhost or an authorized lab network for exercises and keep authentication and encryption decisions separate from transport assumptions.
lessons.example: Two send calls over TCP do not guarantee two matching receive calls. The receiver may get part of one message or several messages together and must parse framing correctly.
lessons.lab: Create a localhost client/server exchange with a length-prefixed message. Pass: split one message across several writes and combine several messages in one write; the receiver reconstructs them correctly.
lessons.reading: R17: TCP service and interface semantics; R16: networking context.

quiz.question: Does TCP preserve application message boundaries?
quiz.answer: No. It supplies an ordered byte stream.

quiz.question: Does high bandwidth imply low latency?
quiz.answer: No. Capacity and delay are different properties.

quiz.question: What behavior must an application add when using UDP?
quiz.answer: Whatever reliability, ordering, congestion control, validation and security its requirements need.

lessons.title: Protocol design, serialization and timeouts
lessons.outcome: Treat every received byte as untrusted structured input.
lessons.teach:
A protocol defines message types, fields, ranges, versioning and permitted sequences. Serialization must specify byte order and numeric representation. Validate lengths before allocation and cap total resource use. A checksum can detect some corruption but is not equivalent to cryptographic authentication.
Timeouts handle missing progress, not certainty about remote state. A timed-out operation may have executed remotely even if its response was lost. Request IDs and idempotent operations help manage retries. Compatibility is a design decision: unknown fields and versions should be accepted, ignored or rejected according to a documented rule.
lessons.example: A repeated "add 10 coins" request can duplicate a reward. A request with a unique operation ID and server-side deduplication can avoid applying the same accepted operation twice under the defined retention policy.
lessons.lab: Add versioned framing, maximum sizes, timeout handling and request IDs to the lab protocol. Pass: reject oversized and truncated messages before dangerous allocation and test duplicate delivery.
lessons.reading: R17: transport failure context; R18: transaction and data-integrity foundations.

quiz.question: Does a timeout prove the remote operation never happened?
quiz.answer: No. The operation may have executed while the response was delayed or lost.

quiz.question: Why validate a length before allocating its buffer?
quiz.answer: An attacker or malformed file could request excessive memory or trigger overflow.

quiz.question: What does idempotence mean?
quiz.answer: Repeating an operation has the same intended effect as applying it once.

lessons.title: Relational modeling, SQL and indexes
lessons.outcome: Represent game data with constraints that survive application mistakes.
lessons.teach:
A relational schema defines tables, keys and relationships. A primary key identifies a row; a foreign key constrains references between tables. Normalization reduces certain redundancy and update anomalies, while deliberate denormalization trades simpler reads for additional consistency work.
SQL queries express desired results, but their execution plans determine physical work. An index can accelerate suitable lookups while consuming storage and adding write cost. Parameterized queries separate data from executable query structure. Do not build SQL by concatenating untrusted text, and do not assume an index helps every query.
lessons.example: A players table and an inventory table linked by player_id avoid embedding an unbounded list in a single ambiguous text field. A uniqueness constraint on (player_id,item_id) can enforce one aggregate row per item type.
lessons.lab: Create a small schema with primary, foreign and uniqueness constraints. Use parameterized queries and inspect one indexed query plan. Pass: demonstrate rejected invalid references and compare a query before/after indexing.
lessons.reading: R18: tables, queries, joins, foreign keys and indexes via the linked manual.

quiz.question: What does a foreign key protect?
quiz.answer: A specified relationship by requiring referenced values to exist, subject to its defined rules.

quiz.question: Why can indexes slow writes?
quiz.answer: The index structures must be maintained alongside the table changes.

quiz.question: Why use parameterized SQL?
quiz.answer: It keeps input data separate from SQL structure and prevents common injection mistakes.

lessons.title: Transactions, consistency and distributed failure
lessons.outcome: Preserve invariants when several operations must succeed together.
lessons.teach:
A transaction groups related database work under defined atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability guarantees. Isolation levels differ; applications must understand which anomalies remain possible. A transfer should not debit one account without the corresponding credit. Concurrency can require retries even when each statement is individually correct.
Across multiple services, a local transaction does not automatically create a global one. Partial failure, duplicate messages and stale reads require explicit coordination. Separate durable authoritative data from caches. A cache miss is recoverable; losing the only authoritative record is a different failure. Test the system's invariants under interruption rather than only normal response codes.
lessons.example: Transferring five items between players requires both inventories to change together and total quantity to remain constant. A failure between updates must not destroy or create items.
lessons.lab: Implement an inventory transfer with transactions and forced failure between updates. Pass: verify conservation, rollback and duplicate-request handling; document what is not guaranteed across processes or services.
lessons.reading: R18: Transactions; R16: persistence and failure reasoning.

quiz.question: What does transaction atomicity mean?
quiz.answer: The transaction's changes are treated as all-or-nothing under the database guarantee.

quiz.question: Does a transaction in one database automatically include another service?
quiz.answer: No. Cross-service coordination needs a separate protocol.

quiz.question: What invariant should an item-transfer test preserve?
quiz.answer: Total item quantity, valid nonnegative balances and the intended ownership changes.

modules.title: Engineering practice, security and maintainability
modules.project: Complete Gate D: a reviewed systems application with a design record, threat model, CI-style local test pipeline, dependency inventory and an incident/recovery exercise.

lessons.title: Requirements, architecture and design records
lessons.outcome: Make tradeoffs explicit and trace implementation back to needs.
lessons.teach:
A requirement states an observable need or constraint. Functional requirements describe behavior; quality requirements describe properties such as latency, reliability or accessibility. Architecture allocates responsibilities and dependencies to meet those requirements. A diagram without contracts and failure behavior is not enough.
An architecture decision record states the problem, constraints, alternatives, chosen approach and consequences. Avoid premature distributed systems or custom frameworks when a smaller design meets the need. Revisit decisions when evidence changes. Traceability links requirements to tests and avoids declaring success merely because all planned code was written.
lessons.example: "Loads quickly" is vague. "Loads the defined test level within a chosen threshold on the declared baseline machine, measured from action to usable state" is testable once the threshold and procedure are filled in.
lessons.lab: Write six measurable requirements and two decision records for the simulation. Pass: every requirement has an acceptance test and each decision includes a rejected alternative and a cost.
lessons.reading: R01: Software Engineering; R02: engineering design and professional practice.

quiz.question: What makes a requirement testable?
quiz.answer: Observable behavior, conditions and an explicit acceptance criterion.

quiz.question: Why record rejected alternatives?
quiz.answer: They preserve the reasoning and make future reassessment more informed.

quiz.question: Is completing planned tasks the same as satisfying requirements?
quiz.answer: No. The implemented result must still meet the specified needs and constraints.

lessons.title: Defensive programming and threat modeling
lessons.outcome: Protect assets and trust boundaries before selecting security mechanisms.
lessons.teach:
A threat model identifies assets, actors, entry points, trust boundaries and plausible failures. Game clients, mods, save files and asset importers are not automatically trusted. Validate input, minimize privileges and isolate risky processing. Memory-safe interfaces, bounds checks, fuzzing and sanitizers help address different defect classes.
Authentication establishes an identity or credential; authorization decides permitted actions. Encryption alone does not enforce game rules or protect a compromised endpoint. Use established security libraries rather than inventing cryptography. Perform testing only against your own code or authorized lab targets; the purpose here is defensive engineering.
lessons.example: A client may request a move, but an authoritative server should validate speed and permissions rather than accepting the client's claimed final position as truth.
lessons.lab: Threat-model the save parser and local service. Add bounds checks and a small malformed-input fuzz harness. Pass: cap work/memory, preserve useful errors and record residual risks instead of claiming complete security.
lessons.reading: R01: Security; R11: bounds/lifetime safety; R02: information-security breadth.

quiz.question: How does authorization differ from authentication?
quiz.answer: Authentication concerns identity; authorization concerns allowed actions.

quiz.question: Why is a game client a trust boundary?
quiz.answer: The player controls that environment and can send incorrect or manipulated requests.

quiz.question: Does encryption replace input validation?
quiz.answer: No. Authenticated or encrypted input can still be malformed, malicious or contrary to game rules.

lessons.title: Build automation, dependencies and release discipline
lessons.outcome: Produce a verifiable artifact from a known source revision.
lessons.teach:
Continuous integration runs repeatable checks when changes are made. A useful pipeline builds, tests and reports failures from a clean environment. Pin dependencies sufficiently to reproduce the result and record toolchain versions. A dependency inventory includes origin, version and license obligations; it is not enough to know that a package downloaded successfully.
Separate secrets from source and limit automation permissions. Preserve symbols or diagnostics needed to investigate crashes, while controlling access to sensitive information. A release artifact should be traceable to a commit and build configuration. Automated success is evidence only for the checks actually run.
lessons.example: A release manifest can record source commit, compiler, build type, dependency versions and asset bundle hash. This helps determine whether a reported defect came from the same artifact that was tested.
lessons.lab: Create a local clean-build script that runs tests and produces a versioned archive plus manifest. Pass: run it from a fresh build directory and deliberately break a test to confirm the pipeline stops.
lessons.reading: R05: workflows and tagging; R12: builds and testing; R01: software engineering.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of dependency pinning?
quiz.answer: To reduce uncontrolled version changes and support reproducible builds.

quiz.question: What should identify a release artifact's origin?
quiz.answer: Its source revision, build configuration, toolchain and dependency/asset versions.

quiz.question: Why test a pipeline with an intentional failure?
quiz.answer: To verify it actually blocks bad changes rather than merely displaying success regardless of checks.

lessons.title: Ethics, accessibility, teamwork and sustainable delivery
lessons.outcome: Evaluate engineering decisions beyond code correctness.
lessons.teach:
Engineering work affects players, colleagues and the public. Accessibility, privacy, intellectual property, honest reporting and sustainable maintenance belong in technical decisions. Obtain permission for assets and code and respect the licenses under which they are supplied. Do not assume publicly visible material is free to redistribute.
Teams need clear responsibilities, respectful review and realistic scope. Crunch is not a substitute for planning and can hide systemic delivery problems. A postmortem should identify contributing conditions and improvements, not scapegoats. For hardware, safety and environmental constraints become additional design requirements, not optional polish.
lessons.example: A performance optimization that removes readable subtitles or makes controls non-remappable may violate the product's requirements despite increasing frame rate.
lessons.lab: Run an accessibility review and a blameless failure retrospective on the project. Pass: identify at least three actionable changes, assign acceptance evidence and document third-party attribution honestly.
lessons.reading: R29: input, text, captions and UI guidance; R01/R02: professional and ethical practice.

quiz.question: Does public availability imply permission to redistribute?
quiz.answer: No. Copyright and license terms still govern use.

quiz.question: Why include accessibility in acceptance criteria?
quiz.answer: Otherwise a technically functioning feature may remain unusable for part of the intended audience.

quiz.question: What should a blameless retrospective seek?
quiz.answer: Contributing system/process conditions and practical improvements rather than personal blame.

modules.title: From geometry to a software renderer
modules.project: Build a CPU renderer that writes a portable image file. It must clip geometry, rasterize triangles, resolve visibility and interpolate attributes correctly. Keep it as a reference implementation for future GPU work.

lessons.title: Images, color and coordinate conventions
lessons.outcome: Define the numerical and geometric meaning of an image buffer.
lessons.teach:
An image buffer stores samples on a two-dimensional grid. Its width, height, channel order, stride and origin must be explicit. A row can include padding, so assuming that every row occupies exactly width times bytes-per-pixel can be wrong. A coordinate convention is a contract shared by geometry, cameras, shaders and tools. Record handedness, axis directions, angle units and matrix multiplication order.
Color values also have meaning. Many image assets use a nonlinear transfer function such as sRGB, while lighting and blending generally need appropriate linear-light values. A normalized channel value is not automatically a physical light measurement. Distinguish color data from non-color textures such as normals or roughness. Treating every texture with the same conversion creates subtle rendering errors.
lessons.example: A 320 by 180 image with four 8-bit channels needs 230,400 bytes of tightly packed pixel storage. A normal-map channel is data; decoding it with a color transfer function changes the represented direction.
lessons.lab: Write a PPM image containing a gradient and coordinate markers. Pass: the dimensions, orientation and channel values are verified by tests, and a README states all coordinate and color assumptions.
lessons.reading: R19: image representation and transformations; R23: Radiometry, Spectra, and Color.

quiz.question: Why must image stride be recorded?
quiz.answer: Rows may contain padding or use a layout different from width times bytes per pixel.

quiz.question: How many bytes are in the tightly packed example image?
Should a normal map automatically receive sRGB decoding?
quiz.answer: No. It represents non-color data, so that transformation would corrupt its intended values.

lessons.title: Projection and clipping before perspective division
lessons.outcome: Transform geometry without confusing visibility with division by depth.
lessons.teach:
A vertex moves through object, world, view and clip spaces according to the chosen convention. Homogeneous clip coordinates retain information needed to clip primitives before perspective division. Dividing by w maps into normalized device coordinates, but blindly dividing vertices behind or across the eye plane can produce enormous or inverted triangles.
Clipping computes intersections with the view volume and retains the visible portion of a primitive. After clipping, perform perspective division and viewport mapping. Different graphics APIs use different conventions for depth ranges and related details; do not copy a projection matrix without checking its contract. Test points on planes, beyond planes and near degeneracies. Back-face culling is a separate decision based on winding and orientation.
lessons.example: For a clip-space component x=2 and w=4, x/w=0.5. A triangle with vertices on both sides of a clipping plane must be clipped as a primitive; dropping one outside vertex alone destroys its shape.
lessons.lab: Implement clipping against one plane, then the complete chosen clip volume. Pass: triangles crossing the near plane remain finite and correctly shaped, and tests cover points exactly on the boundary.
lessons.reading: R19: perspective transformations, clipping and the graphics pipeline; R23: Cameras.

quiz.question: Why clip before perspective division?
quiz.answer: Clipping in homogeneous space handles view-volume boundaries and problematic w values before division.

quiz.question: What normalized component follows from x=2 and w=4?
Is deleting every outside vertex a valid triangle-clipping algorithm?
quiz.answer: No. New intersection vertices are generally needed to preserve the visible polygon.

lessons.title: Triangle coverage, depth and perspective-correct interpolation
lessons.outcome: Produce crack-resistant filled triangles with correct varying attributes.
lessons.teach:
Edge functions determine on which side of a triangle edge a sample lies. Their normalized values yield barycentric coordinates, which sum to one for a nondegenerate triangle. A consistent shared-edge rule prevents neighboring triangles from both missing or inconsistently owning a boundary sample. Degenerate triangles need an explicit rejection policy.
A depth buffer resolves visibility according to the chosen depth representation and comparison rule. Screen-space barycentric interpolation of a general surface attribute is not perspective correct. Interpolate attribute divided by clip w and reciprocal w, then divide the interpolated quantities. Depth interpolation has its own pipeline convention; do not substitute an arbitrary world-space distance. Anti-aliasing estimates pixel coverage rather than pretending a pixel is an infinitesimal point.
lessons.example: For screen-space weights lambda_i, an attribute is a=(sum lambda_i*a_i/w_i)/(sum lambda_i/w_i). When all w values are equal, this reduces to ordinary barycentric interpolation.
lessons.lab: Render two triangles sharing an edge and a receding checkerboard. Pass: no cracks under the documented fill rule, correct overlap ordering, and a visible comparison between affine and perspective-correct texture coordinates.
lessons.reading: R19: rasterization, barycentric coordinates and texture mapping; R23: Sampling and Reconstruction.

quiz.question: What is the sum of barycentric coordinates?
quiz.answer: One for the normalized representation of a point relative to a nondegenerate triangle.

quiz.question: When does perspective-correct interpolation reduce to affine interpolation?
quiz.answer: When all relevant clip w values are equal.

quiz.question: Why specify a shared-edge coverage rule?
quiz.answer: To assign boundary samples consistently and avoid cracks or inconsistent double ownership.

lessons.title: Rays, intersections and acceleration structures
lessons.outcome: Build a second visibility method and compare its costs with rasterization.
lessons.teach:
A ray has origin o and direction d, with points r(t)=o+t*d over a stated interval. The nearest valid positive intersection usually determines a primary visible surface. Directions need not be normalized mathematically, but t is a distance only under suitable normalization and units. Robust intersection tests handle parallel directions, boundary cases and floating-point error.
A bounding-volume hierarchy groups primitives under conservative bounds. Traversal rejects entire groups whose bounds the ray misses. Construction cost, traversal cost, memory and update behavior all matter. An acceleration structure is not a promise of logarithmic worst-case work; difficult overlap can degrade it. Use the brute-force renderer as a correctness oracle before optimizing traversal.
lessons.example: If o=(0,0,0), d=(0,0,2) and t=3, the ray point is (0,0,6); t is not the traveled distance because d has length 2.
lessons.lab: Implement sphere or triangle intersections and a small BVH. Pass: accelerated and brute-force results agree within a defined tolerance over randomized rays, including misses and grazing cases; report build and query costs separately.
lessons.reading: R23: Shapes and Primitives and Intersection Acceleration.

quiz.question: When is ray parameter t directly a distance?
quiz.answer: When direction has unit length and the coordinate units represent that distance.

quiz.question: What point occurs in the worked example at t=3?
Why retain the brute-force implementation?
quiz.answer: It provides a simple reference for testing the accelerated implementation and measuring whether acceleration helps.

modules.title: Explicit GPU programming and graphics APIs
modules.prerequisites: Module 21 plus Modules 18 and 20. Choose one compatible backend, not all at once.
modules.project: Implement a GPU backend for the reference scene. Query device capabilities, enable available validation, document the toolchain and handle resize and shutdown safely. A CPU backend remains a valid fallback while hardware access is arranged.

lessons.title: GPU work submission, resources and pipeline state
lessons.outcome: Separate CPU recording from asynchronous GPU execution.
lessons.teach:
A graphics API lets software describe resources, pipeline state and work for a GPU. The CPU records or encodes commands, then submits them to queues. Submission does not imply immediate completion. The GPU can still be reading data after the CPU has moved to the next frame. This separation is the central source of lifetime and synchronization mistakes.
A pipeline combines programmable stages with fixed-function configuration and resource interfaces. Vulkan, Direct3D 12 and Metal expose related concepts through different contracts; learning one does not make their details interchangeable. Use the API documentation for the installed version and the selected device. Current tutorial feature requirements must be checked, especially on compatibility layers. Start with a minimal scene before adopting a large abstraction framework.
lessons.example: Recording a draw that references a vertex buffer does not copy the entire buffer into the command stream. Destroying that buffer immediately after submission can invalidate in-flight work.
lessons.lab: Create a window or offscreen target and report supported capabilities. Pass: render a clear color, capture validation output and explain which objects belong to CPU recording versus GPU execution.
lessons.reading: R21: Introduction and Drawing a Triangle; alternatively R24 or R25 for one native platform; R22: SDL3 platform setup.

quiz.question: Does queue submission mean the GPU has finished?
quiz.answer: No. Work normally executes asynchronously.

quiz.question: Why can immediate buffer destruction be unsafe?
quiz.answer: Submitted GPU commands may still reference it.

quiz.question: Must a beginner implement three graphics APIs simultaneously?
