quiz.answer: No. One capability-compatible backend plus clear interfaces is the intended first step.

lessons.title: Buffers, shaders, layouts and resource binding
lessons.outcome: Match data representations across CPU and GPU boundaries.
lessons.teach:
Buffers contain bytes; shaders interpret those bytes according to a declared layout. Alignment, padding, matrix convention and element stride must agree between host code and shader code. A C++ structure that looks similar to a shader structure is not proof of binary compatibility. Use explicit offsets or verified layout rules and test small diagnostic values.
Resource binding tells a shader which buffers, textures and samplers it can access. Binding indices and lifetime form an interface contract. Vertex and fragment stages execute with different inputs and responsibilities. Compute shaders are a more general work-dispatch path but still need defined indexing and bounds. Out-of-range threads often occur when dispatch dimensions are rounded upward; guard them rather than assuming exact divisibility.
lessons.example: A workload of 1,000 elements dispatched in groups of 64 needs 16 groups, creating 1,024 logical invocations. The last 24 must not access elements beyond index 999.
lessons.lab: Upload a transform and vertex colors, then add a bounded compute operation. Pass: host/shader layouts are documented, a readback test checks results, and non-multiple work sizes remain correct.
lessons.reading: R21: vertex buffers, uniform buffers and compute; R37: execution configuration and memory organization, only for the optional CUDA route.

quiz.question: Why can matching field names still produce a layout bug?
quiz.answer: The host and shader can apply different padding, alignment or matrix-layout rules.

quiz.question: How many 64-thread groups cover 1,000 elements?
quiz.answer: 16, with bounds checks for 24 excess invocations.

quiz.question: What does a resource binding establish?
quiz.answer: Which resource a shader interface can access, under the API and lifetime contract.

lessons.title: Synchronization, hazards and frames in flight
lessons.outcome: Express dependencies without serializing the entire renderer.
lessons.teach:
A hazard occurs when operations access the same resource in an incompatible order, such as reading before a prior write becomes available and visible. Execution ordering and memory visibility are related but distinct requirements. Barriers, events, semaphores or fences serve different roles depending on the API. Learn their exact scope rather than treating every synchronization primitive as a universal wait.
Frames in flight improve overlap but increase the number of live resources and potentially latency. Per-frame allocations cannot be recycled until the relevant work is complete. A CPU-wide wait after every command may hide a bug while destroying concurrency. First write down the producer, consumer, resource state and required ordering; then choose the narrowest correct mechanism.
lessons.example: A compute pass writes positions and a later draw reads them as vertex data. Correctness requires the appropriate dependency and visibility for that resource, not merely placing source-code statements next to each other.
lessons.lab: Implement a compute-to-draw dependency and two reusable frame contexts. Pass: validation reports no relevant hazards and a stress test never resets a context still used by the GPU.
lessons.reading: R21: synchronization, frames in flight and resource transitions; use R24 or R25 equivalents for the selected backend.

quiz.question: Are execution ordering and memory visibility identical?
quiz.answer: No. Correct synchronization must satisfy the relevant requirements for both.

quiz.question: When may a frame context be reused?
quiz.answer: After the work that references its resources has completed according to the API contract.

quiz.question: Why is waiting for the whole GPU after each command a poor final design?
quiz.answer: It can conceal missing dependencies while eliminating useful overlap and increasing overhead.

lessons.title: Presentation, resizing and device capability policy
lessons.outcome: Treat the window system as a changing environment rather than a fixed image.
lessons.teach:
Presentation connects rendered images to a display surface. The set of presentation images, formats and modes is constrained by the platform and device. A window can resize, become minimized or lose its surface. Rebuilding size-dependent resources requires coordination with in-flight work. A zero-sized drawable should not trigger invalid allocations or divide-by-zero camera calculations.
Define a feature policy: required capabilities, optional enhancements and a fallback. Record why a device is unsupported instead of failing with an obscure assertion. Device errors must preserve useful diagnostics; recovery strategy can range from a clear restart request to a tested rebuild. Keep platform services behind a small interface, while acknowledging that platform-specific behavior cannot always be abstracted away.
lessons.example: A minimized window can report a drawable size of zero. The application should suspend or skip size-dependent rendering until a usable size returns, rather than allocating a zero-height depth target.
lessons.lab: Stress resize, minimize, restore and orderly shutdown. Pass: no stale size-dependent resources, no division by zero, and a readable capability report explains enabled features and fallbacks.
lessons.reading: R21: swapchain recreation and device selection; R22: window events; R24 or R25: presentation and resource lifetime.

quiz.question: Why can resizing require more than changing the viewport?
quiz.answer: Depth images, presentation images and other size-dependent resources may also need safe recreation.

quiz.question: What should happen for a zero-height drawable?
quiz.answer: Skip or suspend dependent rendering and avoid invalid allocation or division.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of an explicit feature policy?
quiz.answer: To distinguish requirements, optional enhancements and fallbacks, making compatibility predictable.

modules.title: Lighting, materials and real-time image quality
modules.project: Create a material-and-lighting demonstration with a documented color pipeline. Compare image quality and frame cost at identical resolution and scene content; include reference images, not only attractive screenshots.

lessons.title: Radiometry, reflectance and physically based materials
lessons.outcome: Explain how lighting models approximate light transport.
lessons.teach:
Radiometry gives precise meanings to quantities such as radiant flux, irradiance and radiance. A bidirectional reflectance distribution function describes how incoming light contributes to outgoing light at a surface. Physically motivated models respect appropriate energy and reciprocity constraints, although real-time implementations often introduce approximations.
A material parameter is meaningful only within its model and encoding. Roughness controls a distribution of microscopic surface orientations in common microfacet models; it is not simply a blur slider. Metallic and dielectric materials have different reflectance behavior. Normals, tangent frames and units must agree. A plausible image can still be numerically or physically inconsistent, so test simple controlled scenes before judging a complex one.
lessons.example: For an ideal diffuse surface, the Lambertian BRDF is reflectance divided by pi. Increasing reflectance beyond one would violate the intended passive energy-conservation interpretation.
lessons.lab: Implement diffuse lighting and one documented microfacet model. Pass: test a constant environment, grazing angles and roughness limits, and state approximations rather than labeling any shiny shader physically exact.
lessons.reading: R23: Radiometry, Reflection Models and Light Transport; R19: shading.

quiz.question: What does a BRDF relate?
quiz.answer: Incoming illumination direction and outgoing reflected radiance direction at a surface, under its formal definition.

quiz.question: What is the Lambertian BRDF for reflectance rho?
quiz.answer: rho/pi.

quiz.question: Why document roughness encoding?
quiz.answer: The numerical value depends on the model and parameter mapping, so incompatible encodings change appearance.

lessons.title: Textures, mipmaps, filtering and tangent-space detail
lessons.outcome: Control aliasing while preserving the meaning of texture data.
lessons.teach:
Textures are sampled signals attached to geometry. When many source texels cover one output pixel, selecting a single texel aliases. Mipmaps prefilter a hierarchy of resolutions; sampling chooses suitable levels and combines samples according to the filtering method. Anisotropic footprints require more than a single isotropic level to preserve oblique detail.
Generate filtered color in an appropriate linear representation, and treat normal or data maps according to their semantics. Tangent-space normal mapping depends on a consistent tangent basis, handedness and mesh UVs. Seams, mirrored UVs and degenerate triangles are valuable tests. Compression trades storage and bandwidth for error; evaluate error in use, not only as a file-size ratio.
lessons.example: A 256 by 256 base texture contains 65,536 texels. A complete power-of-two mip chain adds about one third as many texels beyond the base, approaching four thirds of the base total.
lessons.lab: Render a receding textured floor with and without mipmaps and inspect a normal-mapped seam. Pass: report texture storage including mip levels and explain why non-color data needs its own filtering policy.
lessons.reading: R23: Textures and Sampling and Reconstruction; R21: texture images, samplers and mipmaps.

quiz.question: What problem do mipmaps primarily address?
quiz.answer: Efficient prefiltering for minification, reducing aliasing when many texels map to a pixel.

quiz.question: What is the approximate total mip-chain storage factor?
quiz.answer: Four thirds of the base level for a full large two-dimensional power-of-two chain.

quiz.question: Why can mirrored UVs break normal mapping?
quiz.answer: They can change tangent-frame handedness unless the basis and encoding account for it.

lessons.title: Shadows, light selection and rendering-path tradeoffs
lessons.outcome: Choose a lighting architecture from scene and bandwidth requirements.
lessons.teach:
A shadow map stores depth from a light viewpoint, allowing a later surface sample to test visibility. Resolution, bias and filtering introduce tradeoffs: too little bias causes self-shadow artifacts, while too much separates shadows from contact. A ray-traced visibility query has different costs and artifacts, not automatic perfection.
Forward rendering evaluates material shading while drawing geometry. Deferred approaches store intermediate surface information and light it later, trading bandwidth and storage for different lighting behavior. Tiled or clustered light selection limits which lights a region considers. Transparency, multisampling, material diversity and platform bandwidth affect the choice. Count bytes and work rather than selecting a path because a large studio uses it.
lessons.example: A hypothetical 1,920 by 1,080 G-buffer with 16 bytes per pixel occupies about 33.2 MB for one set of attachments, before depth, extra buffers or repeated reads and writes.
lessons.lab: Implement shadow mapping and compare a simple forward path with tiled light selection or a small deferred prototype. Pass: disclose buffer sizes, light counts, transparency limitations and measured frame costs.
lessons.reading: R19: real-time rendering and shadows; R23: Lights and Light Transport.

quiz.question: Why can excessive shadow bias be visible?
quiz.answer: It can detach the apparent shadow from the casting or receiving surface.

quiz.question: Does deferred rendering remove bandwidth cost?
quiz.answer: No. Writing and reading intermediate surface buffers can consume substantial bandwidth.

quiz.question: What determines whether clustered lighting helps?
quiz.answer: Scene light distribution, overlap, setup cost, shading work and the target hardware, measured under a defined workload.

lessons.title: HDR, tone mapping, temporal reconstruction and validation
lessons.outcome: Separate display mapping from reconstruction and simulation correctness.
lessons.teach:
High-dynamic-range rendering retains scene values beyond a narrow display range. Tone mapping converts those values for a target presentation, while exposure controls the chosen scale. These are not substitutes for correct lighting units or color conversion. Display capabilities and output formats must be handled explicitly.
Temporal techniques reuse earlier samples, often after motion-based reprojection. History can reduce noise or aliasing but can also create ghosting when visibility changes or motion vectors are wrong. Detect invalid history, including disocclusion and camera cuts. A single still screenshot misses temporal artifacts. Evaluate moving sequences, latency, stability and error against a suitable reference. An image-quality metric is evidence, not a complete description of perceptual quality.
lessons.example: A newly revealed background pixel has no valid previous foreground history. Reusing that history without rejection can leave a trailing silhouette even when each individual frame is numerically finite.
lessons.lab: Add exposure, a documented tone mapper and a basic temporal accumulation experiment. Pass: capture a camera cut and disocclusion test, show failure modes, and compare both still-image error and motion behavior.
lessons.reading: R23: Film and Imaging and Sampling; R19: anti-aliasing and image processing.

quiz.question: Are tone mapping and correct light transport the same task?
quiz.answer: No. Tone mapping maps rendered values toward a display representation.

quiz.question: Why reject history at a camera cut?
quiz.answer: The previous frame generally no longer corresponds to the current visibility and coordinates.

quiz.question: Why are still screenshots insufficient for temporal methods?
quiz.answer: Ghosting, instability and delayed response are properties of sequences, not only isolated frames.

modules.title: Engine architecture, simulation and resource ownership
modules.project: Build a small engine with a fixed-step world, generational entity handles, explicit resource ownership and an inspectable task graph. Keep the game rules separate enough to run automated headless tests.

lessons.title: Fixed updates, interpolation and overload policy
lessons.outcome: Separate simulation time from rendering time and real elapsed time.
lessons.teach:
A fixed-step simulation advances by a chosen interval, while rendering may occur at a different rate. An accumulator collects elapsed time and runs enough simulation steps to catch up. Rendering can interpolate between stored simulation states using the leftover fraction. This improves presentation smoothness without changing the simulation step itself.
The system needs an overload policy. An unbounded catch-up loop can consume more time than it recovers. Capping work, dropping accumulated time or reducing quality have different consequences and must be documented. Fixed stepping alone does not guarantee deterministic results: input timing, floating-point behavior, iteration order and parallel execution can still differ. Keep wall-clock measurement outside the deterministic state transition where possible.
lessons.example: With a 10 ms simulation step and 25 ms accumulated, two updates consume 20 ms and leave 5 ms. The interpolation fraction is 0.5 between the relevant stored states.
lessons.lab: Implement an accumulator loop and inject long frames. Pass: simulation advances consistently under normal load, interpolation is bounded, and the overload behavior is tested rather than silently spiraling.
lessons.reading: R27: Fix Your Timestep!; R20: game loops and timing. Use the article as a starting model, not a guarantee of determinism.

quiz.question: What fraction remains after two 10 ms steps from 25 ms?
Does a fixed timestep alone guarantee determinism?
quiz.answer: No. Other ordering, input and numerical differences can still change results.

quiz.question: Why must catch-up work be bounded or otherwise controlled?
quiz.answer: An overloaded system can spend all its time catching up and fall further behind.

lessons.title: Entities, components, handles and data-oriented storage
lessons.outcome: Design identity separately from memory location.
lessons.teach:
An entity is an identity to which state can be attached. A component represents a category of data or behavior according to the chosen architecture. An entity-component-system design is useful when it improves iteration, separation and tooling; it is not a universal requirement for every object.
A handle can contain a slot index and a generation counter. Reusing a slot changes its generation, allowing stale handles to be rejected. Raw pointers into moving arrays cannot provide the same safety automatically. Sparse sets, archetype chunks and ordinary arrays have different iteration and mutation costs. Structural changes during iteration require a policy, such as deferred commands. Evaluate representative access patterns rather than maximizing architectural complexity.
lessons.example: Handle (slot 7, generation 3) must not refer to a new entity placed in slot 7 with generation 4. Matching the index alone would mistakenly resurrect a destroyed identity.
lessons.lab: Implement a small generational entity store with two components and deferred destruction. Pass: stale handles fail safely, iteration survives queued changes, and benchmarks include creation, deletion and common queries.
lessons.reading: R20: game-state organization; R26: gameplay architecture for comparison; R11: lifetime and interface guidance.

quiz.question: Why separate identity from an object address?
quiz.answer: Objects can move or storage can be reused while logical identity must remain controlled.

quiz.question: Is handle (7,3) valid for a slot now at generation 4?
quiz.answer: No.

quiz.question: Why defer structural changes during a component iteration?
quiz.answer: Immediate changes can invalidate iterators or alter which elements are visited.

lessons.title: Allocators, task graphs and frame-resource lifetime
lessons.outcome: Make temporary storage and parallel dependencies observable.
lessons.teach:
Arena allocation groups objects with a shared lifetime and can make allocation and reset inexpensive. It is safe only when no surviving references point into reset storage. A frame arena may outlive the CPU frame when asynchronous jobs or the GPU still reference it. Allocation strategy follows lifetime, not the other way around.
A task graph declares dependencies among units of work. A frame graph can additionally describe resource reads and writes so ordering, transient allocation and synchronization can be derived. Hidden global state defeats this model. Start with a correct serial execution of the graph, then parallelize independent work. Instrument queue delay, execution duration and critical-path length rather than reporting only total task count.
lessons.example: Tasks A and B can run concurrently, but C reading both outputs waits for both. Adding more workers cannot shorten C or remove that dependency.
lessons.lab: Create a serial-then-parallel task graph and a checked temporary arena. Pass: resetting live storage is detected in tests, dependency order is verified, and the critical path is identified from a trace.
lessons.reading: R11: ownership and concurrency; R20: engine architecture; R26: engine systems as a comparative implementation.

quiz.question: When is resetting an arena safe?
quiz.answer: When no live operation or object still relies on its contents.

quiz.question: Can task C consume A before A has completed its required output?
quiz.answer: No. The dependency and visibility requirements must be satisfied.

quiz.question: Why implement a serial graph executor first?
quiz.answer: It provides a simpler correctness baseline before scheduling and synchronization add complexity.

lessons.title: Subsystem boundaries, save formats and reloadability
lessons.outcome: Choose interfaces that make change and failure manageable.
lessons.teach:
An engine subsystem should expose a small contract for initialization, updates, resource ownership and shutdown. Avoid a global manager that silently depends on every other manager. Explicit dependency order makes partial initialization failure and test construction easier to reason about. A plugin boundary adds binary and versioning constraints beyond ordinary source-level interfaces.
Save data should represent durable game meaning rather than raw memory addresses or accidental object layout. Version formats, validate input and define migration or rejection behavior. Hot reload is especially difficult when code, layouts or resources change while old references remain. A safe educational implementation can stop the world, unload controlled state and rebuild it rather than pretending arbitrary live code replacement is simple.
lessons.example: A saved entity reference uses a stable serialized identifier and a reconstruction table, not a pointer value from the previous process. A missing referenced asset needs a fallback or explicit error.
lessons.lab: Add versioned saves and one reloadable asset type. Pass: old supported data migrates, malformed data is rejected without partial world corruption, and subsystem shutdown works after injected initialization failure.
lessons.reading: R20: resource management and tools; R26: serialization and gameplay architecture; R11: interfaces and error handling.

quiz.question: Why is a raw memory pointer unsuitable for a durable save?
quiz.answer: The address has no stable meaning in a later process and may expose unsafe or invalid state.

quiz.question: What must a format version enable?
quiz.answer: An explicit compatibility decision, migration path or clear rejection.

quiz.question: Why test partial initialization failure?
quiz.answer: Shutdown must safely release only resources that were successfully acquired.

modules.title: Asset pipelines, editors and an integrated engine
modules.prerequisites: Module 24 and the software-engineering practices of Module 20.
modules.project: Gate E: deliver a small 3D engine demonstration with an asset cooker, reproducible scene, inspector, save/load, diagnostics and a measured frame/memory budget. A second person must build and run it from the README.

lessons.title: Importing, cooking and content-addressed asset builds
lessons.outcome: Treat assets as compiled inputs with dependency tracking.
lessons.teach:
Authoring assets prioritize editability; runtime assets prioritize loading and execution. An importer reads a source representation, while a cooker transforms it into a platform-appropriate runtime form. The build result depends on source bytes, settings, tool version and dependencies. Caching only by filename can return stale or incorrect output.
A content-addressed key can combine these inputs into a digest. Dependency graphs determine what must be rebuilt after a change. Reproducibility requires stable ordering and controlled metadata, not only hashing the final file. Validate imported geometry, dimensions and resource limits because assets are untrusted inputs. Keep source provenance and license information with the pipeline rather than rediscovering it before release.
lessons.example: Changing a texture compression setting must invalidate the cooked texture even when the original PNG is unchanged. Otherwise the cache key is missing a meaningful input.
lessons.lab: Build a cooker for one mesh and one image representation. Pass: identical declared inputs reproduce the same result, changed settings invalidate the cache, and corrupted sources produce readable failures.
lessons.reading: R20: asset pipelines; R26: asset management and content tools. Apply Module 20 dependency and provenance practices.

quiz.question: Why distinguish source assets from runtime assets?
quiz.answer: Their editing, storage, validation and loading requirements differ.

quiz.question: Must a compression-setting change invalidate a cached build?
quiz.answer: Yes, because it changes the transformation result.

quiz.question: Why include tool version in a cache key?
quiz.answer: A tool change can alter output even when source content is unchanged.

lessons.title: Streaming, residency and memory budgets
lessons.outcome: Load content without allowing asynchronous work to violate ownership.
lessons.teach:
Streaming moves needed content through storage, CPU memory and device memory under a budget. An asset can be requested, loading, decoded, uploaded, resident or failed. Model these states explicitly. A cancellation request must not leave callbacks writing into destroyed owners. Residency policy chooses what remains available when total demand exceeds the budget.
Peak memory matters: compressed input, decoded staging data and final GPU resources can temporarily coexist. Loading one asset at a time is not always sufficient if each individual asset is too large. Level of detail and fallback resources can preserve responsiveness while content is incomplete. Measure misses, stalls and quality changes under controlled constrained budgets.
lessons.example: A 20 MB compressed asset may expand to 100 MB and require another staging copy. Budgeting only the on-disk size substantially understates the transient memory requirement.
lessons.lab: Implement a bounded streaming queue with placeholder assets and cancellation. Pass: a forced small budget produces graceful fallback, no use-after-free, and a report of peak rather than only steady-state memory.
lessons.reading: R20: resource loading; R26: asset management, asynchronous loading and streaming concepts.

quiz.question: Why is compressed file size not the complete memory budget?
quiz.answer: Decoded, staging and final resources may be larger and coexist.

quiz.question: What should rendering do while an optional asset is unavailable?
quiz.answer: Use a defined fallback or deferred behavior rather than dereferencing missing data.

quiz.question: Why model loading as explicit states?
quiz.answer: It makes transitions, failures, cancellation and ownership testable.

lessons.title: Editors, inspection and undoable commands
lessons.outcome: Make engine state understandable and safely editable.
lessons.teach:
An editor is a program for manipulating structured state, not merely a collection of buttons. Separate the document or scene model from its views. Commands can capture reversible changes for undo and redo. Some operations are not trivially reversible, so record enough prior state or use a well-defined transaction.
Inspection tools expose entity identity, transforms, resources, timings and errors. Good tools shorten debugging loops and let non-programmers test assumptions. Input focus matters when an editor and game view share keys. Changes made during a running simulation need a policy: transient preview, committed authoring change or explicit rejection. Keep data validation active in tools; editor-generated data can still be invalid.
lessons.example: A move command can store the entity identifier, old transform and new transform. Undo restores the old transform only if the target identity remains valid under the editor contract.
lessons.lab: Create a scene inspector with transform editing and a ten-command undo/redo test. Pass: invalid inputs are rejected, focus does not trigger unintended gameplay, and save/reload preserves committed changes.
lessons.reading: R20: game tools; R26: editor and reflection concepts. Use a minimal UI toolkit appropriate to the selected platform.

quiz.question: What is the model/view distinction useful for?
quiz.answer: It separates underlying document state from the interface used to display and edit it.

quiz.question: What data can make a transform move reversible?
quiz.answer: The target identity and both the old and new transforms.

quiz.question: Why distinguish preview state from committed authoring state?
quiz.answer: Otherwise running or stopping a simulation can unpredictably overwrite the intended scene.

lessons.title: Engine integration and reproducible demonstration
lessons.outcome: Deliver a small complete system whose limitations are measurable.
lessons.teach:
Integration exposes mismatched assumptions that isolated components hide: units, coordinate systems, thread ownership, asset versions and shutdown order. A useful milestone freezes a small scene and tests the complete path from source assets to presentation. It is better to finish a constrained engine than to accumulate disconnected advanced features.
Define a target machine and operating conditions before claiming a frame budget. Report CPU and GPU timings separately where available, plus resolution, scene counts, build mode and peak memory. Use percentiles or time-series evidence to reveal stutter. A successful demonstration also needs clear controls, error messages and a clean build process. Reviewers should be able to reproduce the result without undocumented files on the author's computer.
lessons.example: A claimed 60 frames per second implies a 16.67 ms frame interval, but an average of 16 ms can still hide repeated 60 ms stalls. The distribution matters to the declared experience.
lessons.lab: Complete Gate E using the project specification in the handbook. Pass: another person follows the README, a headless test scene passes, all assets have provenance, and a limitations section identifies remaining correctness or performance risks.
lessons.reading: R20: project completion; R26: profiling and engine architecture comparison; revisit Module 20 release and review practices.

quiz.question: What frame interval corresponds to 60 frames per second?
quiz.answer: 1/60 second, approximately 16.67 ms.

quiz.question: Why report more than average frame time?
quiz.answer: Averages can conceal stalls and unstable responsiveness.

quiz.question: What does a clean-machine build test reveal?
quiz.answer: Missing dependencies, undeclared assets, environment assumptions and incomplete instructions.

modules.title: Collision detection and physical simulation
modules.project: Build a deterministic test harness for a small physics scene, compare your simple implementation with a maintained physics library, and record precisely which physical and numerical assumptions differ.

lessons.title: Broad phase, narrow phase and geometric robustness
lessons.outcome: Separate possible collisions from confirmed contacts.
lessons.teach:
A collision system first identifies potentially interacting pairs, then performs more expensive geometric tests. The broad phase must be conservative: extra candidate pairs cost time, but missing a real collision breaks correctness. Spatial grids, sweep-and-prune and bounding-volume hierarchies suit different distributions and movement patterns.
The narrow phase determines actual overlap or separation and, when needed, contact positions and normals. Contact normal orientation is an interface contract. Touching, overlapping and nearly parallel configurations need deliberate tolerance policies. Floating-point tolerances should relate to scale and purpose, not an unexplained universal constant. Keep a brute-force pair generator as an oracle for small tests before optimizing.
lessons.example: For 100 objects, checking every unordered pair requires 100 x 99 / 2 = 4,950 pair tests. A broad phase helps only if its maintenance cost and candidate count are favorable for the scene.
lessons.lab: Implement a grid broad phase and circle or box narrow phase. Pass: no true pairs are omitted compared with brute force over randomized scenes, and boundary-touching behavior is documented.
lessons.reading: R28: collision module, shapes and broad-phase concepts; R19: geometry and collision.

quiz.question: May a correct broad phase return false positives?
quiz.answer: Yes. Narrow-phase tests can reject them; false negatives are the dangerous case.

quiz.question: How many unordered pairs exist for 100 objects?
Why document contact-normal orientation?
quiz.answer: Impulse and separation calculations depend on a consistent direction between the two bodies.

lessons.title: Rigid bodies, angular motion and collision impulses
lessons.outcome: Use conservation laws with explicit approximations.
lessons.teach:
A rigid-body model represents position, orientation, linear velocity and angular velocity without modeling deformation. Mass relates force to linear acceleration, while an inertia tensor relates torque and angular acceleration under the chosen frame conventions. Off-center forces and impulses can change rotation as well as translation.
Collision impulses change velocity over an idealized short event. For a frictionless one-dimensional collision, restitution controls the ratio of separating to approaching relative speed under the model. Friction constrains tangential impulses and requires care around resting contact. Infinite-mass or static bodies are commonly represented through zero inverse mass rather than numerical infinity. Conservation tests are powerful when applied to scenarios that actually satisfy the assumptions.
lessons.example: A 2 kg body receiving a 6 N*s impulse through its center changes velocity by 3 m/s. The same impulse away from its center also changes angular momentum.
lessons.lab: Implement center-of-mass impulses and a simple rotational case. Pass: momentum is conserved in isolated tests within tolerance, static bodies remain fixed, and energy behavior matches the chosen restitution model.
lessons.reading: R28: rigid bodies, contacts and simulation; R19: physical simulation.

quiz.question: What velocity change follows from 6 N*s applied to 2 kg?
quiz.answer: 3 m/s in the impulse direction.

quiz.question: Why can an off-center impulse cause rotation?
quiz.answer: It changes angular momentum through the lever arm relative to the center of mass.

quiz.question: Why use zero inverse mass for a static body?
quiz.answer: It naturally produces no velocity change under impulse calculations without relying on infinite numerical values.

lessons.title: Constraints, iterative solvers and continuous collision detection
lessons.outcome: Explain where discrete simulation fails and how solvers control error.
lessons.teach:
A constraint restricts allowed motion, such as maintaining a joint distance or preventing interpenetration. Iterative solvers repeatedly reduce constraint error using local updates. The number of iterations, ordering, timestep and warm starting influence convergence and apparent stiffness. A stable-looking scene is not proof of exact constraint satisfaction.
Discrete collision detection samples configurations at steps and can miss an object passing completely through a thin obstacle. Continuous methods examine motion over an interval or estimate a time of impact. They require motion assumptions and add cost. Use them selectively where speed and geometry justify them. Position correction should not silently create unbounded energy or conceal a broken velocity solver.
lessons.example: An object moving 30 m/s travels 0.5 m during a 1/60 s step. A wall much thinner than that can be crossed between sampled positions without either endpoint overlapping.
lessons.lab: Create a fast-projectile tunneling test and a short chain of constraints. Pass: a continuous or swept test catches the projectile, and a plot or table shows constraint error versus iteration count and timestep.
lessons.reading: R28: joints, solver settings and continuous collision; R19: numerical simulation.

quiz.question: How far does 30 m/s travel in 1/60 second?
Why can increasing solver iterations help?
quiz.answer: It can reduce residual constraint error, though cost rises and other modeling problems can remain.

quiz.question: Does CCD remove every numerical simulation problem?
quiz.answer: No. It addresses certain between-step collision failures under its motion and solver assumptions.

lessons.title: Physics testing, determinism and engine integration
lessons.outcome: Validate simulation with invariants and adversarial scenes.
lessons.teach:
Physics tests should include resting stacks, extreme but supported mass ratios, repeated contacts, long runtimes and objects entering or leaving the world. Define units and supported scales before tuning. NaNs or exploding positions should produce a diagnostic near their origin, not only a later renderer crash.
Deterministic replay requires control of ordering, arithmetic assumptions, random sources and inputs. Bitwise determinism across platforms is a stronger requirement than visually similar behavior on one machine. A library can have explicit determinism limits; record them. Compare analytic solutions where available and use convergence studies elsewhere. Integration tests must verify that rendering interpolation, collision events and entity destruction do not violate the physics system's lifetime rules.
lessons.example: A freely moving body with no force should maintain velocity in the ideal model. A falling body before collision can be checked against an analytic constant-acceleration solution, separating integration error from collision behavior.
lessons.lab: Build a regression suite with replay hashes on one pinned environment, finite-value checks and analytic tests. Pass: failures identify the first divergent tick and reports distinguish same-machine repeatability from cross-platform determinism.
lessons.reading: R28: simulation, determinism and limitations; revisit Modules 08 and 24.

quiz.question: Is same-machine repeatability proof of cross-platform determinism?
quiz.answer: No. Compiler, arithmetic and implementation differences can still matter.

quiz.question: Why identify the first divergent tick?
quiz.answer: It localizes the origin of disagreement before later effects amplify it.

quiz.question: What should happen when a simulation first creates a NaN?
quiz.answer: Capture a useful diagnostic and reject or isolate invalid state according to policy rather than letting it propagate silently.

modules.title: Animation, audio and interactive timing
modules.project: Integrate an animated character or articulated object with event-driven audio. Demonstrate smooth interpolation, bounded audio work, adjustable sound categories and correct behavior when animation rate differs from simulation rate.

lessons.title: Skeletons, transforms and skinning
lessons.outcome: Compute hierarchical animation without mixing coordinate spaces.
lessons.teach:
A skeleton is a hierarchy of local transforms. A joint's world transform depends on its ancestors, so evaluation must respect the hierarchy. Skinning transforms mesh vertices using joint transforms and stored bind information. Inverse bind matrices relate the original mesh pose to the current skeleton; applying a transform in the wrong space creates characteristic stretching or displacement.
Linear blend skinning combines transformed positions using weights that normally sum to one. It is efficient but has deformation limitations. Rotations should be interpolated with a representation appropriate to orientation, such as normalized quaternions with a shortest-path convention. Interpolating arbitrary matrix entries can introduce unintended scale or shear. Test a two-joint example before importing a complex character.
lessons.example: A vertex influenced equally by two joints has weights 0.5 and 0.5. Omitting the bind-pose correction can move it even when the skeleton is supposedly in its original pose.
lessons.lab: Animate a two-joint mesh or line skeleton. Pass: the bind pose reproduces the source geometry, weights are validated and a parent rotation moves descendants consistently.
lessons.reading: R19: transformations and animation; R26: skeletal animation concepts.

quiz.question: Why evaluate parent transforms before dependent children?
quiz.answer: A child world transform depends on the parent world transform.

quiz.question: What should ordinary normalized skinning weights sum to?
quiz.answer: One.

quiz.question: Why avoid directly interpolating arbitrary rotation-matrix entries?
quiz.answer: The result may cease to be a valid pure rotation and can introduce scale or shear.

lessons.title: Animation blending, state machines and inverse kinematics
lessons.outcome: Coordinate authored motion with runtime goals.
lessons.teach:
Animation state machines choose motion states and transitions, while blend systems combine clips using parameters such as speed or direction. Transition conditions, interruption rules and event timing are part of gameplay behavior. A clip completing is not always equivalent to an action becoming interruptible.
Inverse kinematics finds joint configurations that satisfy target constraints, such as placing a foot on a surface. It may have no solution, multiple solutions or a solution outside joint limits. Iterative methods need stopping criteria and stable behavior near unreachable targets. Root motion introduces a policy decision about whether animation or simulation controls displacement. Keep ownership clear to prevent animation and physics from both moving the same body inconsistently.
lessons.example: A two-link arm with lengths 1 and 1 cannot reach a target 3 units from its base. A solver should clamp or report the unreachable condition rather than generating invalid angles.
lessons.lab: Build idle/walk/action transitions and a two-link IK demonstration. Pass: interruptions behave as specified, unreachable targets are handled, and root-motion ownership is documented.
lessons.reading: R19: animation and inverse kinematics; R26: animation blueprints and blending concepts, compared with your own small implementation.

quiz.question: Can every IK target be reached?
quiz.answer: No. Geometry, joint limits and constraints can make targets unreachable.

quiz.question: What is the maximum reach of two collinear links of length 1 each?
quiz.answer: 2 units.

quiz.question: Why define root-motion ownership?
quiz.answer: Animation and physical simulation otherwise may apply incompatible displacement to the same object.

lessons.title: Digital audio, mixing and real-time callback discipline
lessons.outcome: Generate sound without missing the output deadline.
lessons.teach:
Digital audio represents sampled signals. Sample rate, channel layout and sample format describe the buffer contract. Mixing combines signals with controlled gain; clipping occurs when output exceeds the representable or intended range. Resampling is a signal-processing operation requiring filtering, not merely dropping arbitrary samples.
An audio callback usually has a deadline tied to the buffer duration. Avoid unbounded allocation, blocking locks, disk access or unpredictable work on that path. Prepare data elsewhere and communicate through a carefully designed bounded mechanism. Smaller buffers can reduce one source of latency but leave less scheduling margin. Measure underruns and end-to-end response rather than assuming the smallest available buffer is best.
lessons.example: A 256-frame buffer at 48,000 frames per second spans 256/48,000 seconds, about 5.33 ms. A callback that blocks for 20 ms can miss that timing requirement.
lessons.lab: Mix two generated tones with adjustable gains using a platform audio API. Pass: no clipping under the documented gain policy, bounded callback work and a recorded underrun or deadline-stress test.
lessons.reading: R10 from Volume 2: sampling and filtering; R22: SDL3 audio; R20: audio systems.

quiz.question: What duration does 256 frames represent at 48 kHz?
quiz.answer: Approximately 5.33 ms.

quiz.question: Why avoid disk reads inside an audio callback?
quiz.answer: Their unpredictable blocking time can exceed the audio deadline.

quiz.question: Does halving the buffer automatically improve every aspect of audio?
quiz.answer: No. It can reduce buffering latency while increasing deadline pressure and underrun risk.

lessons.title: Spatial audio, animation events and multimodal accessibility
lessons.outcome: Synchronize feedback while preserving user control.
lessons.teach:
Spatial audio approximates cues such as level, direction and environmental filtering. A simple stereo pan is not a full head-related acoustic model. Distance attenuation and occlusion are design choices that should be consistent with the game's spatial scale and readability needs. Avoid treating physically plausible sound as automatically useful feedback.
Animation and gameplay events should reference a deliberate clock and deduplication policy. Rollback or repeated evaluation must not replay every sound unintentionally. Provide category volume controls and alternatives for information communicated only through sound or color. Subtitle timing, speaker identification and visual event indicators are engineering requirements, not a final decoration. Evaluate accessibility with actual task completion where possible.
lessons.example: A predicted footstep may be encountered again during replay. Assigning an event identity and a presentation policy prevents an unintended duplicate sound while preserving the corrected simulation.
lessons.lab: Add spatial panning, separate music/effects controls and a visual equivalent for a critical audio cue. Pass: replay does not duplicate one-shot events and a muted-audio test still allows the required task.
lessons.reading: R20: audio and event systems; R22: audio interfaces; R29 from the resource directory: audio and subtitle accessibility.

quiz.question: Is stereo panning a complete spatial-hearing model?
quiz.answer: No. It represents only some directional cues.

quiz.question: Why give presentation events stable identities during replay?
quiz.answer: To recognize previously presented events and apply a deliberate deduplication policy.

quiz.question: Why provide a non-audio equivalent for a critical cue?
quiz.answer: The player may not hear the cue because of disability, environment or settings.

modules.title: Game AI, decision systems and machine learning
modules.project: Build an inspectable agent that navigates, chooses actions and recovers from blocked plans. Compare a rules-based baseline with one small learned or search-based component; evaluate behavior and runtime cost, not only win rate.

lessons.title: Navigation graphs, steering and dynamic obstacles
lessons.outcome: Separate finding a route from executing movement.
lessons.teach:
Pathfinding chooses a route through an abstract representation; steering controls local motion along or toward that route. A navigation mesh represents traversable regions, while grids and waypoint graphs offer other tradeoffs. The abstraction must include the agent's dimensions and movement constraints. A path valid for a point may be impossible for a wide character.
Dynamic obstacles can invalidate a route or require local avoidance. Replanning every frame for every agent may waste time; never replanning may leave agents stuck. Use bounded work, event-driven invalidation and observable failure states. Local avoidance does not guarantee a globally feasible route. Test narrow passages, opposing traffic and unreachable destinations rather than only empty rooms.
lessons.example: A doorway 0.8 units wide is not traversable by a circular agent with diameter 1.0 under a no-overlap model, even if the navigation graph contains an edge through its center.
lessons.lab: Combine A* with a steering controller and a blocked-path detector. Pass: agent size is respected, unreachable goals terminate or report failure, and repeated replanning has a bounded budget.
lessons.reading: R46: Search; R20: game AI and navigation concepts.

quiz.question: How do pathfinding and steering differ?
quiz.answer: Pathfinding selects a route; steering produces local movement to follow or adjust that route.

quiz.question: Can the example 1.0-wide agent pass through the 0.8-wide doorway?
quiz.answer: Not under the stated no-overlap model.

quiz.question: Why bound replanning work?
quiz.answer: Large or frequent searches can consume the frame budget and harm responsiveness.

lessons.title: Behavior trees, utility systems and explainable decisions
lessons.outcome: Represent behavior so designers can understand its failures.
lessons.teach:
A finite-state machine encodes states and transitions. A behavior tree organizes conditional execution and action status. A utility system scores alternatives and selects according to a policy. These are alternative or complementary organizational tools, not a ranking from obsolete to modern. Choose based on behavior complexity, authoring needs and debugging.
An action should expose progress, success, failure and cancellation semantics. Utility scores need compatible scales and often hysteresis to prevent rapid switching between nearly equal options. Behavior traces should record why an action was selected and why it failed. A black-box agent that occasionally behaves well is harder to improve than a simpler agent whose decisions can be inspected.
lessons.example: An agent choosing between attack score 0.51 and retreat score 0.50 can oscillate as small observations change. A switching threshold or minimum commitment interval can stabilize the policy, with explicit tradeoffs.
lessons.lab: Implement either a small behavior tree or utility selector with a trace viewer. Pass: action cancellation releases resources and three induced failure cases produce understandable explanations.
lessons.reading: R20: game AI; R46: agents, utilities and decision-making foundations.

quiz.question: What statuses should a multi-frame action expose?
quiz.answer: At least a defined running/progress state, success, failure and cancellation behavior.

quiz.question: Why can nearly tied utility scores cause oscillation?
quiz.answer: Small input changes repeatedly reverse the preferred action.

quiz.question: Why is a decision trace valuable?
quiz.answer: It makes selection criteria and failures visible for testing, tuning and designer review.

lessons.title: Adversarial search, planning and simulation budgets
lessons.outcome: Trade decision quality against bounded computation.
lessons.teach:
Minimax reasons about alternating choices under a specified game model. Alpha-beta pruning can avoid exploring branches that cannot affect the result while preserving the minimax value under the same assumptions. Move ordering changes efficiency, not the objective. Evaluation functions approximate the value of states that cannot be searched to completion.
Monte Carlo tree search uses repeated sampled exploration to allocate work. Its behavior depends on sampling, exploration policy and rollout or value estimates. Real-time agents need deadlines and a valid fallback action. Hidden information requires reasoning about beliefs rather than granting the agent access to facts a player could not observe. Compare policies on diverse scenarios, not only against one weak opponent.
lessons.example: A branching factor of 10 searched to depth 6 can produce roughly one million leaf paths before pruning. A 2 ms decision budget cannot be assumed sufficient without measurement and a bounded policy.
lessons.lab: Implement minimax with alpha-beta or a small MCTS agent for a tiny game. Pass: legal moves are always returned within a defined budget or fallback, and evaluation includes multiple seeds and opponents.
lessons.reading: R46: Games, Minimax, Expectimax and Monte Carlo Tree Search.

quiz.question: Does alpha-beta change the minimax objective when applied correctly?
quiz.answer: No. It prunes branches that cannot affect the same result under the search assumptions.

quiz.question: How many depth-6 paths arise from branching factor 10 without pruning?
quiz.answer: About 10^6, or one million.

quiz.question: Why use a fallback action?
quiz.answer: The decision deadline may arrive before the planned search completes.

lessons.title: Learning systems, neural inference and responsible evaluation
lessons.outcome: Understand learning fundamentals without replacing every subsystem with a model.
lessons.teach:
Supervised learning fits parameters from examples; reinforcement learning optimizes behavior through rewards and interaction. A training objective is not the same as the desired player experience. Split data by independent episodes or sources when appropriate so nearly duplicate examples do not leak between training and testing. Establish a simple non-learned baseline first.
A neural network composes parameterized transformations and nonlinearities; gradients update parameters through the chain rule. Inference cost includes preprocessing, memory movement and scheduling, not only arithmetic. Distribution shift can cause failure when gameplay differs from training. Record data rights, privacy and failure policies. Learned components should remain bounded and observable, especially when their output affects authoritative game state.
lessons.example: A model trained and tested on adjacent frames from the same recorded match may appear accurate by exploiting near-duplicates. Holding out complete matches provides a stronger test of generalization.
lessons.lab: Train a small classifier or value estimator on synthetic game data and compare it with a rules baseline. Pass: independent splits, error analysis, inference timing, reproducible seeds and a fallback behavior are reported.
lessons.reading: R46: Machine Learning and Reinforcement Learning; R47: linear models, multilayer perceptrons, backpropagation and generalization.

quiz.question: Why separate complete episodes across data splits?
quiz.answer: It reduces leakage from highly correlated examples belonging to the same episode.

quiz.question: What mathematical rule underlies backpropagation?
quiz.answer: The chain rule applied through the computation graph.

quiz.question: Why retain a rules-based baseline?
quiz.answer: It reveals whether learning adds useful quality relative to its data, runtime and maintenance costs.

modules.title: Multiplayer simulation and online services
modules.prerequisites: Modules 18-20 and 24; Module 26 for physical interaction.
modules.project: Create a local two-client multiplayer demonstration with a network simulator for delay, jitter, loss, duplication and reordering. No public server or paid cloud account is required. Document authority and recovery rules.

lessons.title: Authority, prediction and reconciliation
lessons.outcome: Provide responsive local control without trusting arbitrary client outcomes.
lessons.teach:
An authoritative simulation decides which state is accepted as game truth. Clients commonly send input intentions rather than unrestricted final positions or rewards. Local prediction improves immediate response by simulating the client's own input before server confirmation. Reconciliation compares authoritative state with the corresponding predicted history and reapplies unacknowledged inputs when necessary.
Input sequence numbers or simulation ticks make this correspondence possible. Validation needs resource and rate limits as well as semantic checks. Authority does not eliminate all cheating or fairness problems, but it defines the trust boundary. Presentation smoothing should not rewrite the authoritative rules. Keep correction behavior visible during development so errors are not merely hidden behind interpolation.
lessons.example: The server acknowledges input 40. The client corrects to the returned state for that point and replays locally stored inputs 41 through 44, rather than applying those inputs twice to the wrong starting state.
lessons.lab: Implement a one-dimensional or grid movement server with client prediction. Pass: invalid movement is rejected and induced delay produces documented corrections without permanently diverging state.
lessons.reading: R17: transport semantics; R26: networking and multiplayer concepts; R20: networking in games.

quiz.question: What is authoritative state?
quiz.answer: The state accepted as the deciding game truth under the chosen trust model.

quiz.question: Which inputs are replayed after acknowledgment of input 40 in the example?
quiz.answer: Unacknowledged inputs 41 through 44.

quiz.question: Why send intentions rather than unrestricted reward totals?
quiz.answer: The authority can validate and compute outcomes instead of trusting client-supplied benefits.

lessons.title: Snapshots, interpolation, relevance and lag compensation
lessons.outcome: Manage bandwidth and latency while making fairness assumptions explicit.
lessons.teach:
Remote entities can be rendered between buffered snapshots, trading some added presentation delay for smoother motion under jitter. Extrapolation predicts beyond available data and can be wrong when motion changes. Snapshot sequence numbers, timestamps and baselines must be validated. Delta compression requires agreement about the baseline being referenced.
Interest management sends relevant state rather than every entity to every client. Relevance is also a security concern: sending hidden information can expose it even when the interface does not display it. Lag compensation may evaluate an action against historical state, but history bounds and fairness policy must be explicit. There is no universal policy that makes every latency condition equally fair.
lessons.example: Buffering two snapshots 50 ms apart can interpolate motion during a delay variation, but it intentionally displays a slightly older world. This is a latency-quality tradeoff, not free smoothing.
lessons.lab: Add remote interpolation and relevance filtering. Pass: out-of-order snapshots are handled, missing baselines trigger recovery, and the report explains both visual delay and hidden-state exposure policy.
lessons.reading: R20: networked game state; R26: replication and network smoothing; revisit Module 19 message validation.

quiz.question: What cost does snapshot interpolation commonly add?
quiz.answer: Additional presentation delay from buffering earlier snapshots.

quiz.question: Why must delta-compression baselines be identified?
quiz.answer: The receiver needs the correct prior state to reconstruct the delta.

quiz.question: Why avoid transmitting irrelevant hidden enemy state?
quiz.answer: A modified client may inspect received information even if the normal UI hides it.

lessons.title: Lockstep, rollback and deterministic replay
lessons.outcome: Choose synchronization around the game model rather than genre slogans.
lessons.teach:
Lockstep peers or participants advance a deterministic simulation using agreed inputs. It can reduce state bandwidth, but progress depends on input availability and determinism. A single divergent arithmetic or ordering decision can amplify into different worlds. Periodic state hashes help detect disagreement but do not repair it by themselves.
Rollback predicts missing inputs, then restores a past state and resimulates when the prediction differs. It needs fast state capture, bounded history and careful handling of irreversible presentation or external side effects. The rollback horizon controls memory and correction cost. Neither rollback nor lockstep is automatically appropriate for every RTS or action game; evaluate state size, simulation cost, latency and player experience.
lessons.example: At 60 simulation ticks per second, storing 120 snapshots covers two seconds of history. If each snapshot is 2 MB, raw snapshot storage alone reaches 240 MB before metadata or compression.
lessons.lab: Implement rollback or input lockstep for the tiny deterministic game. Pass: a delayed-input test converges, state hashes detect a deliberately introduced divergence, and audio or reward side effects are not duplicated.
lessons.reading: R20 and R26: multiplayer concepts; derive the implementation using Modules 18, 24 and 26 rather than assuming engine-specific guarantees.

quiz.question: How much time do 120 ticks cover at 60 Hz?
quiz.answer: Two seconds.

quiz.question: How much raw storage do 120 snapshots of 2 MB require?
Why are external side effects difficult during rollback?
quiz.answer: Re-executing a tick must not repeat irreversible actions such as issuing a reward or sending an external message.

lessons.title: Match services, identity, persistence and failure recovery
lessons.outcome: Design a small online service without treating it as part of the render loop.
lessons.teach:
Matchmaking, authentication, session allocation and persistent progression are service responsibilities distinct from frame simulation. A match can continue or fail under a defined policy when a nonessential service is unavailable. Identity and authorization must be checked at the relevant boundary; a valid account is not permission to modify another account's data.
Retries, timeouts and idempotency are essential for reward and progression operations. Use established authentication and cryptographic libraries rather than inventing protocols. Store secrets outside repositories and logs. Operational readiness includes health checks, structured diagnostics, graceful shutdown and recovery tests. For learning, local mock services and synthetic accounts are sufficient and avoid unnecessary privacy and spending risks.
lessons.example: A match-result submission is retried after a timeout. A stable operation identifier lets the progression service recognize the duplicate and avoid granting the same reward twice.
lessons.lab: Build a local match registry and idempotent result store. Pass: duplicate submissions do not duplicate rewards, unauthorized edits fail, and simulated service loss produces a documented client outcome.
lessons.reading: R18 from the directory: transactions; R17: transport; revisit Modules 19-20 for distributed failure and threat modeling.

quiz.question: Is authentication the same as authorization?
quiz.answer: No. Identity verification and permission to perform a specific action are separate checks.

quiz.question: Why identify a match-result operation uniquely?
quiz.answer: Retries can then be recognized and processed without duplicating its durable effect.

quiz.question: Must this lab use a paid public cloud?
quiz.answer: No. Local services and synthetic accounts satisfy the educational objective.

modules.title: Production quality and the undergraduate engine capstone
modules.prerequisites: Modules 21-29 plus Gate D software-engineering evidence.
modules.project: Gate F: release a small original game using your engine, with one complete gameplay loop, settings, save/load, diagnostics, accessibility checks, a tested distribution and a technical postmortem. Scope is judged by quality of evidence, not visual size.

lessons.title: Profiling, frame budgets and performance regression tests
lessons.outcome: Optimize measured bottlenecks without sacrificing correctness.
lessons.teach:
Profiling identifies where time and resources are spent under a specific workload. Instrumentation records explicit events; sampling estimates where execution tends to be observed. Both have overhead and interpretation limits. A CPU trace alone cannot fully explain GPU work, and a GPU timing alone cannot describe input-to-display latency.
Create repeatable scenes with fixed settings and a warmup policy. Record build type, hardware, drivers, resolution and background conditions. Measure distributions and peak memory, then change one hypothesis-driven factor at a time. A microbenchmark speedup is useful only if it improves an important application path without unacceptable regressions. Keep correctness tests alongside performance tests and tolerate normal measurement noise appropriately.
lessons.example: A subsystem taking 2 ms of a 20 ms frame can save at most 2 ms if removed entirely. A 10x speedup in that subsystem alone yields an 18.2 ms frame under the simplified additive model.
lessons.lab: Profile the capstone scene, optimize one verified bottleneck and add a regression benchmark. Pass: repeated before/after results, unchanged correctness and disclosed measurement uncertainty are included.
lessons.reading: R26: profiling and optimization; R45: sanitizer diagnostics; revisit Modules 09 and 18.

quiz.question: What is the ideal frame time after a 10x speedup of the example 2 ms subsystem?
quiz.answer: 18 ms unchanged work plus 0.2 ms optimized work = 18.2 ms.

quiz.question: Why record build type?
quiz.answer: Debug and optimized builds can have very different performance and checks.

quiz.question: Why can a microbenchmark improvement fail to help the game?
quiz.answer: That operation may not dominate the real critical path or may create costs elsewhere.

lessons.title: Compatibility, accessibility, localization and human testing
lessons.outcome: Test whether people can actually use the complete product.
lessons.teach:
A compatibility matrix lists supported environments and input/display configurations. Test cases should include different resolutions, aspect ratios, controllers, keyboard layouts and missing optional devices where relevant. Unsupported cases need clear behavior rather than accidental crashes. Localization affects text length, fonts, layout, number formatting and sometimes text direction.
Accessibility begins with requirements such as remappable controls, readable interface scale, contrast, alternative cues and adjustable timing where the game permits. A guideline checklist supports design but does not replace user testing or establish legal compliance. Use informed, voluntary test participation and collect only necessary data. Observe task completion and confusion rather than asking only whether the game is enjoyable.
lessons.example: A button sized for a short English label can clip a longer translated label. A control prompt that hard-codes a keyboard letter can become wrong after rebinding.
lessons.lab: Test the game at two window sizes, with remapped input and an expanded pseudo-localized text set. Pass: no critical clipped controls, a muted-audio task remains solvable and observed usability issues are tracked.
lessons.reading: R29: input, text, audio, contrast and UI guidelines; R20: playtesting and production.

quiz.question: Why use pseudo-localization before full translation?
quiz.answer: It exposes layout and text-handling problems using expanded or altered test strings.

quiz.question: What should a control prompt show after rebinding?
quiz.answer: The current binding, not an obsolete hard-coded default.

quiz.question: Does checking every accessibility guideline prove legal compliance?
quiz.answer: No. It supports engineering review but is not a legal determination or substitute for user evaluation.

lessons.title: Packaging, patching, modding and supply-chain boundaries
lessons.outcome: Distribute a game without creating an uncontrolled execution path.
lessons.teach:
A release package includes the executable, required runtime assets, dependency information, notices and configuration defaults. Test installation and startup outside the development tree. Patch systems need integrity checks, version compatibility and a rollback or recovery plan; interrupted updates must not destroy the only runnable installation.
Modding expands the trust boundary. Data-only mods still require parsing and resource limits, while executable plugins can run with substantial authority unless isolated. Define supported APIs, compatibility versions and permissions. Do not download and execute arbitrary community code automatically. A script sandbox needs explicit capability and resource limits, and its security depends on implementation, not the word sandbox. Preserve user saves separately from replaceable program files.
lessons.example: A malformed mod declares a texture with dimensions large enough to overflow a byte-count calculation. Validation must check multiplication and total resource limits before allocation, even though the file is nominally data.
lessons.lab: Package the game and implement a data-only mod with a versioned schema. Pass: a clean-folder launch works, oversized or malformed mods are rejected and an interrupted-update simulation preserves a valid version.
lessons.reading: R20: production; R26: packaging and plugins; R45 and Module 20: defensive memory and dependency practices.

quiz.question: Can a data-only mod still be dangerous to robustness?
quiz.answer: Yes. Malformed sizes, structures or resource demands can trigger failures unless validated.

quiz.question: Why separate saves from replaceable installation files?
quiz.answer: Updates or reinstalls should not erase user progress.

quiz.question: Does naming a system a sandbox establish isolation?
quiz.answer: No. Isolation depends on the enforced capability, memory and resource boundaries.

lessons.title: Capstone review, release and technical postmortem
lessons.outcome: Demonstrate ownership of a complete engineering result.
lessons.teach:
A capstone combines requirements, implementation, tests, performance evidence and communication. Freeze a small scope: one complete loop with a clear beginning, success/failure and restart is enough. Review the architecture against actual use, not only the original diagram. List dependencies and distinguish original code from libraries or assistance.
A technical postmortem explains what worked, what failed, evidence behind decisions and what would change next. Avoid rewriting the project history as an uninterrupted success story. An oral review should include a live bug investigation, a design tradeoff and a small code modification. These reveal understanding beyond a polished video. Graduation to advanced work requires the practical artifact and reasoning, not only lesson attendance.
lessons.example: A small game with reproducible builds, bounded memory, clear controls and an honest bug list is stronger evidence of engineering ownership than an unfinished large world with no tests.
lessons.lab: Complete Gate F and the oral questions in the handbook. Pass: another tester finishes a full loop, the release is reproducible, critical defects are resolved or clearly blocked from release, and the postmortem cites measured evidence.
lessons.reading: R20: course projects and critique; revisit the project rubric and professional-practice lessons.

quiz.question: What proves completion beyond a recorded demo?
quiz.answer: A reproducible package, tests, usable controls, documented limitations and independent execution.

quiz.question: Why disclose library and AI assistance?
quiz.answer: It distinguishes the learner's decisions and understanding from supplied work and supports provenance.

quiz.question: Why include a live modification in an oral review?
quiz.answer: It tests whether the learner can reason about and change the system rather than only present a prepared artifact.

modules.title: Circuits, measurement and electronic foundations
modules.prerequisites: Modules 06-10; basic algebra and calculus competence required. Simulation is the default laboratory.
modules.project: Create a circuit laboratory notebook using simulation first: voltage/current prediction, an RC transient, a transistor switch and a sampled input. Physical extensions require a qualified mentor and a documented low-voltage safety review.

lessons.title: Voltage, current, resistance and safe measurement
lessons.outcome: Analyze a simple circuit using units and conservation laws.
lessons.teach:
Voltage is potential difference between two points; current is charge flow. Resistance relates voltage and current for an ideal resistor through V=IR. Kirchhoff's current law expresses charge conservation at a node, while the voltage law applies around a lumped-circuit loop under its modeling assumptions. Always choose reference directions and keep signs consistent.
Power is P=VI, so a circuit can be logically correct but thermally unsuitable. Real components have ratings and tolerances. A voltmeter is connected across the relevant points; measuring current generally changes the measurement arrangement. Incorrect meter configuration can create a short. Begin in simulation and use only reviewed low-voltage educational hardware for physical work. Do not open mains-powered supplies, displays or battery packs.
lessons.example: An ideal 1,000 ohm resistor across 5 V carries 5 mA and dissipates 25 mW. These are model calculations; a physical build also requires component ratings and safe connections.
lessons.lab: Simulate a two-resistor divider and verify node voltages and current conservation. Pass: predictions include units, the source/load assumptions are stated, and a safety checklist precedes any physical experiment.
lessons.reading: R30: lumped-circuit abstraction, resistive networks and basic circuit analysis.

quiz.question: What current flows through 1,000 ohms at 5 V?
What power is dissipated in that ideal resistor?
Why can putting a meter in the wrong current-measurement configuration be dangerous?
quiz.answer: It can create an unintended low-resistance path or short, damaging equipment or causing injury.

lessons.title: Capacitors, inductors, transients and frequency response
lessons.outcome: Relate stored energy to timing and filtering behavior.
lessons.teach:
A capacitor stores energy in an electric field and relates current to voltage change through i=C*dv/dt in the ideal model. An inductor relates voltage to current change through v=L*di/dt. These elements make circuit behavior depend on time and initial conditions. An RC network is a useful first-order model for charging, filtering and delay.
For a simple charging RC circuit, the time constant is tau=RC. Frequency-domain analysis uses complex impedance to describe sinusoidal steady-state behavior, but it does not replace startup analysis. Real parasitic resistance, inductance and capacitance matter increasingly as signal edges become fast. A model should state which nonideal effects it intentionally omits.
lessons.example: With R=10,000 ohms and C=1 microfarad, tau=0.01 s, or 10 ms. Starting from zero, the ideal capacitor reaches about 63.2% of its final step-response voltage after one time constant.
lessons.lab: Simulate an RC step response and a sinusoidal frequency sweep. Pass: the measured time constant agrees with the ideal calculation within numerical tolerance, and the report distinguishes transient from steady-state behavior.
lessons.reading: R30: capacitors, inductors, first- and second-order systems; R10: frequency response.

quiz.question: What is tau for 10 kohm and 1 microfarad?
quiz.answer: 10 ms.

quiz.question: What fraction of a zero-to-final RC charging step is reached at one tau?
quiz.answer: Approximately 1-exp(-1), or 63.2%.

quiz.question: Why do initial conditions matter?
quiz.answer: Energy already stored in capacitors or inductors affects the transient response.

lessons.title: Diodes, transistors, CMOS and analog interfaces
lessons.outcome: Understand the physical devices beneath digital abstractions.
lessons.teach:
A diode has a nonlinear current-voltage relationship; it is not a perfect one-way switch. A transistor can control current and serve as an amplifier or switch depending on its operating region and circuit. MOS devices form complementary networks in CMOS logic. The digital 0/1 abstraction hides voltage ranges, delay, leakage and transition behavior.
Analog interfaces may use amplifiers, comparators and reference voltages. An ideal operational-amplifier model is useful only while feedback and operating limits support its assumptions. Real inputs and outputs have range, bandwidth and loading constraints. Read datasheets as contracts, including absolute maximum ratings and recommended operation, rather than choosing parts from one headline specification.
lessons.example: A logic input specified for one voltage domain is not automatically safe when driven by a higher-voltage output. A logical high in both systems does not imply electrical compatibility.
lessons.lab: Simulate a CMOS inverter and one simple amplifier or comparator stage. Pass: plot input/output behavior, identify valid operating regions and explain one failure of the idealized model.
lessons.reading: R30: MOS transistors, amplifiers, digital circuits and operational amplifiers.

quiz.question: Why is a transistor not only a binary software switch?
quiz.answer: Its electrical behavior is continuous and depends on voltages, currents, device properties and operating region.

quiz.question: Does a logical high guarantee compatibility across voltage domains?
quiz.answer: No. Electrical input limits and output levels must also match.

quiz.question: Why distinguish absolute maximum ratings from recommended operating conditions?
quiz.answer: Absolute limits are not a normal design target or a guarantee of intended performance.

lessons.title: Sampling, ADCs, DACs and noisy controller inputs
lessons.outcome: Convert physical signals into stable digital measurements.
lessons.teach:
An analog-to-digital converter samples and quantizes an input relative to a reference. Resolution describes code granularity, not guaranteed accuracy. Noise, offset, reference error, nonlinearity and acquisition behavior can dominate the nominal bit count. A digital-to-analog converter performs a related reconstruction task with its own filtering and output limits.
An analog signal needs bandwidth control before sampling when aliasing is a concern. Digital filtering afterward cannot generally undo already aliased information. A controller input also needs calibration, dead zones and careful response tuning. Switch debouncing and analog filtering solve different problems. Preserve enough timing information to measure the latency added by filtering.
lessons.example: An ideal 12-bit converter spanning 0 to 3.3 V has a nominal step of about 3.3/4096 = 0.806 mV under that quantization convention. Real usable precision may be lower.
lessons.lab: Simulate a noisy joystick signal, quantization and a simple filter. Pass: report step size, calibration error, added response delay and behavior near the dead-zone boundary.
lessons.reading: R30: mixed-signal and measurement concepts; R10: sampling and filtering.

quiz.question: How many distinct codes does a 12-bit converter provide?
Does 12-bit resolution guarantee 12-bit accuracy?
quiz.answer: No. Noise and other errors can reduce accuracy and effective resolution.

quiz.question: Why filter before sampling to prevent aliasing?
quiz.answer: Once high-frequency content aliases into the sampled band, ordinary later filtering cannot distinguish it from genuine in-band content.

modules.title: Digital logic, state and timing
modules.project: Build and test an arithmetic unit, a finite-state controller and a synchronous queue model. For every block, provide a truth table or transition specification before coding its implementation.

lessons.title: Boolean logic and combinational building blocks
lessons.outcome: Translate a logical specification into a circuit with no stored state.
lessons.teach:
Combinational logic computes outputs from current inputs. Boolean algebra and truth tables specify behavior independently of a particular gate arrangement. Multiplexers select among inputs; decoders map a code to selected outputs; adders combine bit patterns according to arithmetic rules. Equivalent logic can have different area, delay and power.
Minimization is not only reducing the printed expression. Fanout, gate availability and signal arrival times influence implementation. A combinational loop usually indicates a design error in beginner synchronous work. Unknown or invalid input codes require a defined policy.
