State external validity limits, including devices, workloads and quality settings not tested.
lessons.example: Ten thousand frames from one scene are not equivalent to ten thousand independent games. A scene-level comparison across diverse scenes can better test a claim about broad engine behavior.
lessons.lab: Preregister a small experiment with baseline, primary metric, trial unit and exclusion policy. Pass: raw data and analysis scripts reproduce the tables, and an ablation isolates at least one proposed mechanism.
lessons.reading: R09: statistical inference; R42: experimental examples; handbook benchmark and research templates.

quiz.question: Why identify the statistical unit?
quiz.answer: It determines what observations can reasonably be treated as independent for the intended inference.

quiz.question: What does an ablation test?
quiz.answer: Whether removing or changing a component changes the outcome in a way that supports its claimed contribution.

quiz.question: Why reserve held-out workloads?
quiz.answer: They test whether tuning improvements generalize beyond the cases used to choose parameters.

modules.title: Advanced parallel and GPU algorithms
modules.project: Implement a reusable GPU reduction, scan or compaction primitive and integrate it into an engine workload. Compare a simple reference, a competent library baseline when available and your implementation at equal correctness requirements.

lessons.title: Parallel reductions, scans and work-span analysis
lessons.outcome: Prove the structure of a parallel primitive before tuning it.
lessons.teach:
A reduction combines many values with an operator; a scan produces prefix combinations. Associativity supports regrouping mathematically, but floating-point addition is not exactly associative. Decide whether the contract requires bitwise reproducibility, bounded error or an exact integer result. A tree reduction can reduce dependency depth from linear to logarithmic while retaining linear total work.
Work is the total number of operations; span is the longest dependency chain. More processors cannot beat the span without changing the algorithm. A naive parallel scan can have extra logarithmic work, while work-efficient constructions achieve linear work with logarithmic span under their model. Handle partial groups, empty inputs and irregular sizes explicitly. Cross-group coordination must follow the API rather than assuming a global barrier inside an ordinary dispatch.
lessons.example: A balanced reduction over 1,024 elements has 10 combination levels under a binary-tree model and 1,023 total pairwise combinations. Its implementation still pays memory and synchronization costs.
lessons.lab: Implement reduction and either scan or compaction. Pass: derive work/span bounds, test sizes 0, 1 and non-powers of two, and report the numerical/reproducibility contract.
lessons.reading: R37: cooperative execution and synchronization; R48: parallel architectures; derive algorithm bounds using Module 14 methods.

quiz.question: How many levels are in a balanced binary reduction of 1,024 values?
How many pairwise combines does that reduction require?
Why can parallel floating-point sums differ from serial sums?
quiz.answer: Changing grouping changes rounding because floating-point addition is not exactly associative.

lessons.title: Tiling, data reuse and asynchronous pipelines
lessons.outcome: Overlap movement and computation without creating races.
lessons.teach:
Tiling partitions a computation so values can be reused in a faster memory level. Matrix multiplication, image filters and neighborhood operations benefit when the tile fits available storage and exposes sufficient parallelism. Larger tiles can increase reuse but also raise register or shared-memory demand and reduce residency.
Double buffering can overlap preparation of one tile with computation on another. The pipeline needs explicit ownership: no consumer reads an incomplete tile and no producer overwrites data still in use. Asynchronous copy features vary by device; maintain a correct portable baseline. Account for boundary tiles, alignment, synchronization and extra staging work. Compare arithmetic intensity at the memory level actually being optimized.
lessons.example: For C=A*B, reusing a loaded A or B tile across many multiply-adds can raise useful operations per byte. A tile that spills heavily can erase that advantage.
lessons.lab: Implement a tiled matrix multiply or image filter, then one overlap variant where supported. Pass: adversarial dimensions match the reference, synchronization is checked and the end-to-end comparison includes staging overhead.
lessons.reading: R37: shared memory, synchronization and asynchronous operations where supported; R43: operational intensity.

quiz.question: Why can larger tiles hurt performance?
quiz.answer: They can increase resource usage, reduce residency or cause spills and boundary overhead.

quiz.question: What ownership rule is essential for double buffering?
quiz.answer: A buffer must not be consumed before preparation completes or overwritten before its current consumer finishes.

quiz.question: Why retain a non-asynchronous baseline?
quiz.answer: It provides a simpler correctness and portability reference for evaluating the extra pipeline complexity.

lessons.title: Irregular workloads, wavefront scheduling and load balance
lessons.outcome: Design around variable work rather than assuming identical threads.
lessons.teach:
Ray traversal, graph processing and variable-length simulation tasks have irregular work. A fixed assignment can leave some workers idle while a few long tasks dominate the tail. Work queues, compaction and wavefront processing reorganize active tasks, trading scheduling and memory traffic for better coherence or load balance.
Persistent-worker designs keep workers alive to fetch tasks, but need bounded queues, termination detection and a memory-ordering contract. Global progress cannot depend on every workgroup being resident when the hardware does not guarantee that. Sorting tasks by similarity can improve coherence but has a cost and can alter latency. Evaluate both balanced and skewed distributions, including rare expensive tasks.
lessons.example: If 99 tasks take 1 unit and one takes 100 units, static one-task assignments can leave the final completion dominated by the long task. Splitting or scheduling work differently may help only when the task is divisible.
lessons.lab: Implement an irregular workload using static assignment and a queue or compaction alternative. Pass: prove or test termination, handle queue capacity safely and measure tail behavior as well as mean throughput.
lessons.reading: R37: execution, atomics and synchronization; R48: multithreaded scheduling; R23: wavefront rendering as an application.

quiz.question: Why can average task cost hide poor completion time?
quiz.answer: A few long tasks can dominate the final tail after most workers become idle.

quiz.question: Why avoid a global spin barrier requiring every group to be resident?
quiz.answer: Unschedulable groups may never run while resident groups wait, causing deadlock.

quiz.question: Is sorting tasks always beneficial?
quiz.answer: No. Sorting cost, added latency and data movement can exceed coherence gains.

lessons.title: Portable performance and integration-quality evaluation
lessons.outcome: Separate algorithmic benefit from one device-specific tuning win.
lessons.teach:
A performance-portable implementation preserves correctness and obtains useful efficiency across its stated target set. This does not mean identical code or identical speed everywhere. Capability dispatch can select specialized paths while keeping a tested fallback. Tuning parameters should be bounded and recorded rather than silently selected from the final test set.
Compare against a competent baseline and include small, large and irregular workloads. Report speed, memory, numerical error and integration cost. A kernel that is faster only after excluding transfer or conversion work should make that boundary explicit. Reproducible artifacts include build scripts, device capability reports, raw data and failure cases. Lack of access to multiple GPUs is a limitation to disclose, not a reason to invent portability evidence.
lessons.example: A tile size tuned on one GPU can reduce occupancy or exceed shared-memory limits on another. Capability checks and independent tuning prevent that choice from becoming an invalid universal default.
lessons.lab: Integrate the selected primitive into the engine and evaluate at least two workload regimes. Pass: application impact is measured, unsupported features fall back safely and any untested device claims are explicitly excluded.
lessons.reading: R37 and R21: capability contracts; R43: performance models; Module 41 experimental protocol.

quiz.question: Does portable performance require one fixed launch configuration?
quiz.answer: No. Valid specialization or bounded tuning may be necessary across targets.

quiz.question: What should be said when only one GPU was tested?
quiz.answer: The evidence is limited to that tested configuration; broader portability remains unverified.

quiz.question: Why measure integration cost?
quiz.answer: A standalone kernel gain may not survive real data preparation, scheduling and result consumption.

modules.title: Advanced rendering and reconstruction
modules.project: Reproduce a bounded rendering result and add one justified extension. Derive the estimator or reconstruction objective, compare equal-quality cost, include temporal failure cases and preserve source scenes and evaluation scripts.

lessons.title: Monte Carlo light transport and multiple importance sampling
lessons.outcome: Derive estimators with correct densities and measures.
lessons.teach:
The rendering equation expresses outgoing radiance as emission plus an integral of incident radiance, scattering and geometry factors. Monte Carlo estimation samples an integral: for samples from density p, average f(x)/p(x) where p is positive over the relevant nonzero support. Correct units and probability measures matter; area and solid-angle densities are not interchangeable without a Jacobian.
Importance sampling aims to reduce variance by matching useful structure. Multiple importance sampling combines strategies with weights that sum appropriately under the estimator. The balance heuristic uses relative weighted densities, but sample counts and support must be included correctly. Russian roulette can terminate paths without bias when surviving contributions receive the proper probability compensation. Finite-variance independent sampling gives the familiar inverse-square-root standard-error scaling; do not assume it for every estimator.
lessons.example: With one sample from each of two strategies and densities p1=2 and p2=6 at a point, the balance weight for strategy 1 is 2/(2+6)=0.25.
lessons.lab: Implement a path tracer with explicit light sampling and MIS. Pass: derive the estimator, verify a simple known integral, compare variance at equal cost and test emission and grazing-angle edge cases.
lessons.reading: R23: Monte Carlo Integration, Light Transport and sampling strategies. Work the associated mathematical exercises, not only the implementation.

quiz.question: What is the balance weight for strategy 1 in the example?
quiz.answer: 0.25 under equal sample counts.

quiz.question: Why is p(x)>0 on relevant support important?
quiz.answer: Otherwise nonzero contributions can never be sampled and the estimator can be biased or undefined.

quiz.question: What sample-count increase ideally halves standard error for independent finite-variance samples?
quiz.answer: Approximately four times as many samples.

lessons.title: Real-time ray tracing, dynamic acceleration and hybrid pipelines
lessons.outcome: Budget traversal, building and shading as one system.
lessons.teach:
Ray-tracing acceleration structures trade build cost, memory and query cost. Dynamic scenes may update or rebuild structures; the best policy depends on movement, geometry and traversal degradation. A refit can be cheaper initially but leave poor bounds after large changes. Hardware-assisted traversal still needs correct synchronization and resource lifetime.
Hybrid renderers combine rasterized visibility with ray-traced shadows, reflections or indirect lighting. Each path needs a consistent material and coordinate model. Screen-space or cached approximations require fallbacks where information is absent. Measure acceleration build/update, tracing, shading, denoising and synchronization separately, then report total frame impact. Compare equivalent scene motion and image quality rather than static screenshots alone.
lessons.example: A faster traversal variant that adds 4 ms of build work to save 1 ms of tracing is a regression for a scene rebuilt every frame, but might help a scene reused for many frames.
lessons.lab: Add one ray-traced effect to the engine or build a software hybrid prototype. Pass: dynamic-scene tests include total update cost, missing-information fallbacks and resource synchronization evidence.
lessons.reading: R23: intersection acceleration and light transport; R21, R24 or R25: supported ray-tracing interfaces for an optional hardware route.

quiz.question: Why can a cheap BVH refit become a poor long-term choice?
quiz.answer: Large motion can degrade bounds and increase traversal cost.

quiz.question: Is saving 1 ms of tracing worth 4 ms of per-frame rebuild cost?
quiz.answer: Not under that stated per-frame workload; total time increases by 3 ms.

quiz.question: Why compare animated scenes?
quiz.answer: Dynamic updates and temporal behavior can dominate costs or artifacts absent in a static scene.

lessons.title: Spatiotemporal reuse, reservoirs and denoising
lessons.outcome: Evaluate variance reduction together with bias, history validity and motion.
lessons.teach:
Temporal and spatial reuse exploit related samples across frames or nearby locations. Reusing data changes the sampling and correlation structure, so the estimator and weights must be derived rather than improvised. Reservoir sampling can retain a compact representative sample under a defined weighted selection rule; its rendering use requires additional treatment of target distributions and reuse.
Denoising reconstructs a signal from noisy observations using assumptions about spatial, temporal or learned structure. It can suppress noise while introducing bias, blur or ghosting. Visibility changes and incorrect motion vectors invalidate history. Distinguish estimator bias from reconstruction bias and assess moving sequences at equal total cost. The original 2020 ReSTIR paper is a historical reproduction option, not a claim to represent the latest technique.
lessons.example: If a moving object reveals a background, old foreground samples are not valid background evidence merely because they occupy the same pixel coordinate. History acceptance must account for correspondence and visibility.
lessons.lab: Reproduce a small weighted-reservoir example or temporal denoiser, then evaluate on motion and disocclusion sequences. Pass: the selection/weight rule is derived, bias limitations are stated and results include sequence-level failure cases.
lessons.reading: R44: original ReSTIR paper and its estimator assumptions; R23: sampling theory; read only the selected bounded method before expanding scope.

quiz.question: Why cannot reused samples always be treated as new independent samples?
quiz.answer: Reuse can introduce correlation and change the estimator's sampling structure.

quiz.question: Why is same-pixel history not enough to establish correspondence?
quiz.answer: Different surfaces can occupy that pixel after motion or disocclusion.

quiz.question: What should be compared in a denoised rendering benchmark?
quiz.answer: Quality, bias/artifacts, temporal behavior and total runtime, not only the raw ray count.

lessons.title: Differentiable and neural rendering under engineering constraints
lessons.outcome: Test learned or gradient-based methods against explicit baselines.
lessons.teach:
Differentiable rendering studies how outputs change with scene or model parameters. Visibility discontinuities, stochastic sampling and approximations complicate gradients. A useful derivative must match the actual objective and parameterization; automatic differentiation alone does not guarantee the right physical or statistical estimator. Validate on small scenes with finite differences and known cases.
Neural rendering or learned reconstruction can trade preprocessing, training and memory for runtime quality or speed. Training data coverage, scene specificity, temporal stability and inference hardware constrain deployment. Compare a non-learned baseline and include training or preprocessing cost where the claim requires it. Separate interpolation within familiar conditions from generalization to new scenes, lighting or motion.
lessons.example: A reconstruction network tested on frames from its own training sequence may perform well without generalizing to a new level. Holding out entire scenes tests a stronger claim.
lessons.lab: Implement a small inverse-rendering optimization or learned reconstruction experiment. Pass: gradient or generalization checks, a non-learned baseline, compute/memory accounting and a distribution-shift failure analysis are included.
lessons.reading: R47: automatic differentiation, optimization and generalization; R23: light transport and sampling foundations; select one original method with Module 41's paper-review protocol.

quiz.question: Does automatic differentiation guarantee the desired gradient estimator?
quiz.answer: No. The modeled computation, discontinuities and stochastic estimator must still match the intended objective.

quiz.question: Why hold out entire scenes for some rendering evaluations?
quiz.answer: It tests generalization beyond correlated frames or content seen during training.

quiz.question: When should training cost be included?
quiz.answer: When the claimed practical benefit depends on total preparation, deployment or repeated use, not only one isolated inference.

modules.title: Advanced engine systems and simulation research
modules.project: Conduct an engine-system experiment with a formal model or numerical argument, a reference implementation and stress-tested integration. Choose one main depth area: world streaming, simulation, distributed state or reliability.

lessons.title: Large-world scheduling, streaming and critical-path control
lessons.outcome: Design a bounded system under changing content and workload.
lessons.teach:
Large-world engines coordinate visibility, simulation, streaming and resource residency under changing demand. A frame graph can make dependencies explicit, but hidden shared state or unpredictable tasks can still expand the critical path. Partition work by ownership and locality while controlling cross-partition communication.
World-coordinate precision can degrade far from the origin; origin rebasing, hierarchical coordinates or higher precision each affect physics, rendering and networking interfaces. Streaming priorities should reflect gameplay deadlines and resource availability, not only distance. Build a workload model with bursts, cancellation and scarce memory. Evaluate tail latency and quality degradation under stress rather than only steady travel through a preloaded scene.
lessons.example: A camera teleport invalidates a distance-based prefetch assumption and can create a sudden working-set change. The engine needs placeholders and a bounded recovery policy rather than an unlimited synchronous load.
lessons.lab: Implement a bounded world-streaming scheduler or large-coordinate experiment. Pass: teleport and memory-pressure tests preserve correctness, peak resources are measured and the critical path is explained with a trace.
lessons.reading: R26: world, task and streaming systems for comparison; R20: engine architecture; R54: numerical conditioning where coordinate precision is studied.

quiz.question: Why can a camera teleport defeat ordinary prefetching?
quiz.answer: It changes the needed content abruptly, bypassing assumptions about gradual motion.

quiz.question: Why is origin rebasing an interface issue?
quiz.answer: Physics, rendering, networking and stored references must agree on coordinate changes.

quiz.question: What distinguishes a bounded degradation policy?
quiz.answer: It limits work and resource use while explicitly choosing which quality or availability guarantees may temporarily relax.

lessons.title: Deformable simulation, variational models and solver tradeoffs
lessons.outcome: Derive a physical or constraint model before comparing visual results.
lessons.teach:
Deformable simulation represents degrees of freedom and a model of forces, energies or constraints. Spatial discretization, boundary conditions and time integration together define the numerical problem. Finite-element or mass-spring approaches approximate different structures; a visually similar result does not prove equivalent material behavior.
Implicit methods can improve stability for stiff systems while requiring nonlinear or linear solves and introducing other errors. Position-based and compliant-constraint methods offer alternative formulations with their own parameters and convergence behavior. Derive one simple energy or constraint, explain its units and study timestep/iteration sensitivity. Separate stability, accuracy and physical fidelity. A stable method can be inaccurate, and an accurate local solver can still use an inappropriate material model.
lessons.example: For spring energy E=0.5*k*(x-rest)^2, the force is -dE/dx=-k*(x-rest). This derivative supplies a check before extending to a multi-particle system.
lessons.lab: Implement a small cloth, elastic bar or compliant-constraint model and compare two integration/solver choices. Pass: derive the core equations, check gradients, quantify constraint or energy error and reproduce one bounded result from the assigned research.
lessons.reading: R54: equilibrium, variational and differential-equation methods; R55: 2016 XPBD and related position-based simulation course notes.

quiz.question: What force follows from the example spring energy?
quiz.answer: -k*(x-rest).

quiz.question: Does numerical stability guarantee physical accuracy?
quiz.answer: No. A stable trajectory can still have large discretization error or use an unsuitable physical model.

quiz.question: Why vary timestep and solver iterations independently?
quiz.answer: They affect different sources of error and can reveal hidden parameter dependence.

lessons.title: Distributed game state, consistency and overload behavior
lessons.outcome: Specify which guarantees survive network delay and partial failure.
lessons.teach:
Distributed engine services divide state across processes or machines. Some operations require a single authoritative order, while others tolerate delayed or approximate views. Consistency is a property of a specified operation and model, not a single adjective that applies equally to every subsystem. During communication failure, availability and agreement requirements can conflict.
Partition ownership, migration and recovery need explicit protocols. A world handoff must not create two authorities granting the same irreversible outcome. Queues require bounds and backpressure; retry storms can magnify overload. Test fault sequences involving delayed messages, crashes and duplicate requests. Use local process simulation before public infrastructure, and never claim internet-scale behavior from a two-process happy-path demo.
lessons.example: If two servers both accept ownership of the same entity during a failed handoff, both might award a unique item. A versioned ownership or fencing mechanism must prevent stale authority from committing that effect.
lessons.lab: Model a two-partition entity handoff with injected failure. Pass: a stated safety invariant holds, recovery assumptions are explicit and overload is bounded without unbounded retry amplification.
lessons.reading: R17-R18: transport and transactions; R20: game-state architecture; use Module 41's claim and experiment discipline for the distributed model.

quiz.question: Why is duplicate authority dangerous?
quiz.answer: Two participants may both commit effects that should occur only once under one owner.

quiz.question: What is a retry storm?
quiz.answer: Many failed or slow requests trigger additional retries that worsen overload.

quiz.question: Can a small local demo establish internet-scale reliability?
quiz.answer: No. It supports only the tested model and scale unless broader evidence is provided.

lessons.title: Formal specifications, replay and reliability-oriented engine design
lessons.outcome: Use precise invariants to reduce the space of subtle failures.
lessons.teach:
A formal model abstracts a system to states and transitions so properties can be examined precisely. Safety states that something bad never happens; liveness states that something good eventually happens under assumptions. An engine resource manager can have safety invariants about ownership and liveness obligations about eventual completion or cancellation.
Model checking explores the chosen abstraction, not every detail of the production implementation. Connect model transitions to real code and tests. Deterministic replay, fault injection and property-based testing complement formal reasoning by exercising implemented behavior. Avoid vacuous proofs from impossible environment assumptions. A reliability claim should identify the property, model, bound and implementation evidence separately.
lessons.example: For an asset request, safety might require that a released owner never receives a callback touching its memory. Liveness might require that each accepted request eventually completes or cancels, assuming the worker continues to run.
lessons.lab: Model a small engine lifecycle or queue protocol and connect it to implementation tests. Pass: at least one safety and one conditional liveness property are defined, a deliberate violation is found and abstraction limits are documented.
lessons.reading: R50: safety, liveness and assumptions as a formal-methods reference; R11 and Module 18: ownership/concurrency contracts; R26: system comparison.

quiz.question: How do safety and liveness differ?
quiz.answer: Safety excludes forbidden events; liveness requires eventual progress under stated assumptions.

quiz.question: Why must liveness assumptions mention scheduling or worker progress?
quiz.answer: An environment that never lets work run can prevent completion regardless of the local algorithm.

quiz.question: Does proving an abstract model automatically prove all implementation code?
quiz.answer: No. The relationship between the model and implementation must be established and checked.

modules.title: Compilers, shader languages and engine specialization
modules.project: Gate I: deliver a research-quality reproduction and extension in rendering, simulation, GPU algorithms or compilation. This module also requires a small compiler optimization with semantic tests, generated-code inspection and end-to-end measurements.

lessons.title: Intermediate representations, SSA and dataflow analysis
lessons.outcome: Represent program meaning so transformations can be justified.
lessons.teach:
An intermediate representation makes control flow, values and operations explicit. Static single assignment gives each value one defining assignment; merge points use a representation such as phi nodes to select values from predecessor paths. SSA simplifies many analyses but does not by itself establish program correctness.
Dataflow analysis computes properties over a control-flow graph, often through iterative fixed points on a chosen domain. Liveness identifies values that may be used later; constant propagation tracks values known under the analysis. Soundness means the analysis does not exclude behavior relevant to its guarantee, while precision controls how much useful information it retains. Dominance and control-flow edges must remain consistent after transformations.
lessons.example: After an if/else assigning x=1 or x=2, a merge can represent x=phi(1 from then, 2 from else). Replacing it with 1 unconditionally would be wrong unless the else path is proven unreachable.
lessons.lab: Extend the tiny compiler with a control-flow IR and one dataflow analysis. Pass: derive transfer functions and a fixed-point stopping condition, test loops and merges, and verify transformed programs against an interpreter.
lessons.reading: R14: LLVM frontend, control flow and optimization tutorials; R48: compiler/architecture interaction.

quiz.question: What does SSA require of each value?
quiz.answer: One defining assignment in the representation.

quiz.question: Why is the example phi node not always constant 1?
quiz.answer: The else predecessor supplies 2 unless that path is proven unreachable.

quiz.question: What is the role of a fixed point in dataflow analysis?
quiz.answer: It marks a state where further propagation under the analysis rules no longer changes the computed facts.

lessons.title: Alias analysis, vectorization and legal optimization
lessons.outcome: Separate transformations that are fast from transformations that preserve meaning.
lessons.teach:
An optimization must preserve the language's permitted observable behavior under its assumptions. Alias analysis determines which references may identify overlapping storage. Incorrectly assuming no aliasing can make loop reordering or vectorization wrong. Undefined behavior, overflow rules and floating-point options affect what transformations are legal, so record the compilation contract.
Vectorization groups iterations only when dependencies and semantics permit it. Reductions, exceptional values and rounding can require special handling. Register allocation maps values to a limited physical register set; spills introduce memory traffic. Inspect generated code and test adversarial inputs. A faster compiler output that silently changes required results is a correctness failure, not an optimization.
lessons.example: For a[i]=a[i-1]+1, iterations depend on previous results. Treating all iterations as independent changes behavior unless a valid alternative algorithm preserves the recurrence.
lessons.lab: Implement or study a loop transformation with an explicit legality check. Pass: overlapping-memory and boundary cases are tested, compiler flags are recorded and speed claims exclude transformations that violate the required numerical contract.
lessons.reading: R14: optimization and code generation; R11: aliasing, lifetime and arithmetic guidance; R37: vector/parallel execution consequences.

quiz.question: Why is alias analysis important for reordering loads and stores?
quiz.answer: Two apparently different references may access the same storage, creating dependencies.

quiz.question: Are iterations of a[i]=a[i-1]+1 independent?
quiz.answer: No. Each depends on the previous result.

quiz.question: Why record floating-point compiler options?
quiz.answer: They can permit transformations that change rounding, exceptional-value handling or other required semantics.

lessons.title: Domain-specific languages, specialization and safe JIT execution
lessons.outcome: Trade generality for predictable game-engine computation.
lessons.teach:
A domain-specific language restricts expression to make authoring, validation or optimization easier. A material graph, particle formula or animation expression can expose structure that a general compiler cannot easily infer. Define types, allowed effects and resource limits before implementing code generation.
Specialization precomputes decisions known from material or scene parameters, potentially reducing runtime branches at the cost of more variants and compilation work. Just-in-time compilation introduces startup latency, code-cache management and execution-security concerns. Cache keys must include meaningful inputs and tool versions. Untrusted scripts or graphs need capability and complexity limits. A restricted interpreter remains a useful fallback and semantic reference.
lessons.example: Specializing four binary material options can create up to 2^4=16 variants before other parameters are considered. Uncontrolled variant growth can increase build time and runtime cache misses.
lessons.lab: Build a typed expression or material DSL with constant folding and a bounded interpreter or JIT route. Pass: invalid graphs fail safely, variant counts are measured and compiled outputs match the reference.
lessons.reading: R14: language implementation and JIT; R26: material and scripting concepts for comparison; Module 20: trust boundaries.

quiz.question: How many combinations do four independent binary options create?
Why limit the effects allowed in a DSL?
quiz.answer: Restrictions make validation, optimization and safe execution more tractable.

quiz.question: Why keep an interpreter alongside compiled execution?
quiz.answer: It provides a portable fallback and a simpler reference for semantic testing.

lessons.title: Compiler/hardware co-design and graduate artifact review
lessons.outcome: Connect a transformation to architecture and application evidence.
lessons.teach:
Compiler decisions influence memory layout, instruction mix, register demand and parallel scheduling. Hardware features are useful only when software can express and exploit them efficiently. A co-design experiment changes one interface, representation or instruction opportunity and measures its complete effect. Avoid attributing a gain to hardware when it actually comes from a stronger software baseline.
Graduate review requires a defensible claim, mathematical or semantic argument, implementation and reproducible evaluation. Gate I can focus on one earlier graduate topic, but must include baselines, ablations, uncertainty and limitations. Publication acceptance is not required; credible independent evaluation is. Preserve unsuccessful experiments and distinguish a reproduced known result from the learner's actual extension.
lessons.example: A new vector instruction that saves arithmetic but increases packing and spills may lose in the full engine. The experiment must measure both the generated kernel and its application integration.
lessons.lab: Complete Gate I and defend one compiler transformation's legality. Pass: an independent reader reruns the central experiment, the claimed extension is precisely identified and raw evidence supports the conclusions.
lessons.reading: R14 and R48: compilation and architecture; R49: co-design methodology; Module 41: research evaluation protocol.

quiz.question: Why can a faster instruction fail to improve the application?
quiz.answer: Packing, spills, data movement or unaccelerated work can outweigh the arithmetic savings.

quiz.question: What distinguishes reproduction from extension?
quiz.answer: Reproduction recreates an existing result; extension changes or adds a clearly identified method, setting or analysis.

quiz.question: Is publication acceptance mandatory for Gate I?
quiz.answer: No. The requirement is rigorous, reproducible work and an independent technical review.

modules.title: Advanced computer architecture for gaming workloads
modules.project: Perform an architecture study using a pinned simulator or a carefully bounded analytical model. Compare at least three configurations on representative and adverse game-related workloads, and validate the model against a known reference where possible.

lessons.title: Cache coherence, memory consistency and synchronization
lessons.outcome: Separate agreement about a location from ordering across locations.
lessons.teach:
Cache coherence governs how cached copies of a location interact, including ownership and visibility of writes. Memory consistency defines which orderings of operations across locations are observable. A coherent machine can still expose behaviors disallowed by a stronger consistency model. Programming-language memory rules add another layer between source code and hardware.
Protocols such as MESI use states and messages to preserve coherence invariants, but real implementations include transient states and races among requests. A useful invariant is that no two participants simultaneously hold conflicting write ownership under the protocol. Directory designs track sharers while snooping designs observe suitable interconnect traffic. False sharing and invalidation storms are performance effects of otherwise correct coherence. Use small litmus tests and state models to connect abstract rules to software synchronization.
lessons.example: A producer writes data and then publishes a flag. Correct consumer behavior depends on an appropriate release/acquire or equivalent synchronization contract; coherent caches alone do not justify ordinary unsynchronized C++ access.
lessons.lab: Model a small coherence protocol and evaluate message-passing litmus tests under stated language and hardware models. Pass: ownership invariants hold, transient races are considered and coherence is not confused with data-race freedom.
lessons.reading: R48: multiprocessors, coherence and consistency; R35: selected memory-ordering specification; R11: language-level concurrency.

quiz.question: How do coherence and consistency differ?
quiz.answer: Coherence concerns copies and writes of a location; consistency constrains observable ordering across memory operations and locations.

quiz.question: Do coherent caches make unsynchronized C++ shared access safe?
quiz.answer: No. Language data-race and synchronization rules still apply.

quiz.question: Why include transient states in a protocol model?
quiz.answer: Requests and responses overlap in time, creating states and races absent from a purely stable-state diagram.

lessons.title: Out-of-order execution, speculation and precise state
lessons.outcome: Increase instruction overlap without changing architectural outcomes.
lessons.teach:
Out-of-order processors schedule ready operations while older operations may be waiting. Register renaming removes false name dependencies such as write-after-read and write-after-write, but true data dependencies remain. A reorder or retirement mechanism preserves the required architectural order and supports precise exceptions.
Branch prediction and memory speculation create work before all conditions are known. Incorrect speculation must discard inappropriate architectural effects, while microarchitectural traces may still matter to security and performance. More execution width helps only when useful parallelism, instruction supply and memory behavior support it. Analyze queue capacity, issue limits and dependency chains rather than assuming a larger core always improves a latency-sensitive game thread.
lessons.example: For two instructions that both write architectural register r1 but whose values are consumed separately, renaming can assign different physical destinations. A later instruction that truly consumes the first result still waits for that result.
lessons.lab: Use a simulator or detailed scheduling model to compare in-order and out-of-order execution on independent and dependent instruction streams. Pass: architectural results agree and bottleneck explanations include true dependencies and resource limits.
lessons.reading: R48: superscalar, out-of-order, prediction and exception handling; R38: CPU models and configuration.

quiz.question: Which dependencies does register renaming primarily remove?
quiz.answer: False name dependencies such as write-after-read and write-after-write, not true read-after-write data dependencies.

quiz.question: Why retire architectural effects in a controlled order?
quiz.answer: To preserve the instruction-set contract and support precise state at exceptions or recovery.

quiz.question: Why may a wider core fail to improve one game thread?
quiz.answer: The thread may be limited by dependencies, cache misses, branch behavior or insufficient instruction-level parallelism.

lessons.title: Architecture simulation, traces and model validation
lessons.outcome: Use simulation as evidence with a stated fidelity boundary.
lessons.teach:
A functional simulator checks what computation does; a timing model estimates when events occur under modeled resources. A cycle-oriented model is not automatically accurate for every real device. Workload inputs, cache warmup, sampled regions and operating-system effects influence results. Trace-driven studies can lose feedback between timing and program behavior.
Validate simple cases against analytical expectations and available measured hardware before trusting complex comparisons. State which pipeline, memory and interconnect mechanisms are modeled or omitted. Sensitivity analysis varies uncertain parameters to see whether conclusions survive. Preserve simulator revision, configuration and workload binaries. Relative comparisons can still be misleading when a model error favors one design disproportionately.
lessons.example: If a simulated memory latency is uncertain, sweep a plausible declared range. A proposed design that wins only at one finely chosen value has a weaker claim than one that remains useful across the range.
lessons.lab: Run a cache, scheduling or accelerator study with at least one validation case and a sensitivity sweep. Pass: raw configurations reproduce results, modeled versus measured quantities are labeled and conclusions do not exceed the tested fidelity.
lessons.reading: R38: simulation models, statistics and configuration; R48: architecture evaluation; R43: analytical bounds.

quiz.question: Does cycle-oriented simulation guarantee real-hardware accuracy?
quiz.answer: No. Accuracy depends on the modeled mechanisms, calibration and workload assumptions.

quiz.question: Why perform sensitivity analysis?
quiz.answer: It reveals whether conclusions depend strongly on uncertain or selected parameters.

quiz.question: What can a trace-driven model omit?
quiz.answer: Feedback in which timing changes the future execution or interaction pattern that generated the trace.

lessons.title: Memory systems, chiplets and multi-objective design
lessons.outcome: Choose an architecture across performance, power, cost and complexity.
lessons.teach:
Memory bandwidth, latency, capacity and energy are distinct design dimensions. More channels or wider interfaces can improve bandwidth while increasing pins, routing, power and controller complexity. Cache size changes miss behavior but also area and access characteristics. Packaging and chiplet approaches introduce interconnect and partitioning tradeoffs; no packaging label guarantees a superior system.
A Pareto frontier contains designs not dominated on every chosen objective. Define constraints and compare alternatives at consistent workload quality and manufacturing assumptions. Cost and yield models require credible inputs; educational estimates should not be presented as production quotations. Include verification and software complexity in the design discussion because a theoretically efficient architecture may be impractical to support.
lessons.example: Design A takes 10 ms at 40 J per task; B takes 8 ms at 50 J. Neither dominates the other on latency and energy. A third design at 12 ms and 60 J is dominated by both under those two metrics.
lessons.lab: Construct a Pareto comparison of at least three architecture configurations. Pass: objectives and assumptions are explicit, dominated designs are identified correctly and a recommendation changes appropriately when a hard constraint changes.
lessons.reading: R48: memory and quantitative design; R49: packaging and system tradeoffs; R38: architecture alternatives.

quiz.question: Does A dominate B in the example?
quiz.answer: No. A uses less energy but B has lower latency.

quiz.question: Why is the 12 ms, 60 J design dominated?
quiz.answer: Another design is no worse on either metric and strictly better on at least one; here both A and B improve both metrics.

quiz.question: Why not present an educational chip-cost model as a quote?
quiz.answer: Its manufacturing, yield, packaging and commercial assumptions are not verified production terms.

modules.title: VLSI, timing and physical implementation
modules.prerequisites: Modules 31-34, 40 and 46. Use educational libraries and licensed or open tools only.
modules.project: Carry a verified small RTL block through an educational synthesis and physical-design flow. Report constraints, timing, area and power-estimation assumptions. The result is a learning artifact, not fabrication-ready commercial signoff.

lessons.title: CMOS logic, transistor sizing and delay models
lessons.outcome: Connect gate-level choices to electrical load and timing.
lessons.teach:
CMOS gates charge and discharge capacitances through transistor networks. Propagation delay depends on drive strength, load, input transition, topology and process/voltage/temperature conditions. Increasing device size can reduce effective resistance while increasing input capacitance and area, moving cost to the previous stage.
Logical-effort-style models separate gate topology, electrical effort and parasitic delay to reason about sizing and staging. These are approximations, not substitutes for characterized library timing. Series transistor stacks and fanout affect delay differently. Dynamic switching, leakage and short-circuit effects contribute to power. Study an inverter chain and a small logic path before optimizing a large synthesized block.
lessons.example: In the simplified normalized model d=g*h+p, a stage with g=1, h=4 and p=1 has delay 5 units. Those normalized units require a technology-dependent scale before becoming nanoseconds.
lessons.lab: Analyze and simulate an inverter chain or compare library-cell drive strengths under several loads. Pass: assumptions are stated, input loading is included and model predictions are compared with available characterized or simulated results.
lessons.reading: R49: CMOS devices, combinational circuits and delay; R30: MOS circuit foundations.

quiz.question: What is d for g=1, h=4, p=1?
quiz.answer: 5 normalized delay units.

quiz.question: Why can enlarging one gate slow an earlier stage?
quiz.answer: The enlarged gate presents greater input capacitance to its driver.

quiz.question: Can normalized logical-effort delay be reported directly as nanoseconds?
quiz.answer: No. It needs a justified technology-dependent scale or characterized timing model.

lessons.title: Static timing analysis, clocks and timing exceptions
lessons.outcome: Check every required path under the correct timing contract.
lessons.teach:
Static timing analysis evaluates path delays without enumerating every input waveform. Setup checks constrain maximum data arrival before capture; hold checks constrain minimum delay around the capture edge. Clock-to-output, combinational delay, setup/hold requirements, skew and uncertainty all participate. Different corners can dominate different checks.
Clocks, generated clocks, input/output delays and exceptions define what the tool analyzes. An unconstrained path is not a fast path; it may be an unexamined path. False-path and multicycle exceptions must follow real functional guarantees, not serve as a way to hide violations. Review exception reachability and clock-domain boundaries. Functional correctness and timing correctness require separate evidence.
lessons.example: With zero skew and uncertainty, tCQ_max=0.10 ns, logic_max=0.50 ns and setup=0.05 ns require T>=0.65 ns. Real signoff adds the relevant clock, interconnect and corner details.
lessons.lab: Constrain a small sequential block and inspect worst setup and hold paths. Pass: no unexplained unconstrained endpoints, every exception is justified and a deliberately tightened clock produces an understood violation.
lessons.reading: R39: timing analysis and flow constraints; R49: sequential timing and clocking.

quiz.question: What minimum simplified period follows from the example?
quiz.answer: 0.65 ns before omitted effects and margins.

quiz.question: Does marking a path false make a real timing problem disappear physically?
quiz.answer: No. It only removes that path from analysis and is valid only when the functional contract justifies it.

quiz.question: Why examine both maximum and minimum delays?
quiz.answer: Setup and hold impose different requirements and can fail at different corners or paths.

lessons.title: Synthesis, placement, clock trees, routing and physical checks
lessons.outcome: Understand how a logical netlist becomes a physical layout.
lessons.teach:
The implementation flow maps logic, places cells, constructs clock distribution and routes interconnect under design constraints. Placement changes wire length and congestion; routing adds parasitic resistance and capacitance that affect timing and power. Clock-tree design must distribute a usable clock while controlling skew and other requirements.
Physical checks include geometry rules and connectivity consistency between layout and the intended circuit. Passing one tool stage does not establish all manufacturing, electrical or reliability requirements. Educational process kits and libraries have specific scope and licensing. Preserve exact versions and distinguish pre-route estimates from extracted post-route results. A failed route or timing closure attempt is useful evidence about congestion or unrealistic constraints.
lessons.example: A netlist can meet an idealized pre-route timing estimate and fail after long interconnect is included. The logical cell count alone does not reveal that physical bottleneck.
lessons.lab: Run a small block through an educational OpenROAD-compatible flow or inspect a provided open example. Pass: capture stage reports, identify a routing/timing change and state which physical checks were and were not performed.
lessons.reading: R39: flow stages, placement, clock tree and routing; R49: physical-design methodology and EDA.

quiz.question: Why can timing worsen after routing?
quiz.answer: Actual interconnect parasitics and placement/routing choices add delays not captured by simpler estimates.

quiz.question: Does synthesis success prove a manufacturable layout exists?
quiz.answer: No. Physical implementation and many additional checks remain.

quiz.question: Why preserve process-kit and library versions?
quiz.answer: They define rules and models that materially affect implementation and reported results.

lessons.title: Power, area, process corners and design-space closure
lessons.outcome: Report PPA with enough assumptions to make comparison meaningful.
lessons.teach:
Power-performance-area evaluation depends on workload activity, clocking, voltage, cell library and physical implementation. A common simplified dynamic-power model is P=alpha*C*V^2*f, where alpha represents switching activity under a stated convention. Leakage and other contributions are additional. A power estimate without activity assumptions can be badly misleading.
Process, voltage and temperature corners model variation but do not cover every reliability or manufacturing issue. Compare designs under consistent constraints and report whether timing actually closes. Clock gating and operand isolation can reduce unnecessary switching but require functional and timing verification. An educational area reduction is meaningful only alongside performance, power and correctness effects. Keep fabrication and production signoff outside the claim.
lessons.example: Under the simplified dynamic model with unchanged alpha, C and f, reducing voltage to 0.9 of its original value scales dynamic power to 0.9^2=0.81. In practice the achievable frequency and margins may also change.
lessons.lab: Compare two verified RTL implementations using identical flow assumptions. Pass: report area, worst timing and activity-based power estimates where supported, with uncertainty and no unsupported commercial-silicon claim.
lessons.reading: R49: power, timing and implementation tradeoffs; R39: reports and analysis; R30: energy and electrical models.

quiz.question: What dynamic-power factor follows from 0.9x voltage under fixed other factors?
quiz.answer: 0.81, or a 19% reduction in the simplified dynamic component.

quiz.question: Why is an activity assumption necessary for power estimation?
quiz.answer: Switching frequency of nodes strongly affects dynamic power.

quiz.question: Why can lower voltage invalidate a timing target?
quiz.answer: Transistor behavior and circuit delay change, so the original frequency may no longer meet margins.

modules.title: Verification, reliability and hardware trust boundaries
modules.project: Create a verification dossier for the hardware capstone: requirements-to-tests traceability, assertions, coverage, clock/reset review, fault injection and a clearly bounded assurance claim.

lessons.title: Formal properties, abstraction and assume-guarantee reasoning
lessons.outcome: Prove useful properties without hiding failures in assumptions.
lessons.teach:
Formal verification reasons about a mathematical model and properties under assumptions. Decompose a large system into contracts: a block assumes valid inputs and guarantees specified outputs or progress. The system review must show that connected blocks actually satisfy each other's assumptions. Circular or inconsistent contracts can make local proofs meaningless.
Bounded model checking, induction and equivalence checking answer different questions. A timeout is not a proof or a counterexample. Vacuity checks and cover properties help reveal environments that never exercise the intended behavior. Abstraction can make proof tractable but must conservatively preserve the property of interest. Track proof scripts, tool versions and unresolved properties as part of the artifact.
lessons.example: An arbiter property stating that every request is eventually granted becomes vacuous if the environment assumes requests are always zero. A cover goal requiring contention exposes that missing behavior.
lessons.lab: Prove a queue, arbiter or transaction property and inject a violation. Pass: assumptions are reviewed independently, contention is covered and bounded, proven, failed and unknown results are reported separately.
lessons.reading: R50: safety, liveness, induction, cover and assumptions; R49: verification methodology.

quiz.question: Is a solver timeout evidence that the property is true?
quiz.answer: No. It is an unresolved result under that run and resource limit.

quiz.question: Why can the no-request assumption make an arbiter proof vacuous?
quiz.answer: The required service behavior is never exercised.

quiz.question: What must assume-guarantee integration establish?
quiz.answer: Each block's environment, including other blocks, actually satisfies its assumptions without circular or inconsistent reasoning.

lessons.title: Clock/reset crossings and asynchronous FIFO verification
lessons.outcome: Check digital protocol correctness while acknowledging analog risk.
lessons.teach:
Clock-domain crossings require both a sound transfer protocol and an appropriate physical synchronizer implementation. Asynchronous FIFOs often use local binary pointers with Gray-coded values transferred between domains, because adjacent Gray values change one bit. Correct full/empty detection, pointer widths, reset behavior and synchronization delay still need verification.
Gray coding is not a substitute for routing/skew constraints or correct sampling assumptions. Multi-bit coherence and pulse capture need distinct reasoning. Reset deassertion must be coordinated with each domain's requirements, and resetting one side of a live link needs a recovery policy. Digital formal analysis proves the modeled protocol; analog metastability probability needs device and timing information beyond that model.
lessons.example: A one-bit source pulse can occur entirely between two destination clock edges and be missed. A level handshake or suitable event-transfer scheme is needed when every event must be observed.
lessons.lab: Model an asynchronous FIFO or event handshake with independent clocks and reset sequences. Pass: no loss/duplication under the stated protocol, full/empty behavior is checked and physical synchronizer assumptions are listed separately.
lessons.reading: R50: multiclock modeling and verification; R49: sequential circuits and synchronization; revisit Module 32 timing boundaries.

quiz.question: Why is Gray code useful for pointer transfer?
quiz.answer: Adjacent values change one bit, reducing ambiguity from simultaneous multi-bit transitions under the intended crossing design.

quiz.question: Can an unsynchronized one-cycle pulse be missed by another domain?
quiz.answer: Yes, especially when it occurs between destination sampling edges.

quiz.question: Does a digital FIFO proof quantify real metastability failure rate?
quiz.answer: No. That requires physical device, timing and implementation assumptions not captured by ordinary digital logic alone.

lessons.title: Fault models, ECC, testability and recovery
lessons.outcome: Design for detectable failures rather than assuming perfect hardware.
lessons.teach:
A fault model specifies the failures considered, such as stuck-at logic, transient bit flips or communication corruption. Detection and correction capability depend on the code or mechanism and the fault pattern. Parity detects an odd number of flipped bits but does not locate and correct an arbitrary single error by itself. Error-correcting codes add structured redundancy with explicit guarantees.
Design-for-test techniques improve controllability and observability of internal state, with area, timing and security implications. Built-in self-test and scan are not interchangeable with complete functional verification. A detected error needs policy: retry, isolate, reset, degrade or fail safely. Fault injection tests the policy as well as detection. Report unmodeled common-mode or multi-bit failures instead of assuming independence without evidence.
lessons.example: With one parity bit over a word, a single flipped data bit changes parity and is detectable. Two flipped bits can leave parity unchanged, so the same scheme cannot guarantee detection of every double-bit error.
lessons.lab: Implement a parity and a small single-error-correcting code model, then inject faults. Pass: enumerate the supported correction/detection claims, test multi-bit counterexamples and define a recovery response.
lessons.reading: R49: testing, DFT and reliability context; R51: error detection/correction reporting concepts; R06: coding and combinatorial reasoning extension.

quiz.question: Can simple parity detect every two-bit error?
quiz.answer: No. Two flips can preserve parity.

quiz.question: Why specify a fault model before claiming reliability?
quiz.answer: The guarantee applies only to the modeled failure types and assumptions.

quiz.question: What is missing when a system detects an error but has no recovery policy?
quiz.answer: It lacks a defined safe response, so detection alone may not preserve useful or correct operation.

lessons.title: Hardware security, thermal limits and assurance review
lessons.outcome: Include isolation and failure containment in the design contract.
lessons.teach:
Hardware interfaces control powerful resources: memory access, privilege, interrupts and firmware execution. Validate descriptors, restrict DMA and separate trusted control from untrusted data. Boot authenticity, update integrity and rollback policy require established cryptographic mechanisms and careful key handling, not a homemade cipher. Debug interfaces need a lifecycle access policy.
Shared caches, timing and power behavior can expose information even when architectural results are isolated. Study threat models and defensive mitigations without attacking systems outside an authorized lab. Thermal and electrical protections remain active during experiments. An assurance review connects threats and hazards to requirements, mechanisms, tests and residual risks. Passing a educational checklist is not security certification.
lessons.example: A device accepting an unchecked memory address in a work descriptor can cross the intended buffer boundary. A protected mapping and validated length constrain that authority even when the computation itself is correct.
lessons.lab: Write a threat-and-failure review for the accelerator and test malformed descriptors, denied access and reset under load in simulation. Pass: isolation limits, protection assumptions and unresolved risks are explicit; no unauthorized target testing occurs.
lessons.reading: R51: device access, DMA and isolation; R49: implementation and verification; R50: enforceable protocol properties.

quiz.question: Why validate both address and length in a work descriptor?
quiz.answer: Their combination determines the memory range the device may access and can overflow or exceed authorized bounds.

quiz.question: Can correct architectural output coexist with a side-channel risk?
quiz.answer: Yes. Timing, shared resources or other observable behavior may reveal information.

quiz.question: Does this review constitute a security certification?
quiz.answer: No. It is bounded educational evidence with stated assumptions and residual risks.

modules.title: Master's thesis: proposal, implementation and evaluation
modules.prerequisites: Gate I and relevant advanced-track modules; independent technical mentorship strongly recommended.
modules.project: Prepare and execute a thesis-scale project in one primary specialization. Budget 400-800 focused hours as a planning range, with scope adjusted through review. The deliverable is a defensible contribution and reproducible artifact, not a promise of publication.

lessons.title: Question selection, literature map and thesis scope
lessons.outcome: Turn a broad interest into a falsifiable, feasible research question.
lessons.teach:
A thesis question identifies a problem, intervention or method, evaluation setting and meaningful outcome. Narrowness improves rigor: one well-tested engine subsystem or hardware tradeoff is preferable to a promise to build an entire commercial console. Distinguish an engineering integration contribution, a new method, a replication study and a negative result.
Build a literature map with seminal work, strong baselines and relevant newer work reviewed when the thesis begins. The dated anchor papers in this curriculum are not a complete current literature review. Identify the gap and explain why it matters. Check data, hardware, tool access, licenses and mentorship before committing. Write explicit exclusions so the project remains feasible.
lessons.example: Instead of "make a faster engine," ask whether a bounded task-scheduling policy reduces p99 frame time under specified streaming bursts without exceeding a declared memory budget, compared with two competent baselines.
lessons.lab: Write a 3-5 page proposal with a research question, 8-15 relevant sources, baseline plan, constraints and exclusions. Pass: a reviewer can explain what observation would weaken or refute the main hypothesis.
lessons.reading: Use Module 41's paper method and the chosen track's original papers; R44, R48, R49 or R55 are starting anchors, not a substitute for the literature search.

quiz.question: What makes a research question falsifiable?
quiz.answer: It specifies an observation or result that could count against the proposed claim.

quiz.question: Why state explicit exclusions?
quiz.answer: They prevent uncontrolled scope growth and make the intended contribution assessable.

quiz.question: Are the curriculum's historical anchor papers a complete current literature review?
quiz.answer: No. Relevant newer and competing work must be reviewed when the project begins.

lessons.title: Proposal review, baselines and risk-reduction milestones
lessons.outcome: Make failure cheap before the expensive implementation phase.
lessons.teach:
A credible proposal includes a baseline that already runs, an evaluation protocol and a risk register. Technical risks include insufficient performance, unavailable data, unsupported tool features and an inability to measure the claimed effect. Resolve the highest-impact uncertainties with small prototypes before building a large framework.
Milestones should produce evidence: a reference result, a validated instrument, a working minimal method, an ablation and a reproducible final comparison. A calendar date alone is not a technical milestone. Define stop or pivot criteria in advance. Independent review can reveal an unfair baseline or an untestable objective. Keep project decisions in a versioned log so later changes are transparent.
lessons.example: Before implementing a new GPU scheduler, confirm that the target platform exposes enough timing information to distinguish scheduling delay from execution time. Otherwise the proposed mechanism may be impossible to evaluate directly.
lessons.lab: Deliver a running baseline, risk register and milestone plan. Pass: the primary metric can be measured, a small feasibility experiment exists and each major risk has a mitigation or explicit acceptance decision.
lessons.reading: R49: project milestone and reporting structure; Module 41: experimental design; chosen method's primary documentation.

quiz.question: Why require a running baseline early?
quiz.answer: It establishes feasibility, comparison quality and the measurement path before major new implementation.

quiz.question: What makes a milestone evidence-based?
quiz.answer: It produces a reviewable artifact or result rather than only consuming time.

quiz.question: Why define pivot criteria before final results?
quiz.answer: It reduces ad hoc decisions that hide failure or endlessly expand the project.

lessons.title: Implementation, ablations and controlled evaluation
lessons.outcome: Execute the study without changing the question to fit a favorable result.
lessons.teach:
Implement the smallest method that tests the research question. Keep a correct reference path and add tests before optimizing. Separate development experiments from final evaluation, and record changes to the protocol with reasons. A method that fails on some supported inputs must report those failures rather than silently removing the cases.
Ablations test the contribution of individual components. Sensitivity sweeps examine parameter dependence; held-out workloads examine generalization. Statistical analysis should match the trial structure and metric. Preserve raw data, seeds, binaries or build manifests and analysis scripts. When results are negative, investigate correctness, measurement and assumptions, then report the supported conclusion. Honest negative evidence can be a substantial contribution.
lessons.example: If a new allocator reduces average time but worsens p99 frame time beyond the stated requirement, the original latency hypothesis is not supported even though one secondary number improved.
lessons.lab: Run the approved evaluation with baselines, at least one ablation and one sensitivity study. Pass: scripts regenerate results, failed cases remain visible and claims use the preregistered primary metric or clearly disclose deviations.
lessons.reading: R09 and Module 41: uncertainty; chosen track's original methods and implementation references; handbook experiment manifest.

quiz.question: Does improving a secondary metric prove the primary hypothesis?
quiz.answer: No. The original target must be evaluated on its own terms.

quiz.question: Why retain failed supported cases?
quiz.answer: They define the method's actual reliability and prevent selective reporting.

quiz.question: What should happen after a negative result?
quiz.answer: Check implementation and measurement, examine assumptions, and report the conclusion supported by the evidence rather than manufacturing a success story.

lessons.title: Thesis writing, reproducibility and contribution boundaries
lessons.outcome: Write a technical argument another engineer can audit.
lessons.teach:
A thesis report connects motivation, prior work, method, implementation, experiments, results and limitations. Each major claim should point to a derivation, test, table or figure. Separate observations from interpretations and specify uncertainty. Explain enough detail for a competent reader to reconstruct the central method without depending on undocumented conversations.
Include an artifact guide with environment, commands, expected outputs and resource needs. Record third-party code, assets, datasets and AI assistance with their relevant licenses and provenance. Do not include confidential material without authorization. The contribution statement should identify what is new, what is reproduced and what remains unverified. A polished document cannot compensate for missing experiments or an irreproducible implementation.
lessons.example: A report saying "the method is 30% faster" should specify the baseline, workload, metric, aggregation, hardware, quality constraint and uncertainty. Otherwise the number lacks an interpretable claim boundary.
lessons.lab: Produce a thesis-style report, typically 30-60 pages plus appendices as a planning guide, and a complete artifact package. Pass: a reviewer traces five major claims to evidence and reproduces the central table or experiment.
lessons.reading: R49: final project reports; chosen original papers for reporting comparisons; handbook thesis outline and evidence checklist.

quiz.question: What must accompany a speedup claim?
quiz.answer: A defined baseline, workload, metric, environment, comparison quality and uncertainty or measurement context.

quiz.question: Why distinguish observation from interpretation?
quiz.answer: The data may support several explanations, and an inferred cause needs its own evidence.

quiz.question: What belongs in the contribution statement?
quiz.answer: The exact new work, reproduced components, scope and remaining unverified claims.

modules.title: Thesis defense, professional practice and continued development
modules.prerequisites: Module 49 and all prerequisites for the selected specialization.
modules.project: Gate J: defend the thesis, pass an independent artifact reproduction, complete a maintainable handoff and publish an honest portfolio where rights permit. This completes the self-study program, not an accredited degree.

lessons.title: Oral defense and independent artifact reproduction
lessons.outcome: Show that the learner owns the reasoning and implementation.
lessons.teach:
An oral defense tests the relationship between the research question, assumptions, implementation and conclusions. Begin with the central claim and evidence, then invite scrutiny of the weakest assumptions. Be prepared to derive a key equation, explain a failed experiment and modify a small part of the implementation live. Saying that a tool generated the code is not an explanation of its correctness.
An independent reproduction uses the supplied artifact instructions without hidden files or undocumented manual repairs. Record what the reviewer could reproduce and what failed. A defense can pass with limitations when the claims are narrowed honestly; it should not pass on presentation alone while the central evidence remains unavailable. Revisions should respond directly to review findings.
lessons.example: A reviewer changes a supported workload parameter. The learner should predict which resource or error term may change, run the test and explain agreement or disagreement with that prediction.
lessons.lab: Hold a 30-45 minute technical defense with a qualified reviewer or peer panel and a separate artifact run. Pass: the central result is reproduced, major questions receive evidence-based answers and required revisions are completed.
lessons.reading: R49: design-project evaluation as a reference; handbook defense questions and rubric.

quiz.question: What does a live modification test beyond a prepared presentation?
quiz.answer: Whether the learner can reason about, predict and change the actual system.

quiz.question: Must every thesis result be positive to pass?
quiz.answer: No. A rigorous negative or limited result can pass when the claim and evidence are sound.

quiz.question: Why separate independent reproduction from the author's demo?
quiz.answer: The author's environment may contain undeclared dependencies or manual steps absent from the artifact.

lessons.title: Mature-codebase integration, review and maintainable contributions
lessons.outcome: Transfer a prototype into an engineering environment with other owners.
lessons.teach:
A research prototype and a maintained engine component face different requirements. Integration needs style consistency, tests, platform support, migration behavior, documentation and ownership. Study an existing codebase through a narrow feature path: entry point, data flow, invariants, tests and build configuration. Avoid rewriting a subsystem before understanding why it exists.
A good contribution starts with a focused issue and a reproducible case. Discuss design where project norms require it, make a small patch and respond constructively to review. Open-source maintainers are not obligated to accept educational work. A local integration exercise can satisfy this lesson when no appropriate public contribution is available. Respect licenses and never upload employer or proprietary SDK code without authorization.
lessons.example: A faster container may break serialization ordering or iterator expectations elsewhere in the engine. Integration review must examine those contracts before accepting the local benchmark improvement.
lessons.lab: Integrate one tested improvement into a mature open codebase or a maintained local fork. Pass: a focused patch, regression test, design rationale and reviewer response are included, whether or not an upstream project accepts it.
lessons.reading: R05: distributed workflows and contributing; R11: interfaces and maintenance; R26: mature-engine comparison where authorized.

quiz.question: Why can a locally faster component be an integration regression?
quiz.answer: It may violate ordering, lifetime, serialization or platform contracts outside the benchmark.

quiz.question: Is upstream acceptance required to prove learning?
quiz.answer: No. A reviewed local contribution with evidence can satisfy the educational objective.

quiz.question: Why avoid a large rewrite as the first contribution?
quiz.answer: It increases risk before the learner understands the codebase's hidden constraints and maintenance needs.

lessons.title: Portfolio, technical interviews and role-specific evidence
lessons.outcome: Present concrete engineering competence without inflated claims.
lessons.teach:
A portfolio should show a small number of complete artifacts with clear ownership, build instructions, tests, measured results and limitations. Tailor emphasis: engine roles need runtime architecture and debugging; rendering roles need graphics mathematics and GPU evidence; platform roles need systems and latency; hardware roles need RTL, verification and timing or board evidence.
Technical interviews often probe fundamentals through unfamiliar problems, so practice explanation, assumptions, edge cases and tests rather than memorizing only known answers. Revisit algorithms, memory, concurrency and mathematics using transfer tasks. Do not label this self-study program an accredited degree or imply professional chip signoff from educational tools. Honest scope and a reproducible artifact are stronger than a list of fashionable technologies.
lessons.example: A portfolio entry can state: "Implemented a verified FIFO and compared two storage mappings under one pinned synthesis flow; physical silicon and production signoff were not performed." That is precise and defensible.
lessons.lab: Prepare three portfolio case studies and complete one systems, one algorithm and one specialization mock interview. Pass: every claimed result is supported by an artifact and assistance or third-party contributions are clearly attributed.
lessons.reading: R01-R02: breadth review; R11: engineering explanation and contracts; handbook role map and portfolio template.

quiz.question: What makes a portfolio claim defensible?
quiz.answer: Clear scope, ownership, reproducible evidence and stated limitations.

quiz.question: Should completing this program be described as earning an accredited master's degree?
quiz.answer: No. It is a self-study curriculum unless separately assessed and credited by an accredited institution.

quiz.question: Why practice unfamiliar transfer tasks?
quiz.answer: They test whether concepts generalize beyond memorized exercises or copied implementations.

lessons.title: Long-term learning, maintenance and final handoff
lessons.outcome: Keep the knowledge and artifacts useful after the course ends.
lessons.teach:
Engineering knowledge includes durable concepts and changing interfaces. Preserve principles such as invariants, measurement and ownership while periodically checking toolchains, specifications and platform documentation. A dependency update should run tests and benchmarks rather than assume compatibility from a version number. Maintain an evidence log of what was actually revalidated.
Create a handoff document describing architecture, build, tests, known risks and next decisions. Archive raw research data and source in accessible formats with appropriate backups. Choose a next specialization from demonstrated interest and gaps, not pressure to master every field simultaneously. The final review should identify strengths and unresolved areas honestly. Continuing with mentorship, collaboration and real projects is part of professional development, not a failure of the curriculum.
lessons.example: Updating a graphics SDK can change tutorial requirements or validation behavior. A pinned working environment preserves reproducibility while a separate upgrade branch tests the new toolchain.
lessons.lab: Complete Gate J: archive the thesis artifact, produce a maintainer handoff and write a 90-day learning plan with one primary gap and one real contribution goal. Pass: another person can locate, build and understand the project without the author's machine.
lessons.reading: R05: maintenance workflows; R01-R02: periodic breadth review; current official documentation for the selected tools when an update is undertaken.

quiz.question: Why keep a pinned environment while testing an upgrade separately?
quiz.answer: It preserves the known reproducible baseline while evaluating compatibility and regressions.

quiz.question: What belongs in a maintainer handoff?
quiz.answer: Architecture, build/test commands, ownership, known risks, data locations and the next decisions.

quiz.question: Why choose one primary next specialization?
quiz.answer: Depth and sustained evidence usually benefit from focused work rather than simultaneous shallow pursuit of every advanced topic.
